title: AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be
description:
Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis.

Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board said it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has announced additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns.

Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him.

Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN.

The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses.

Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait?

Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it.

“AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.”

AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology.

THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM

Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker.

Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise?

Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players.

“Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub says. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.”

Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products.

“The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.”

That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on.

In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve users as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices.

Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing.

“The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says.

She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning.

“I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says.

For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations.

Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance.

THE BILL IS COMING DUE

Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology.

Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save.

“The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.”

Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive.

Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost.

Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified.

The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive.

Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with.

“Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company.

This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models?

Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow.

“I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.”

WHO GETS THE VALUE?

Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software.

Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods.

“There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.”

His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient.

“Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?”

Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work.

“These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says.

Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify.

For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most important operations.

“The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary.

A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running.

And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want.

During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.”

He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them.

WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE

A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money.

O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models.

“For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.”

But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves.

Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies.

Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward.

AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

title: Bambu Lab P3C is here: Tool changer, now standard
description:
Surely, they could have made many other decisions to reduce the price, but delivering it with 2 nozzles, would not really make it competitive to the U1 or any other tool changer.

And the P3C is an answer to the U1.

It swaps tools (and therefore materials) in less than 4 seconds, but people complain about the initial loading time of the filament. It is still a hobby machine.

When you know on forehand that you constantly need to load different materials, you can always go for the U1 or another machine from the competition if you think it better. Don’t underestimate all the other hassle that comes with those machines.

It’s an entry tool changer machine with a competitive price.

And it’s pretty hard to build a one-size-fits-all solution in 3D Printing. I bet the engineers and marketers will have had many discussions over this topic for sure.

And maybe in the near future, an Automatic loading AMS will be released.

title: Loud Clattering/Clicking,
description:
Hello,

This is the response from Bambu Lab Support.

Dear Customer,

Thank you for your reply.

We’ve reviewed your video, and there’s nothing obviously abnormal during the manual movement. The sound isn’t coming from the idler pulley.

The sound you hear while printing is most likely caused by the toolhead starting and stopping quickly over short distances, which produces a mechanical sound as the motion absorbs the impact. This is normal and won’t affect the printer’s performance.

Because the H3C prints with higher speed and acceleration than our other models, this sound tends to be more noticeable on the H3C.

If the sound bothers you and you’d like to reduce it, there are two things you can try: 1. Turn on Silent Mode. You can switch it on directly in “Settings” on the printer’s screen, and it can effectively reduce operating noise. 2. Adjust the slicer settings. In your slicer (such as Bambu Studio), lower the maximum acceleration a little, then re-slice and print again. This can also noticeably reduce the sound.

If you still have any issues after making these adjustments, please don’t hesitate to contact us.

Best regards,
Bambu Lab Customer Support

The support team’s response isn’t entirely satisfactory, but it makes sense. The print quality is good. The only real downside: Compared to the H2C, it’s significantly louder.

excerpt: Doerkson orders SOGI materials out of B.C. schools | Williams Lake Tribune As one of his first orders of business, Premier Lorne Doerkson ordered materials and resources created through the Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123 schools initiative to be removed from government websites as he tries to wipe out a program he calls a “lightning rod for division.” “A lot of parents feel as though they haven’t had enough say in what their kids are being taught,” he said. “And I think that they have a point.” SOGI 123 is a set of resources introduced in B.C. schools starting in 2016 to prevent bullying. An organization called the ARC Foundation created and administered the resources but lost its contract with the government last summer, effectively ending SOGI as an active program. It is now up to individual school districts whether to continue using SOGI resources. Doerkson says the education minister will work with districts to remove the materials from individual classrooms. “We’ve asked for it to be removed from the room, so if it’s not, they’re not just going to get pushback from the parents; they’re going to get pushback from me as well,” he said. B.C. Teachers’ Federation President Carole Gordon said this decision is “rooted in misinformation,” questioning what this will mean in practice and what specific resources will be removed. title: Are AI companies ‘glosslighting’ you with misleading jargon? This report says yes
description:
Ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “co-pilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry.

“Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the AI industry is doing in spades.

Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice around the industry takes on extra weight.

What is glosslighting?

For the study, researchers analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion.

The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. 

“Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,'” the authors write.

How AI jargon causes harm

The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following:

  • “Hallucination,” “co-pilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them
  • “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development
  • “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns
  • “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy
  • “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laymen to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin

The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that either simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go more in-depth to provide greater accuracy to AI’s impact.

One author, assistant professor of computing science Nicholas Vincent, told Tech Xplore that “issues where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.”

“Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent said. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”

title: 1Password Security Breach: What Was Accessed and What Wasn't
description:
Popular password management app 1Password today said it experienced a security breach earlier this month. 1Password says some customer names and email addresses were accessed, but no customer vault contents were compromised.


On November 19, 1Password saw indications that an employee's GitHub account had been breached and began investigating. The company says the breached GitHub account was used to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, with the code downloading some customer data. Here's a list of what the hacker was able to get:

  • Names and email addresses customers use to sign into 1Password

  • Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

  • Public keys

  • Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (1Password says this can't be used for account access)

  • Tokens in emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

  • Other non-secret account data related to 1Password's internal architecture, like version numeric identifiers and file numeric identifiers

  • 1Password source code, which 1Password says does not include customer data or user secrets

  • Access to 1Password's CI/CD system, which it says has infrastructure-related secrets for the service to work


According to 1Password, there is no impact to its services, availability, or product security. Customer vaults and the items in them were not accessed, nor were the keys that protect vaults. The hacker did not have access to account recovery keys or 1Password apps and browser extensions. 1Password vaults are encrypted and protected by keys on the user end, so content is not accessible to 1Password or anyone who hacks the 1Password servers.

The biggest risk comes from the token breach. Tokens can be used for account recovery, but they only work when paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to a user's email address. Codes have now been changed from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them more difficult to brute force.

The affected GitHub account has been disabled, and the attacker's token was revoked. Internal credentials that may have been exposed have been revoked. Internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls have been "tightened," with new detection methods for similar attacks. The company found no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using the exposed account provisioning tokens, and it has hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its response.

1Password users who had a token accessed were notified, but it is unclear if 1Password has sent notices about the breach to all users. While the blog post is titled as "update on" a security incident, it does not seem that the breach was disclosed when 1Password first learned of it six days ago.

1Password will not contact users to ask for an account password or Secret Key, and the information should be entered only in the official 1Password app or official website. It recommends all users be cautious about phishing attempts like emails, texts, and calls that mention 1Password or account recovery.

Users do not need to update or change anything in their 1Password accounts.

title: Inverting process dynamics in knowledge production
description:
Boozhoo News River Readers,

Today’s edition of the news features an article about lived experience, relationality and community in the process of knowledge generation. It reminds me of one of our most popular stories our readers clicked from last month on indigenous jurisprudence. Together they might make a great pair to contemplate  with a warm cup of tea.  

Here’s the rest of this weeks news…

In the age of AI, Indigenous ways of knowing remind us why lived experience matters

The Big Picture: Universities, long entrusted with teaching, research and knowledge production, are confronting one of their most significant challenges: The rising use of artificial intelligence. As UNESCO has acknowledged, generative AI raises questions about the importance of human participation in knowledge production. For universities, these developments invite an uncomfortable question: If AI can produce knowledge more efficiently, what makes human contributions to knowledge production valuable?

Why lived experience matters: Knowledge is not necessarily confined to information that can be collected, analyzed and reproduced. It can also emerge from the meanings people develop through participation in the world. This distinction is especially important when considering Onkwehón:we (Indigenous) understandings of knowledge.

Indigenous ways of knowing: Although Onkwehón:we knowledge traditions are diverse, many emphasize that knowledge emerges through relationships among people, communities and the natural world. Onkwehón:we scholarship on relationality demonstrates how knowledge and relationships are inseparable from the people and communities in which they are developed.

Read the full article here. 

More curated reads

Utah Has a New Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives Database

A Native-led organization in Utah has unveiled a new database dedicated to Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives (MMIR). The database, dubbed Traces, was launched Monday by MMIR Utah, a nonprofit that advocates for MMIR victims and families. The group’s co-founder and executive director, Tammy Dee Platero (Diné), said Traces aims to be a balm against the lack of media attention Native victims receive, compared to non-Native victims. Platero, who co-founded MMIR Utah after the MMIR Task Force was disbanded in 2024, said the database was inspired by the movement for Indigenous data sovereignty and the OCAP framework — ownership, control, access and possession — created by the First Nations Governance Center to determine how data about Native people is collected and used. It’s by this model that the database allows families to submit information at their discretion, whether it be a full case entry or simply a photo of a loved one. And it remains private, accessible only to MMIR Utah staff, and information is shared with law enforcement only at a family’s request.

To do better research with Indigenous communities, share the driver’s seat

The partnership model IIF developed was a deliberate departure from how academic research typically works. Often, universities set the questions, communities provide access or data and outcomes circulate within institutions the communities rarely encounter. IIF inverted this. Community members developed their own future imaginaries, with IIF providing support and encouragement, and research questions were developed in response. That inversion took shape through four interconnected pillars: workshops that built technical capacity; residencies supporting artists’ deep engagement with the technology, along with commissions to help populate the future with Indigenous images; symposia and lecture series that circulated these methods more widely; and preservation of digital media artworks for future generations. 

UNBC researchers secure $800K to study potential impacts of proposed NeToo Hydropower Project

An extensive research project out of the University of Northern British Columbia (UNBC) has secured funding for its fourth phase of research involving the Nechako River Basin, this time to examine the potential impacts of the proposed NeToo Hydropower Project at the site of the existing Kenney Dam. “The overarching goal of the research is to collect baseline data and information on the Nechako Canyon for integrative responses to climate, water and community connections in the Nechako Watershed,” Martins said. “Water stewardship is strongest when it reflects local knowledge, priorities and lived experience,” said Garcia-Becerra. According to UNBC, partners include the Lheidli T’enneh First Nation, Nulki-Tachick Lakes Stewardship Society, Yinka Dene (Nechako First Nations), Nechako Environment and Water Stewardship Society and Nechako Watershed Roundtable. The project also includes other UNBC researchers, researchers from the University of British Columbia and BC Hydro.

Camosun opens applications for tuition-free Indigenous technology program

A tuition-free, 12-week program at Camosun College is giving Indigenous learners an opportunity to explore careers in technology and engineering, with no previous experience required. The province-funded Indigenous Peoples in Technology Pathways (InTech) program begins its next cohort on Jan. 11, 2027, at the college’s Interurban Campus. It is open to Indigenous Canadian citizens and permanent residents, with no age restrictions or academic prerequisites. “Indigenous learners bring knowledge, experiences, and perspectives that our technology industries need,” said Olga Gould, Camosun’s program co-ordinator for Technology Pathways.

Community collaboration preserves Indigenous history online

For more than a decade, Rudy De La Cruz Jr., director of the Texas Heritage Project (THP), an initiative of American Indians in Texas at the Spanish Colonial Missions (AIT-SCM), has worked to preserve the histories of Indigenous families in South Texas and connect students with that history beyond the classroom. De La Cruz has built a collection of more than 30,000 digital assets, including family photographs, genealogical records, and historical documents. Making those materials accessible to researchers, educators and the public while respecting the families who entrusted their histories to the THP presented a challenge. As the collection grew, so did the need for a digital archive. That’s when UT San Antonio Libraries’ Community Engaged Digital Scholarship Hub (CEDISH) stepped in. Through the Preserving Archives of Texas Heritage (PATH) program, launched in 2025, CEDISH provided technical expertise, student support and resources to help the THP develop a digital archive.

SFU and Tsawwassen First Nation collaborate on Indigenous-led greenhouse project

While modern greenhouse operations typically rely on private software, automated sensors, AI and predictive algorithms to maximize harvests, an emerging research partnership in Delta is taking a different approach to agricultural technology. Backed by seed funding from SFU’s Climate Innovation Amplification Grant, researchers and Tsawwassen First Nation (TFN) lead a plan to turn an existing community greenhouse into a living laboratory. The project will address four elements rarely combined in agricultural research: upholding Indigenous governance, knowledge authority and data sovereignty; developing low-carbon, climate-resilient greenhouse systems; adopting locally repairable agritech with transparent operation and safe manual fallbacks; and creating viable community operations along with training and career pathways for local youth. Crucially, the framework centres on Indigenous governance and data sovereignty. Too often, technological ventures collect operational data that remains locked behind corporate firewalls or academic databases.

title: Ozempic is changing the way Americans shop and eat, even if they’ve never taken it
description:
The new class of drugs led by Ozempic and Wegovy don’t just have transformative effects on the people who take them – they’re reshaping the lives around them too.

Patients prescribed GLP-1s are eating less and drinking less, but those behavioral shifts are trickling down to people in their life who aren’t taking the medications themselves. Nearly one in four U.S. consumers have adjusted the way that they shop, eat, and drink based on knowing other people who take GLP-1s, according to a new survey from market research firm Escalent. 

The survey homed in on a group that the market research group calls “echo consumers,” which refers to people who don’t take a GLP-1 themselves but are changing their habits based on others in their social circles who do. The survey included data from 315 U.S. and 335 U.K. respondents who haven’t taken a GLP-1 drug but know someone who does and report changes to their own behavior based on those social connections.

“Much of the attention surrounding GLP-1 medications has focused on the people taking them, and those living in their households,” Escalent Europe Managing Director Melissa Bane wrote. “… For retailers, food and beverage brands and restaurants, that’s a significant consumer group whose changing habits have gone largely unnoticed.”

Among the echo consumers, 42% reported exercising more, 36% said they consume more wellness products, and 27% are drinking less. When eating out, 49% said they are ordering less at restaurants when eating with someone taking a GLP-1, while 21% are opting for alternative activities instead of socializing while eating and drinking. Almost one in five say they have picked different gifts for GLP-1 users they’ve shopped for, and many say they are buying different food and drinks to bring along to social gatherings in light of smaller appetites and friends and family who aren’t drinking as much.

Industry-shifting numbers

While the new survey only offers a small snapshot of consumer behavior, GLP-1 medications are clearly causing some seismic cultural shifts that we’re only beginning to understand. In the U.S., a massive 11% of the population are currently prescribed GLP-1s and 15% say they have tried them for weight loss before. That huge swath of Americans is already walking, running, and cycling more, buying fewer sweet treats, spending less on groceries, and drinking less alcohol.

Habit shifts among GLP-1 users alone already represent a massive amount of change for industries to adapt to across just a few short years. Beyond those consumers, Escalent’s survey suggests that there are 1.7 times as many people shifting their behavior in light of the widespread use of weight management drugs than there are GLP-1 users. If similar numbers play out in future research, that’s an even more massive chunk of the population suddenly eating, drinking, and buying differently than they did prior to the advent of drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound.

“For Echo Consumers, a box of chocolates or a bottle of wine may no longer be the gift of choice, and social occasions could increasingly revolve around activities rather than going out for food and drink,” Bane said, calling the changes a “major shift” that will be even more evident during the holiday season. 

“Brands, retailers and hospitality businesses will need to find ways to adapt their offerings to reflect changing demand as these habits continue to spread through social networks.”

title: Why isn’t AI changing career advice?
description:
Ask a 17-year-old where their career plan came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table. A parent, maybe an uncle. These are people who love them and want the best for them. They are also, in most cases, working from a job market map that is 20 or 30 years out of date.

The school counselor rarely enters the picture. Most U.S. school counselors spend no more than 20% of their time on career counseling while serving hundreds of students. The available capacity works out to well under an hour per student per year, even before accounting for group programming and administrative responsibilities.

Meanwhile, nearly the entire AI and jobs conversation is about what this technology will take away from young workers. That concern is fair. I’ve argued here before that AI will reduce the need for some entry-level white-collar roles, and employers need to plan for that now.

But we have become so focused on what AI will do to young workers that we have stopped asking what it can do for them. And there is an irony sitting right in front of us. One of the hardest problems in workforce development is getting accurate, real-time labor market information to the people who need it most. That happens to be the kind of problem AI is unusually good at.

THE DATA EXISTS BUT FEW CAN READ IT

Labor market data is not scarce. Governments, job boards, and industry groups publish enormous amounts of it every month. The trouble is that it is dense, scattered, and close to illegible for anyone without a statistics background. A 16-year-old is not going to read a state workforce projection. Neither is her dad.

So young people make one of the biggest decisions of their lives with the least information. We are preparing them for yesterday’s jobs while tomorrow’s technology sits on the phone in their pocket.

They know the system is failing them. In the Broken Marketplace, a Schultz Family Foundation and HarrisX survey of more than 5,700 young Americans ages 16 to 24, more than four in 10 said the education system and the employment resources available to them are broken. Seven in 10 said they learn about career pathways on social media.

We know that young people are already asking algorithms for career advice. They are just asking the wrong ones.

WHAT A GOOD AI COUNSELOR SOUNDS LIKE

At the International Youth Foundation, we’ve been testing this idea with a chatbot called Clara, a partnership we have with the Salesforce Foundation. The premise is straightforward: Take labor market data that would make most people’s eyes glaze over and turn it into a conversation.

Picture a young woman who has just finished a technical program and doesn’t know where to apply. Instead of a spreadsheet, she gets something closer to a knowledgeable friend. A chat that says, “Did you know they’re hiring electricians a few miles from you? A couple of things in your background could make you competitive. Let me ask you some questions and see whether it’s worth pursuing.”

From there, the tool can explain what training she would need, how long it takes, and whether that field is growing where she lives. That is the guidance a great counselor gives. But most students never get it. Nearly half of career and technical educators say their school’s counselors spend less time on career pathways than on college prep.

AI can close that gap at a scale no hiring plan ever could. Big data sets, updated in real time, delivered to one person at a time in plain language. That is what these models do best.

THE RISK AND FIX ARE REAL

To be clear, this is not without risk. General-purpose AI models can sound authoritative while missing the details that matter. When researchers at Renaissance Philanthropy tested leading models on thousands of real career questions from young people, most would have earned a C-minus. For a young person making a first career decision, a confident wrong answer can cost years.

That is a reason to build these tools carefully, and to build them now. If AI makes the labor market more volatile, good information becomes increasingly valuable. The work of measuring whether AI gives young people good career advice has barely started, and it deserves far more investment than it is getting.

The AI labs should be paying attention, too. Millions of young people are already typing some version of “what job should I go for?” into their products. Making sure those answers are accurate and grounded in real local demand would cost a fraction of what is being spent on the next generation of models.

AI can’t save every job. But it could help a young person find the next one. Employers, funders, and the companies building this technology spend a great deal of energy worrying about what AI will do to the next generation of workers. They should spend at least as much making sure it works for them.

Christina Sass is president and CEO of the International Youth Foundation.

title: Implementing OpenCart Browser & Server-Side Tracking with GTM, Stape & Cloudflare Workers
description:
This post is part of Web Tracking Series Earlier I shared how I implemented both browser and server side tracking on a Shopify store using GTM and direct CAPI implementation via a Custom Pixel. This time we are going to see how one can implement browser and server tracking on an OpenCart store. Read on! So, someone approached me to take care web tracking on their OpenCart store. I was like, why not! I had never worked with OpenCart before. Most of my ecommerce tracking work has been with Shopify or WooCommerce. I thought it would be an easy task: find a free plugin, install it, configure GTM, and move on. To my surprise, there are very few OpenCart extensions (the OpenCart version of plugins) for this. Secondly, pretty much everything I found was paid. The minimum was around $30, with some going close to $100. Initially, I thought of simply buying one. But there were no trial versions, and I wasn’t even sure whether they’d give me the flexibility I wanted. Then the developer in me whispered: “Hey, why don’t you make one?” Hmm… not a bad idea. Especially because I wanted control over exactly how the tracking data was generated. So I started exploring the OpenCart documentation and, with the help of docs + AI, started building my own extension. Instead of relying on DOM scraping or modifying the theme, the extension hooks into OpenCart’s built-in event architecture and generates the tracking data itself Implementation Extension Development and Browser Side Tracking We used OpenCart’s event hooks to run our custom PHP controller at key points in the storefront and checkout. For purchases, the controller pulled the order details, products, and totals from OpenCart, stored them in the session, and injected a dataLayer.push() call just before </body> on the order confirmation page. Below is the interface of the extension I made. Below is the screenshot of the fired events in the GTM interface. Meta Pixel viewer extension shows fired events And Meta’s event manager was also recording events Server side implementation via Stape and Cloudflare workers Unlike previous post in which we directly called CAPI APIs, we are going to rely on Stape. Stape is a server side tagging platform that helps us to create and manage server containers. When you signup you see an interface like below to create your first container: You select the location that is nearest to your visitors. Next, once the sGTM running you will see something like below: It will generate a tagging server URL like http://xxx.apd.stape.io/ for you that you could use for testing purpose. Next, we will be using this URL in the server container within GTM so that it can serve tags from the custom domain instead of GTM’s Now, let’s test it: Next, I am gonna Add Data Tag template by Stape in webGTM Set the server container URL and save tag: We don’t want to send hard-coded event names so we’d make it dynamic: We are gong to use the Event variable to use the info of the incoming event name. If all goes well, we’d see server GTM in action: Next, we need to configure Meta CAPI. We are going to add Facebook Conversion API template by Stape. We will be adding all required tags to interact with Meta servers. If all goes well you’d see something like: Similarly we’d be configuring other events as well. Custom domain configuration in Cloudflare We needed the tracking requests to be processed via the domain of the store itself so that the GTM Server Side configuration could have the same-origin endpoint and be able to create first-party cookies. We set up a custom tagging subdomain for our Stape-hosted server-side GTM container and configured its DNS records in Cloudflare. We also deployed a Cloudflare worker under a separate path of the OpenCart store domain which then stripped the path and forwarded the request to the Stape tagging subdomain. We made the necessary adjustments to the web GTM Data Tag and checked whether the endpoint is working correctly by sending an event through a product view page. Conclusion That’s how we set up browser and server-side tracking for the OpenCart store. I’ve kept this post focused on the implementation steps and left the code and configuration details for another time. Setting up server-side tracking for OpenCart with Stape takes some care. Once the OpenCart data layer, web GTM, and server container are wired together, you can test the full flow from the storefront to Meta Events Manager. If you run an OpenCart store and want to set up tracking or check whether your existing setup is working correctly, book a call with me. After this project, I also released a free GTM extension for OpenCart.

title: Church and Cultural Centre, Veneux-les-Sablons, France / Bertrand Taquet Architectes
description: In Veneux-les-Sablons, south-east of Paris, the church of Saint-Philippe-et-Saint-Jacques reopens ten years after the fire that partly destroyed it in 2016. Built in 1828 by subscription among the villagers, it had been enlarged in 1959 by a second nave set at right angles to the first. The fire destroyed that extension and most of the roof of the original nave. The Town of Moret-Loing-et-Orvanne decided to restore the church and rebuild its extension as a shared building: the historic nave remains a place of worship, the new extension becomes a cultural hall.

title: Borrowed References, Local Languages: Blended Styles on Latin American Façades
description: Architectural styles are often identified through a familiar set of characteristics: particular forms, materials, proportions, and decorative elements. A classical column may appear on a self-built house, a modernist ceramic composition may be reproduced across a residential façade, or a chalet may become part of a multistory commercial building. Each retains something recognizable from its precedent, although its application reflects a different set of architectural decisions.

Fukushima Daiichi’s reactor fuel melted down after the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami.

title: Israeli opposition leader Eisenkot wins first coalition pact, majority remains elusive
description:
Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief who leads the centre-right Yashar party, agreed to sign the first coalition pact since Israel’s Oct. 27 election with Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Israel Our Home party. The deal gives Eisenkot a partner but not a majority: his bloc holds 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, Israel’s parliament, while the alliance backing caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has 53. Parties representing Israel’s Arab minority hold 19 seats and could support Eisenkot, but Lieberman has opposed relying on them.

The parties remain divided over the makeup of a government. The left-wing Democrats party, led by Yair Golan, suspended talks with Yashar, citing progress in unity-government discussions between Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s Likud party and deadlock over forming a government without Netanyahu. Eisenkot could also seek support from ultra-Orthodox parties; negotiations with United Torah Judaism have focused on arrests for draft evasion and the enlistment of ultra-Orthodox men.

President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot a 28-day mandate to form a government, running through Dec. 6, with the possibility of a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu can try to form a government; if neither succeeds, Israel is expected to hold another election next year.

title: WHO warns drug-resistant Klebsiella threatens vulnerable hospital patients across Europe
description:
The World Health Organization warned that drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is spreading in Europe, putting hospitalized patients with existing health problems at greatest risk; the resistant strains circulate mainly in hospitals and clinics. Bloodstream infections caused by the strain increased 72% from 2019 to 2025, with reported fatality rates of 40% to 70%. WHO experts assess the risk of the strain becoming established across the European Union and European Economic Area as very high.

Jean-Pierre Njemazi, director of WHO's antimicrobial-resistance department, cited estimates that resistance could be directly linked to 39 million deaths over the next 25 years. Member states aim to cut deaths attributed to resistance by 10% by 2030, but Njemazi said current trends and action are not on course to meet that goal. Experts also point to antibiotic use in people and animal farming, and to resistant microbes moving through wastewater and the environment.

title: B.C. premier directs cabinet to reverse Indigenous, climate and drug policies
description:
British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson has directed his new cabinet to reverse key policies on Indigenous rights, climate action and substance use, while pursuing tax relief and tighter government spending. The government released the mandate letters Tuesday, after Doerkson and his cabinet were sworn in on Friday.

The government says ministers must focus on affordability, economic growth, health care, community safety and provincial pride, and submit new funding requests to the Treasury Board for an affordability review. The letters also call for an independent review of provincial finances as the government pledges to address a record $13.8-billion deficit.

title: EU weighs €50 billion fund for AI and quantum firms
description:
The European Union is considering a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund that could mobilize up to €50 billion for European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies as Brussels seeks to reduce reliance on U.S. and Chinese technology. The proposal, reported by the Financial Times citing two officials involved in the discussions, would make larger, riskier and longer-term investments than existing EU financing schemes. Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report.

The European Commission plans to use EU money as seed capital to attract private investment, aiming to mobilize as much as €6 for every euro committed. An independent manager would run the fund, while the precise financing arrangements remain under discussion. The European Investment Bank could provide financial expertise without taking on investment risk.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged an ambitious proposal for technology-sovereignty funding after EU leaders discussed artificial intelligence earlier this month. The Commission is expected to present details of how the fund would operate at EU leaders’ competitiveness retreat in Alden Biesen, Belgium, in February 2027.

title: Somalia orders UAE ambassador out within 72 hours in diplomatic rift
description:
Somalia’s government on Nov. 19 ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador to leave within 72 hours and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi after President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of interfering in Somali affairs, backing armed groups and making port deals with regional administrations without federal approval. The UAE rejected Mogadishu’s accusations, calling its approach “escalatory and hostile,” and said it had already closed its embassy and withdrawn its diplomats in January after Somalia canceled bilateral agreements.

The dispute involves UAE relations with Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, as well as disagreements within Somalia over constitutional changes and election arrangements. Parliament amended the constitution in March to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from four years to five; regional administrations and opposition figures rejected the changes. Somalia’s Supreme Court later ruled that the current leaders’ terms had expired and set deadlines for an election framework and polls.

title: Car bomb in Villavicencio leaves more than 20 injured on anniversary of peace deal
description:
On November 24, Colombia commemorated the tenth anniversary of the peace deal signed in Bogotá between the government and the FARC guerrillas. The day before, a car bomb exploded in Villavicencio, leaving more than 20 people injured. President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed the attack on FARC dissidents and ruled out negotiating with armed groups. The agreement ended more than half a century of conflict between the government and the guerrillas; more than 13,600 combatants laid down their arms.

A decade later, the Kroc Institute estimates that 36% of the commitments have been fulfilled. The Office of the Ombudsman records 521 signatories killed, and the Armed Forces estimate that armed groups total around 29,000 members across 165 structures, compared with approximately 13,000 in 2022. After the FARC withdrew, the government failed to establish a sufficient presence in several areas, which were left vulnerable to disputes among other groups.

De la Espriella has cut the budget of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), the court created by the agreement, and ended talks with armed groups. Former president Juan Manuel Santos maintains that the problems stem from the failure to implement the agreement. At the request of the Colombian government and with the backing of the United States, the UN verification mission will stop monitoring rural reform; its overall mandate was renewed for one year.

title: Study links sperm mitochondrial DNA retention to lower pregnancy odds
description:
A study of 327 men with normal semen-test results found that higher levels of mitochondrial DNA retained in sperm were associated with lower monthly chances of pregnancy, researchers reported Nov. 24. The association remained after accounting for factors including both partners’ ages, body mass indexes and smoking status.

The study does not show that retained mitochondrial DNA causes infertility. Researchers said further work is needed to explain why some sperm retain it and whether it affects fertilization or embryo development.

title: From Policy to Pavement: Preparing Cities for El Niño in the Greater Horn of Africa
description: To limit the toll of El Niño's October-December rains, IGAD's specialized climate institution, the Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC), has released a practical guide with UN-Habitat for Horn of Africa cities. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) is a regional bloc in Eastern Africa of governments from the Greater Horn of Africa, and their High-Level Call to Action on El Niño Preparedness establishes a regional commitment to move from reactive disaster response to proactive action for long-term resilience. Emphasizing cross-border coordination and crediting local knowledge, the call states: "We recognize that climate and disaster risks do not respect national borders, and that no single country or institution can manage them alone."

title: Singapore says Megaspeed chips never entered country, seeks U.S. data
description:
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Nvidia chips bought by cloud company Megaspeed never physically entered Singapore. His government is seeking more information from the United States to identify the chips' end users and verify transaction documents. Singapore is investigating possible breaches of its own laws while working with Washington on checks to help the United States enforce its export controls.

Wong said the chips were routed to other countries, limiting what Singapore can investigate on its own. “We did ask for some information. Not all of it was forthcoming,” he said. The U.S. Commerce Department placed Megaspeed and six related companies in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand on its Entity List on Nov. 23, requiring licenses for U.S. exports. The department cited the risk of advanced computing technology reaching unauthorized users or uses.

Singapore's inquiry remains active, and Wong said companies found to have violated local law would face firm enforcement. During his visit to Canberra, Wong and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also signed an agreement to secure essential supplies, including food, pharmaceuticals and agricultural inputs.

title: U.S. survey: 44% of GLP-1 users who drank when starting treatment reported drinking less
description:
A survey of U.S. adults found that 44.2% of people who drank alcohol when they began taking GLP-1 medications reported drinking less during their first three months on the drugs. Researchers surveyed 2,009 adults in March and April 2026; 242 respondents said they drank when they started taking a GLP-1 medication.

The findings do not establish that the drugs caused the reported changes or are effective in treating alcohol use disorder, which the study did not assess. Participants recalled their drinking, and researchers did not measure how much consumption changed. Larger clinical trials are needed to test whether the medications reduce unhealthy alcohol use.

title: Researchers model helium bubbles to limit metal buildup in molten-salt reactors
description:
Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute used computer simulations to study how replenishing helium bubbles could prevent radioactive metal particles from accumulating in molten-salt reactor systems. The particles can coat heat exchangers, trapping heat and reducing reactor efficiency; the models indicate that adding fresh bubbles can sustain the bubbles’ ability to collect the metals.

The team combined experimental data from the 1960s and 1970s with Argonne’s SAM reactor-safety software to track tellurium-132 under different bubble-flow conditions. The study was published in the journal Nuclear Technology. Its findings are based on simulations, not experimental validation of the proposed operating approach.

title: Hackers breach U.S. spy analysis network, risking exposure of priorities
description:
Hackers breached an unclassified open-source intelligence analysis network used by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), exposing some information, according to people familiar with the incident. A source told The Associated Press that the breach had been resolved and involved no classified information.

The network processes publicly available and commercially sourced material, including social media, satellite imagery and paid data feeds. Investigators have not identified the attacker or specified which records were exposed. Reports also indicated that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was affected and that information at other government agencies may have been exposed.

Access to analysts’ activity could reveal what U.S. intelligence agencies are tracking, even without access to classified files. Nextgov reported that investigators believe hackers used ARTEX, an AI-enabled intrusion tool, but U.S. officials have not publicly attributed the breach to a person, group or government.

title: B.C. towns issue evacuation alerts as storm tides threaten coast
description:
Squamish declared a local state of emergency as communities across British Columbia issued evacuation alerts and closed waterfront areas Tuesday amid coastal flooding risks from king tides, storm surge and heavy rain. Squamish said the declaration would allow it to carry out flood-mitigation work. Parksville and the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation warned shoreline residents to be ready to leave.

Environment Canada warned that tides could run 20 to 50 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides through Thursday. Forecasts called for up to 225 millimetres of rain on parts of Vancouver Island, wind gusts up to 90 km/h in Greater Victoria and rapidly rising rivers across Vancouver Island and the South Coast.

The alerts cover coastal areas from Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island to Haida Gwaii and the central and Sunshine coasts. Victoria closed sections of its Dallas Road waterfront seawall, and Ucluelet closed beaches and trails. The province increased highway patrols and warned that debris or flooding could force sudden road closures.

title: Trump’s tariff plan could add 2% to 7.5% to import duties
description:
A new round of U.S. tariffs could add 2% to 7.5% to import duties if the administration uses the new levies to restore rates imposed before the Supreme Court struck them down, trade-policy expert Deborah Elms estimated. President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing country-specific duties on China, the European Union and 14 other economies following an investigation into industrial subsidies by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR); final rates and effective dates remain unsettled. The duties would focus largely on manufactured goods and could raise costs for importers and consumers. The July tariffs tied to forced-labor enforcement have already contributed to higher U.S. consumer-goods prices, the Associated Press reported.

The administration is expected to keep overall tariff rates within ceilings set by existing trade deals rather than apply a single blanket rate. The European Union, Japan and South Korea face ceilings of 15% or less, while China’s ceiling is expected to remain at 20% if its trade truce with Washington is extended.

The USTR is expected to release its findings shortly. Targeted economies can then seek changes through hearings, public comments and talks before rates are finalized. The administration could also reduce duties if countries take steps to address excess production capacity; the exact product list and start date remain unclear.

title: Argentina's recession hits employment and consumption ahead of the 2027 elections
description:
Between November 2023 and August 2026, Argentina lost 274,300 registered private-sector jobs, and real wages in the sector remained 2.3% below their November 2023 level. Economists estimate that economic activity fell 1.8% between July and September, after contracting 0.6% in the second quarter; the final quarterly figure will be released in December.

In September, ten of the 15 sectors surveyed posted year-on-year declines: fishing fell 48.6%, financial intermediation 11.5%, and manufacturing 1.8%. Mining grew 11.1%; consultancy ACM attributes nearly all of the year's accumulated growth to agriculture and mining.

The government has not confirmed a recession ahead of the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC) publishing third-quarter GDP, scheduled for December 16. Finance Secretary Federico Furiase attributed the July decline to temporary factors and said August and September showed a recovery. Analysts warn that a possible interest-rate hike to contain currency-market pressure would make credit more expensive and hinder the recovery of consumption and investment.

title: Australia’s inflation hits 4.9%, complicating rate and budget decisions
description:
Australia’s annual consumer inflation rate climbed to 4.9% in October from 4.3% in September, while the Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred underlying measure rose to 3.8%, above forecasts of 3.6%. Inflation remains above the central bank’s 2%-3% target, while unemployment has risen and economic activity shows signs of slowing.

Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation. Electricity prices rose 25.2% over the year as government rebates ended, and new-home costs also increased. The Reserve Bank’s next rate decision is due Dec. 8; economists differ on whether rates will stay on hold or rise again. Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government will set out substantial savings in its mid-year budget update, due before Christmas.

title: Judge lets Epstein survivors’ privacy claim over file disclosures proceed
description:
A federal judge in San Jose on Tuesday allowed five Jeffrey Epstein survivors to pursue a Privacy Act claim against the U.S. government, rejecting its bid to dismiss the case. The plaintiffs allege that the Justice Department’s release of investigative files in late 2025 and early 2026 exposed personal information identifying about 100 victims without their consent.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi said the allegations plausibly supported a claim of intentional or willful disclosure but did not rule that the department broke the law. The government cited the 30-day release mandate and acknowledged mistakes, arguing that the plaintiffs had not shown deliberate conduct. The claim can proceed; separate claims against Google and X.AI over AI services that allegedly republished the information remain under challenge.

excerpt: A federal judge in San Jose on Tuesday allowed five Jeffrey Epstein survivors to pursue a Privacy Act claim against the U.S. government, rejecting its bid to dismiss the case. The plaintiffs allege that the Justice Department’s release of investigative files in late 2025 and early 2026 exposed personal information identifying about 100 victims without their consent (courthousenews.com, reason.com). U.S. Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi said the allegations plausibly supported a claim of intentional or willful disclosure but did not rule that the department broke the law. The government cited the 30-day release mandate and acknowledged mistakes, arguing that the plaintiffs had not shown deliberate conduct. The claim can proceed; separate claims against Google and X.AI over AI services that allegedly republished the information remain under challenge (courthousenews.com, law360.com, reason.com). Proposed class: The proposed class would cover Epstein victims whose names, images, phone numbers, email addresses or residential details appeared in unredacted government documents. A subclass seeks removal of information still accessible through government, Google or X.AI services (reason.com). Legal threshold: A Privacy Act disclosure claim requires allegations that the information was contained in a system of records, was improperly disclosed, caused an adverse effect and resulted in actual damages. The agency must also have acted willfully or intentionally; the motion addressed that element (reason.com). Government response: The Justice Department said it created a confidential website for victims to request additional redactions after acknowledging inadvertent disclosures (courthousenews.com, reason.com).

title: Microsoft launches Code Red after outage, sets one-hour recovery goal
description:
Microsoft has launched an internal “Code Red” overhaul after a Nov. 12-13 failure disrupted Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for about 24 hours. The company aims to resolve future global incidents within one hour. Microsoft attributed the outage to a Windows scalability defect introduced in July and said neither cyber activity nor AI agents caused it. The disruption affected government agencies, trading firms and airline communications across several countries.

The company’s review found that diagnostic information scattered across internal systems hampered its response: engineers exchanged more than 11,000 messages in 11 Teams chats without maintaining a single shared view of the incident. Microsoft plans to limit system load, separate traffic by region and speed recovery, with AI agents intended to help engineers interpret system-health data.

The company has not said when it expects to meet the one-hour target. Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team and weekly reviews. In a separate recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days to reach users worldwide.

title: More than 120 climate scientists urge House to reject energy permitting bill
description:
More than 120 climate scientists urged the U.S. House to reject a sweeping energy permitting bill that the Senate passed 62-33 on Nov. 19, warning it could lock in fossil-fuel projects while weakening environmental safeguards. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten federal reviews and make it harder to challenge some projects in court; its supporters say faster approvals could help connect clean power and lower electricity costs.

The House is expected to take up the measure after the Thanksgiving recess, but no vote date has been announced. Lawmakers also face year-end legislation, including government funding due by Dec. 11. If the House passes it, the bill would go to President Donald Trump, whose administration has endorsed it.

title: Dell raises fiscal 2027 outlook as AI-server orders hit $132 billion
description:
Dell Technologies raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to $202 billion from $192 billion after third-quarter revenue more than doubled to $54.94 billion, beating analysts’ estimates. Adjusted earnings reached $9.45 per share, and Dell lifted its forecast for AI-optimized server revenue to $78 billion. Its AI-server backlog reached a record $132.3 billion after $60.2 billion in orders during the quarter.

The infrastructure business drove the gains, while Dell’s PC revenue rose 3% and fell short of forecasts. The company also authorized another $25 billion in share repurchases. For the current quarter, Dell forecast revenue of $56.3 billion and adjusted earnings of $8.40 per share. It expects memory-chip supply constraints to continue into 2027 and said its infrastructure operating margin could dip below 15% as lower-margin AI servers account for more sales.

It expects memory-chip supply constraints to continue into 2027 and said its infrastructure operating margin could dip below 15% as lower-margin AI servers account for more sales (reuters.com, pb.pl, cnbc.com). title: Tiny solar tracker records hummingbird’s 4,055-mile migration to Alaska
description:
Researchers used miniature solar-powered transmitters to track a male Rufous hummingbird from Alabama to Alaska, recording a 4,055-mile journey in 38 days—the longest hummingbird migration documented to date. They tagged the bird in Lillian, Alabama, on March 27, 2025, and it reached Juneau on May 3.

The team fitted 11 hummingbirds with the devices in coastal Alabama and Florida in spring 2025 to track their movements across North America. The study authors said Rufous and ruby-throated hummingbird populations have recently declined; further research is needed to assess any long-term effects of wearing the transmitters.

title: EFPIA says faster EU trial approvals won't fix hospital delays
description:
A study commissioned by the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) says a proposed European Union Biotech Act could shorten regulatory approval times for clinical trials but would not, by itself, eliminate delays before hospitals open trial sites. Under the proposal, approvals would take 75 days, or 47 days if regulators request no additional information; patients in Europe would still face an estimated wait of 294 to 339 days before a trial site opens.

The study compares Europe’s projected timelines with 168 to 276 days in the United States and 126 to 291 days in China, while cautioning that international comparisons have limits. EFPIA says hospitals need more staff, funding and research infrastructure alongside streamlined approvals. The proposed law remains under legislative negotiation.

Research share: The European Economic Area’s share of commercial clinical trials worldwide fell from 22% in 2013 to 12% in 2023, the study said (consalud.es). Industry target: EFPIA backs a target of 500 additional multinational trials in Europe over five years, potentially allowing 35,000 more patients to participate in research (consalud.es). The company is preparing enterprise pilots for 2027 and completing security audits and SOC 2 compliance work.

excerpt: Conservative candidate Kristina Loewen won the Kelowna Centre riding by 132 votes on election night, Oct. 24, 2026. Conservative Party of BC candidate Kristina Loewen has won Kelowna Centre following a judicial recount, widening her margin over the BC NDP’s Loyal Wooldridge, to 46 votes. In a Facebook post, Loewen announced that the recount was complete. Elections BC posted the results on its website Tuesday (Nov. 23) afternoon, confirming the totals. “The Kelowna Centre recount is done!!! I’ve now won with a margin of 46 votes (up from 43)!!!!” Loewen wrote on Facebook. “I’m ready to be able to fully move forward in my role as an MLA representing Kelowna Centre – as well as in my new role as Minister of Children and Family Development.” Loewen also thanked Wooldridge and OneBC candidate Bill Desrossier for contesting the seat. Following election night on Oct. 24, Loewen held a lead of 132 to 137 votes over Wooldridge before mail-in, absentee, and telephone ballots were counted during Elections BC’s final count between Nov. 6-8. Once those ballots were factored in, Loewen’s advantage narrowed to 43 votes—11,689 votes to Wooldridge’s 11,646 votes. Because the margin fell below Election BC’s automatic judicial recount threshold of one-500th of total ballots cast (48 votes in Kelowna Centre), the riding headed back to a judicial recount which started Nov. 23. The finish echoed the 2024 provincial election where Loewen and Wooldridge also battled down to the wire, and a judicial recount was also needed.

title: Utah seeks to drop Kalshi charges after platform halts trading
description:
Utah has asked a state court to dismiss 14 criminal charges against prediction-market operator Kalshi and co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara after the company stopped accepting new trades from Utah residents. The charges alleged illegal gambling. The state seeks dismissal without prejudice, allowing prosecutors to refile if Kalshi returns. A judge must still approve the request. The executives had been scheduled to appear in court on Dec. 4.

Kalshi halted new trading after a federal judge declined to block Utah’s enforcement of its gambling laws while a federal case over regulatory authority proceeds. Kalshi and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission argue that the platform’s event contracts fall under federal commodities law, while Utah and other states say sports-related contracts constitute gambling subject to state law. Utah’s separate civil case seeking Kalshi’s profits continues, and the company says it will continue challenging the state’s authority.

title: Canada puts 100,000 temporary-worker residency slots under provincial control
description:
Canada’s immigration minister, Lena Metlege Diab, says provinces and territories will decide whether to nominate up to 100,000 temporary workers for permanent residency under a one-time 2027 measure; unused places will not be filled. The government’s regular target is 380,000 permanent residents, while one-time measures could bring total admissions to as many as 662,000 next year.

Diab says most people counted are already in Canada and changing status, while Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argues the plan could add pressure to housing, jobs and public services. The House of Commons debated a Conservative motion to block the plan; the Bloc Québécois says it will support the motion, which needs backing from some Liberal MPs to pass.

title: Bank of Canada warns oil costs may prolong inflation
description:
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said Tuesday that inflation pressures could persist even as global energy prices ease because businesses may pass earlier increases in production and transport costs on to consumers. He said the bank’s inflation forecast was somewhat lower than its October projection of 3.5% at year-end.

Businesses have so far absorbed much of the cost increases, but Macklem said surveys and historical lags point to further price increases in the year ahead. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter-point to 2.5% in October; before its Dec. 9 decision, it will assess third-quarter gross domestic product and November employment data.

title: ESA's Euclid telescope finds record quasar beyond its survey reach
description:
The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope identified a quasar candidate in its wide-area survey data, beyond the distance the mission was designed to map; ground- and space-based observatories then confirmed it. European Southern Observatory astronomer Julien Wolf led the discovery.

The object, J1504+6252, was seen as it existed about 630 million years after the Big Bang. Follow-up observations with the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes, among other observatories, established its record distance. Euclid launched in 2023 to survey galaxies and help investigate dark matter and dark energy; the team published its findings in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

title: Missouri court approves Bayer's $7.25 billion Roundup settlement
description:
A Missouri state court approved a class settlement worth up to $7.25 billion to resolve current and future claims that Bayer-owned Monsanto’s glyphosate-based herbicide Roundup caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The agreement calls for declining annual payments over as long as 21 years; an appeal could delay payments until the challenge is resolved.

The deal follows a June 2026 U.S. Supreme Court ruling barring state failure-to-warn claims that federal pesticide law pre-empts. The settlement remains subject to appeal, and people who opt out may pursue individual cases on other legal grounds.
