title: IAEA moves to appoint sanctioned Russian regulator as deputy chief despite Ukraine’s protest
description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is preparing to appoint Alexey Ferapontov, a sanctioned Russian nuclear regulator, as a deputy director general. A senior diplomat said he is expected to take up the post in January 2027. Ukraine’s foreign and energy ministries demanded that the appointment be canceled, saying Ferapontov was involved in efforts to legitimize Russian regulatory control over the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant. Ukraine sanctioned him in February 2023.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi defended the choice as a staffing decision based on professional qualifications, not nationality or geopolitics. Ferapontov is also expected to head the agency’s Department of Nuclear Energy, which oversees programs on nuclear power development, fuel cycles and technical cooperation. Ukraine has urged IAEA member states, especially the Board of Governors, to use the agency’s statutory procedures to review the decision; preparations for the January appointment are continuing.

title: Archaeological studies trace ancient diets and Roman Britain’s diversity
description:
Three separate archaeological studies offer new evidence about past diets and migration. A study of “Rodhals Man,” excavated in 1956, describes him as a rare source of evidence about the shift toward farming. Research at two sites in Western Australia challenges the idea that ancient people widened their diets only when preferred foods became scarce.

A study of cremated remains from Colchester, Britain’s first Roman capital, found that some residents had origins in the Mediterranean, including Italy, Spain and Lebanon. The researchers used strontium and lead isotope ratios in dense skull bone to trace the origins of people whose cremated remains would otherwise be difficult to study.

The researchers used strontium and lead isotope ratios in dense skull bone to trace the origins of people whose cremated remains would otherwise be difficult to study (discovermagazine.com). Australian evidence: Animal bones from Riwi and Barrow Island show diets that included varied prey; at Riwi, these included wallaby, echidna, possum, flying fox, lizards and snakes (scimex.org). Seasonal hunting: Kangaroos were easier to ambush near waterholes in arid periods, while bandicoots remained a good option because they switched to eating insects (scimex.org). Colchester Vase: It depicts gladiatorial combat and animal hunts; researchers suggest its occupant may have been a gladiator trainer or a wealthy patron (discovermagazine.com).

title: Norway’s Equinor signs 18-year gas deal to supply Germany through 2044
description:
Norwegian energy company Equinor signed an 18-year contract with German gas importer VNG on Nov. 24 to supply up to 15.3 terawatt-hours, or about 1.4 billion cubic meters, of natural gas annually. title: Valve releases Proton 11.0-3, adding support for 15 games and fixing regressions
description:
Valve released Proton 11.0-3 on Nov. 24, adding support for 15 Windows games on Linux and SteamOS and introducing experimental support for 32-bit OpenXR applications. Proton is Valve’s compatibility layer for running Windows games on Linux through Steam without requiring native Linux versions.

The update also fixes 19 regressions in the Proton 11 line, along with graphics, audio, controller and game-launch problems. Valve updated underlying components, including DXVK and VKD3D-Proton, which handle graphics compatibility, as well as Wine Mono, Xalia and FEX. Steam distributes the stable release through its client; users can also select a different Proton version for an individual game.

title: DR Congo suspends cobalt exports again as prices fall
description:
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will suspend all cobalt exports from Nov. 30 until further notice, its strategic minerals regulator, ARECOMS, announced on Nov. 23. The government says it is responding to falling prices, weak global consumption and rising inventories. The DRC supplies nearly three-quarters of the world’s cobalt, used in batteries for electric vehicles and consumer electronics.

The suspension is due for review four months after it takes effect. Kinshasa previously replaced an export halt with quotas. Industry participants warn that restricting shipments may not clear the glut if copper mining continues to produce cobalt as a byproduct while demand remains weak.

title: China and India set Russian oil import records as demand shifts
description:
China and India are on track for record seaborne Russian oil imports averaging 3.4 million barrels per day in 2026, based on figures through mid-November, about 530,000 barrels per day more than a year earlier. The Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, while temporary U.S. sanctions waivers eased purchases and Ukrainian drone attacks reduced Russian refining capacity, leaving more crude available for export.

Traders and analysts expect purchases to ease in 2027 if Middle Eastern supply recovers. China’s Russian oil imports averaged 2.34 million barrels per day in January-October, while India’s averaged 1.87 million barrels per day over the same period.

title: Japan plans medical AI study as countries weigh oversight rules
description:
Japan’s health ministry plans to study the use of artificial intelligence in diagnosis and treatment next fiscal year, assess its accuracy and patients’ views, and examine who bears legal responsibility. The ministry has requested 120 million yen for the study and will use the findings to convene experts and consider changes to existing rules.

The Czech Republic has introduced a strategy through 2029 covering safety, reimbursement, data protection and clinician training, while Poland has begun offering hospitals a public platform with certified AI tools for imaging. Health-system leaders are calling for ongoing performance checks and clear clinical accountability.
summary: Japan’s health ministry plans to study the use of artificial intelligence in diagnosis and treatment next fiscal year, assess its accuracy and patients’ views, and examine who bears legal responsibility. The ministry has requested 120 million yen for the study and will use the findings to convene
excerpt: Japan’s health ministry plans to study the use of artificial intelligence in diagnosis and treatment next fiscal year, assess its accuracy and patients’ views, and examine who bears legal responsibility. The ministry has requested 120 million yen for the study and will use the findings to convene experts and consider changes to existing rules (yomiuri.co.jp). The Czech Republic has introduced a strategy through 2029 covering safety, reimbursement, data protection and clinician training, while Poland has begun offering hospitals a public platform with certified AI tools for imaging (lidovky.cz, newsmed.pl). Health-system leaders are calling for ongoing performance checks and clear clinical accountability (beckershospitalreview.com). Study scope: The review will include interviews with doctors and examine how the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approves and regulates medical AI devices (yomiuri.co.jp). Adoption gaps: A Czech ministry survey found that 39% of participating health facilities lacked internal rules for AI use, while nearly 30% relied only on informal procedures (lidovky.cz). Implementation consensus: A two-round international Delphi study found agreement on 22 of 26 recommendations; 97.3% backed identifying suitable tasks and workflows before design, extensive testing before deployment and real-world evaluation (bioengineer.org). Adoption levels: In 2025, 77% of U.S. hospitals used generative AI, surpassing the 69% using predictive AI for the first time (beckershospitalreview.com).

Perspective: Czech Health Minister Adam Vojtěch: Vojtěch says verified AI should reach patients wherever it can improve care, while insisting that a human must retain the final treatment decision (lidovky.cz). (Lidové noviny)
Perspective: Czech Health Ministry Patient Council: Council chair Simona Zábranská called for human oversight, protection of patient rights and clear disclosure of when and how AI contributes to care (lidovky.cz). (Lidové noviny)
Quote: "AI that isn’t embedded in the EHR is like having a capable assistant who sits outside the room." (Muhammad Siddiqui, CIO of Reid Health, Becker’s Hospital Review)
Background: Japan’s health ministry issued guidance in 2018 stating that doctors remain responsible for diagnosis and treatment even when AI is used (yomiuri.co.jp).

title: Salvadoran tribunal registers Bukele to seek a third term
description:
El Salvador’s Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) officially registered the candidacy of President Nayib Bukele and Vice President Félix Ulloa, of the Nuevas Ideas party, on November 23 for the elections on February 28, 2027. Bukele will thus seek a third consecutive term.

The candidacy is possible thanks to the constitutional reform approved by the Legislative Assembly in July 2025, which enabled indefinite reelection, extended presidential terms from five to six years, and eliminated the runoff. The TSE said the other presidential tickets had pending documentation and gave them three days from notification to submit it; afterward, it will decide which ones are definitively registered.

title: Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including critical vCenter bypass
description:
Broadcom released patches Nov. 24 for 23 vulnerabilities across VMware products, including a flaw with a severity score of 9.8 that could let an attacker with network access to vCenter bypass authentication. Two other critical flaws in the ESX I/O filter service could allow remote code execution on affected hosts.

The new vCenter bug, CVE-2026-123903, is separate from another vCenter authentication bypass, CVE-2026-123890, which Broadcom patched days earlier. Rapid7 said attackers had exploited the earlier flaw as a zero-day. Broadcom did not report any exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws in the wild. Fixed versions include vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m; administrators must check the relevant builds for ESX and other products separately.

title: AI investment drives U.S. growth, complicating Fed's inflation choices
description:
Artificial intelligence investment has become a major contributor to U.S. economic growth through spending on data centers, chips, computing equipment, power systems and cooling. It has also boosted activity among businesses serving construction projects. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has called AI central to U.S. leadership, while the central bank faces strong inflation data and financial markets signaling weaker inflation expectations.

Hotels near data centers have reported revenue growth, and snowmobile maker Polaris has reported demand from contractors building data centers. Evercore ISI Vice President Krishna Guha, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official, said the Fed must avoid both undermining its inflation credibility and being seen as having halted the AI boom. Separately, Seeking Alpha analyst Nicolas Bolsinger argues that rapid capital spending and credit links among AI infrastructure firms could spread financial stress if growth falters. His assessment is based on his own credit-risk model, not an official forecast.

title: England's 5,258 heat deaths spur calls for climate adaptation
description:
An estimated 5,258 heat-associated deaths in England in summer 2026, a record, have intensified calls to prepare homes, health services and public infrastructure for rising temperatures. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) warned that climate change will make extreme heat longer, more frequent and more intense. The estimate covers May to September and remains provisional because death-registration data are incomplete.

The summer was also dry: drought was declared across Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires damaged parts of the country. The agency said heat protection should start early in the season because people and public services may be less prepared for heat episodes in May and June. It also urged longer-term adaptation alongside emissions cuts.

title: Canada-U.S. tariff deal nears, but auto duties and China divide negotiators
description:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington and Ottawa are fairly close to a tariff-relief agreement, but Canada’s trade relationship with China and tariffs on autos remain sticking points. Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the talks had made progress but cautioned that Canada was not about to sign. The two governments have not published proposed terms or a list of tariff changes.

The talks resumed after negotiations collapsed in August and President Donald Trump imposed tariffs of up to 50% on about $28 billion of Canadian goods under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. Ottawa’s counter-tariffs and U.S. duties on vehicles and industrial goods remain in dispute. Canadian automakers are seeking an interim arrangement to narrow the tariff gap between plants on either side of the border. Auto industry representatives say the terms must preserve production in Canada, while Greer has criticized Ottawa’s recent trade agreements with China.

Retaliation costs: University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates Canada’s counter-tariffs average about 30% on affected imports and could add nearly $4 billion to consumer costs, with lower-income households losing a larger share of disposable income (thehub.ca). China agreement: Under the November trade truce, China is to suspend additional duties on about $400 million a year of Canadian frozen pork and seafood from Jan. 1, 2027, through 2028; Canada extended exemptions for some Chinese steel and aluminum (thehub.ca). Tariff arithmetic: Tariffs and parts exemptions put effective duties at about 12.5% on Canadian vehicles entering the U.S. and 21.25% on U.S. vehicles entering Canada, though rates vary by model and plant (autonews.com). Export reliance: The United States accounted for close to 70% of Canadian exports in the spring, down from 76% a year earlier, according to RBC (thehub.ca).

title: NASA opens lunar reactor competition, requiring nonnuclear ground tests first
description:
NASA has opened its formal competition for Lunar Reactor-1, a proposed 20-kilowatt fission system intended to power a future Moon base. The initial contract work focuses on design and ground testing, not building a flight reactor. Industry proposals are due Dec. 21, and NASA is targeting a launch-ready system by 2030.

The first phase calls for refining the flight design and demonstrating a nonnuclear engineering test unit that uses electrical heaters in place of nuclear fuel. NASA’s plan includes component radiation testing and an integrated demonstration of heat transport, power conversion, heat rejection and power management in a thermal-vacuum environment simulating lunar conditions. Selected contractors would have 18 months to complete that work.

NASA describes the current effort as technology development, testing and flight design; any later flight-system work would require further procurement. The reactor is intended to provide electricity through lunar nights lasting about two weeks, when solar generation is unavailable. NASA says the solicitation may also support other space-nuclear projects through additional task orders.

title: EU seeks climate summit rule changes after COP31 deadlock
description:
The European Commission plans to propose changes to the United Nations climate summit process after the COP31 summit ended in Antalya without a political agreement. The European Union wants to revisit the consensus rule that lets any country block a decision. EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said Brussels also wants more transparency and a greater focus on carrying out existing commitments.

Climate-vulnerable countries say they need financing and practical ways to identify where adaptation is most urgent. COP31 backed work on adaptation indicators adopted at the previous summit and asked countries to improve and test them nationally. Brazilian climate and environmental justice adviser Thaynah Gutierrez said breaking down data by race, gender and age could help identify vulnerable communities, but funding remains necessary.

South Korea’s climate ministry said it will convene about 80 experts on Nov. 26 to discuss COP31, the Paris Agreement, carbon budgets and national emissions-reduction pathways. The European Commission says it will develop its proposals in consultation with EU member states.

title: ESA revises BepiColombo maneuvers after Mercury insertion software fault
description:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software fault cut short the joint European-Japanese mission’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. ESA says the revised sequence can correct the spacecraft’s trajectory without additional thruster burns, keeping the separation of its two science orbiters and the start of science operations on schedule.

The fault involved attitude guidance and thruster control, and the spacecraft entered a protective safe mode when the burn stopped. The spacecraft reached a stable Mercury orbit; ESA and its partners continue to investigate the software problem.

The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mio orbiter remain joined and are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with routine science operations planned for April 2027. The European orbiter is expected to reach its final orbit in March, while Mio will investigate Mercury’s magnetosphere.

title: Australia awards top science prize to melanoma oncologist and physicist
description:
Australia jointly awarded its 2026 Prime Minister’s Prize for Science to oncologist Professor Georgina Long and physicist Professor Anthony Thomas at a ceremony in Canberra on Tuesday night. Long’s research led to effective melanoma drug therapies, while Thomas was recognized for work on protons, neutron stars and dark matter.

Among other recipients, Professor Asha Bowen received the life scientist award for research that helped deliver the first significant reduction in skin infections among Aboriginal children in 50 years. Professor Mark Smythe won the innovation prize for turning Australian research into medicines approved to treat conditions including psoriasis and a blood cancer.

Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

title: UK seafood groups welcome EU trade deal, seek transition clarity
description:
UK seafood and agricultural trade groups have welcomed the UK-EU sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, intended to reduce food-trade paperwork and routine checks, while seeking clarity on the transition. The agreement is due to take effect on March 1, 2028, but still requires formal approval. Until then, exporters and producers must follow existing requirements.

The Shellfish Association of Great Britain said the agreement could restore access for some shellfish from Class-B waters, which EU rules have barred unless the catch is purified. Scottish seafood representatives said removing paperwork and checks could reduce costs and help smaller producers return to European markets, but stressed that businesses need time to comply with the aligned rules. The German agricultural trade association has also sought clear provisions for transition periods and existing stocks.

title: EU sets hybrid import limits as European carmakers lose market share
description:
European carmakers are losing ground in their home market as hybrid demand grows. German manufacturers’ European Union sales fell 5.7% in October, and their market share dropped from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to figures cited by DW. On Nov. 24, the European Commission published temporary import quotas for hybrids from China and other exporters after its investigation found an imminent threat of serious injury to EU producers.

The limits cover imports from major suppliers including Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the United Kingdom. The Commission said the restrictions are tightest for China, while most other countries’ allocations exceed recent shipments. German automakers have announced widespread layoffs as their market shares shrink. The Commission has linked import growth to global production overcapacity and trade barriers in other markets.

The provisional measures run for up to 200 days, through June 18, 2027, while the Commission continues its investigation. Any longer-term measures would require backing from EU member states.

The project secured key consents and a 400-megawatt UK government Contract for Difference in 2024, but still needs further contracts and investment before construction.

title: AI-assisted Riemann proof fuels debate over understanding and value
description:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge’s claim to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with AI has prompted debate over whether a machine-checked result can advance mathematics when researchers cannot yet explain its reasoning. Alpöge said he developed the proof with Anthropic’s Claude model and released it as about 17 million lines of Lean code. The Lean and Mathlib organizations expressed confidence in its correctness, while the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved pending publication and broad acceptance.

Researchers are trying to extract an intelligible argument from the formal code. More than 60 people on the Principia Math platform are using AI agents to translate sections and have completed work on more than 3,000 pieces. The platform’s chief executive, Anton Shakov, told WIRED that a conceptual account could take months. Mathematicians say they need to understand the reasoning—not just confirm its formal validity—to build on the result.

The Association for Human Mathematics criticized the announcement’s lack of accountability and accessibility, while Google DeepMind researcher Seb Krier said a pure-math result does not immediately improve Anthropic’s operating margins. Cybersecurity specialists say the result itself does not weaken RSA encryption, though they argue AI’s growing ability to explore and verify mathematics warrants renewed attention to cryptographic readiness.

But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

title: Ottawa seeks faster land seizures for Toronto-Quebec City rail line
description:
Canada’s federal government has proposed giving Alto, the Crown corporation developing a high-speed rail line between Toronto and Quebec City, expanded powers to acquire land through expropriation without public hearings and transfer property directly to a private consortium. Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the measures would prevent land acquisition disputes from delaying the project for years and argued they do not remove due process.

The proposals, included in a Budget 2026 motion published Nov. 20, would exempt Alto from the federal Expropriation Act and parts of several rail and environmental laws. The project is expected to cost $60 billion to $90 billion; construction of its first phase, between Montreal and Ottawa, is scheduled to begin in 2029 or 2030. Farmers, opposition politicians and municipal representatives have raised concerns about property rights, farmland and consultation, while Alto says it will pay fair compensation and limit the impacts.

title: Battery developers expand four-hour storage as power markets shift
description:
Battery developers are planning longer-duration projects as solar growth and rising electricity demand increase the need to shift power into evening peaks. In France, BW ESS and local developer Wattmen plan to develop about 500 megawatts of battery projects over three years, with at least four hours of storage per site. In the United States, utility-scale battery capacity reached nearly 52 gigawatts by June 2026.

U.S. developers are competing with gas peaker plants, while French batteries could earn revenue from wholesale power, balancing services and capacity markets. Japan’s storage market faces uncertainty over whether strong early revenues from ancillary services can sustain projects over their 20-year lifetimes, Umer Sadiq said.

title: Iraq orders federal takeover of Kurdish oilfields and border crossings
description:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal agencies to take over the Kurdistan Region’s border crossings and manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahaddin and Nineveh provinces. He also barred the regional government from approving oil exports outside the federal Oil Ministry. The directives followed an investigation into suspected oil smuggling involving the state-run North Oil Company and are part of al-Zaidi’s campaign to assert state authority over oil and border security.

The measures also direct security forces to close unofficial crossings and routes, station federal personnel at checkpoints and monitor fields and pipelines. Baghdad dismissed the head of its border authority and Kirkuk security commanders and suspended North Oil Company executives pending investigations. The government has not specified when or how it will carry out the takeovers.

Kurdish leaders, including Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, reject the orders as unilateral and unconstitutional but say they remain open to dialogue based on Iraq’s Constitution. The two main Kurdish parties, the Kurdistan Democratic Party and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, issued a joint statement opposing the measures. The dispute is also complicating negotiations over Iraq’s 2027 budget and oil-revenue arrangements.

title: Does Your Building Work or Does It Just Photograph Well? What Neuroscience and Use Data Could Teach Architects
description: Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

title: EU probes European Coca-Cola bottler over suspected limits on Spanish imports
description:
The European Commission is investigating whether Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP), a UK-headquartered bottler, offered retailers incentives to restrict soft-drink imports into Spain and used country-specific packaging to impede cross-border sales. The formal investigation concerns suspected barriers to trade between EU countries and restrictions on wholesale buyers’ ability to negotiate purchases across several markets; the Commission has not established that CCEP broke the law.

CCEP is the largest supplier of carbonated soft drinks in eight member states: Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. The case concerns wholesale supply to supermarkets and other retailers, rather than sales to restaurants, hotels and cafes. The Commission says the suspected practices could limit retailers’ access to lower-cost supplies from other countries and reduce consumer choice.

The Commission is also consulting on possible tools to address territorial supply restrictions that competition law may not cover. A separate EU initiative on those restrictions is expected around spring 2027 and could take the form of legislation or a voluntary code of conduct.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin end Shenzhen summit without concrete agreements
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit but reached no concrete agreements. Their joint statement called for United Nations reform, increased oil-product supplies and talks to reduce nuclear risks, while omitting the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Some analysts described the meeting as largely symbolic, while a Chinese foreign-policy expert said he expected U.S.-China relations to remain broadly stable in 2027 even as tensions rise. Da Wei, director of Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said future stability would depend partly on whether Washington recognizes the two powers’ “mutual vulnerability”.

title: Chinese maker brings foldable off-grid solar EV charger to Australia
description:
Chinese portable solar equipment maker Gaotu Innovation has introduced a roof-mounted, off-grid electric-vehicle charger in Australia that combines a foldable solar array with up to 1,600 watts of input and a 2.5-kilowatt-hour battery. Gaotu says the system can provide up to 80 kilometres of daily driving range without grid power and is aimed at drivers travelling in remote areas or camping.

The company says the battery buffers solar input and supplies regulated alternating-current power to a vehicle. The unit can also provide backup power during mains outages. Gaotu offers the system to Australian distributors and says it can customize versions for local partners.

title: COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities
description: The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

title: BepiColombo adjusts Mercury orbit plan after software glitch
description:
The European Space Agency (ESA) says it has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software problem cut short the spacecraft’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. The joint ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency mission to study Mercury remains in a stable orbit. The revised plan is expected to correct its trajectory without additional thruster burns.

ESA’s analysis points to a software problem involving attitude and thruster control, though the precise cause remains under investigation. The revised sequence is intended to maintain the mission’s schedule: the orbiters are still due to separate in December, with routine science operations planned for April 2027.

title: UK-EU food deal would remove checks from 2028, pending ratification
description:
The United Kingdom and European Union have concluded negotiations on a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement intended to reduce routine certification, inspections and other barriers to trade in food, farm products, animals and plants. Britain would align its rules with EU requirements in covered areas, including future updates, and have a role in discussions on new rules. The agreement is scheduled to take effect on March 1, 2028. Customs procedures and rules of origin would remain in place.

The agreement still requires signing and ratification, and businesses must follow current rules until it takes effect. The UK government says the arrangements could reduce exporters' costs and ease trade, but some British farmers question having to follow EU standards for production for the domestic market. Animal-welfare groups warn the deal could complicate planned reforms. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said legislation to implement the summit agreements would be introduced to Parliament on November 26.

title: Singapore and Malaysia tighten checks on AI chip routes
description:
Malaysia will tell data-centre operators not to host, rent space to or provide services to seven companies placed on a U.S. trade blacklist, including Singapore-based Megaspeed and two firms it identifies as Malaysian entities, Speedmatrix and MSFusion. Malaysia’s trade ministry said another listed company, PT Megaspeed International, is neither registered in Malaysia nor operating there as a data-centre operator or tenant.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said during a visit to Canberra that Singapore is investigating whether Megaspeed breached local laws and is working with Washington to share information and develop a mechanism for U.S. authorities to enforce their own chip controls. He said tracking chips’ eventual destinations is complex and that the U.S. had not provided all the information Singapore requested.

The U.S. Commerce Department added seven companies across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to its Entity List on Nov. 23, citing diversion risks; future licence applications face a presumption of denial. Malaysia accounts for more than half of Southeast Asia’s data-centre capacity under construction.

title: NASA seeks partners for 20-kilowatt Moon reactor by 2030
description:
NASA has opened a competition for industry partners to design, build and test Lunar Reactor-1, a 20-kilowatt fission system intended to be ready for launch by 2030 and operate on the Moon for at least five years. Proposals are due Dec. 21, and the reactor must meet U.S. Department of Energy safety standards for nuclear operations.

The system is designed to provide continuous electricity for future lunar habitats, communications, rovers and scientific equipment, including through lunar nights that last about two weeks. NASA revised its solicitation after releasing a draft in August and holding an industry day in September; the agency says it may also commission additional work on other space nuclear power systems.

title: Macron weighs January vote on French constitutional budget rule
description:
President Emmanuel Macron is weighing whether to revive a 2011 constitutional budget amendment and convene France’s lawmakers in Congress in January to reassure investors over borrowing costs and a deficit the government has struggled to reduce. Macron told Le Figaro he would explore the proposal if market volatility persisted into January; he is also watching whether lawmakers pass the 2027 budget by year-end. France expects a 2026 deficit of 5.4% of gross domestic product, while public debt is about 119% of GDP.

The proposal would require multi-year plans to restore balance rather than impose an immediate numerical deficit ceiling. Both houses approved the 2011 text, but it never went to a final vote in Congress. Adoption at Versailles would require three-fifths support from lawmakers.

Even if the constitutional change passes, lawmakers would need to adopt an organic law defining how the framework works, followed by a first budget framework law. Macron’s January decision remains conditional on market volatility and the budget debate; lawmakers would still need to establish the measure’s implementing rules.

title: Bird flu outbreaks prompt poultry culls in France and Delaware
description:
France reported a highly pathogenic H5N1 outbreak at a poultry farm in Pas-de-Calais, where the virus killed 80 of 4,300 birds and authorities culled the remaining flock. Delaware separately announced a presumptive positive H5 test result in a commercial flock in Sussex County; officials quarantined the farm and began culling its birds, which will not enter the food supply.

Authorities detected the French outbreak as bird flu cases rose seasonally in Europe. France had raised its national risk level to high. Researchers also reported that mammary tissue in several livestock species contains receptors that influenza viruses can use, while noting that infections in those species have been reported only sporadically. French authorities suspect contact between farmed poultry and wild birds in the Pas-de-Calais case.

title: Studies link Parkinson’s to lysosome signaling and women’s hormone profiles
description:
Yale researchers have identified a previously unknown pathway through which stressed cell compartments called lysosomes recruit and activate LRRK2, an enzyme linked to inherited Parkinson’s disease. In cultured immune cells, Rab proteins—especially Rab12—helped attract LRRK2 under one type of stress. Removing the ClC-7 transporter prevented the lysosomes from swelling and kept the enzyme inactive. The findings suggest that different cellular stresses can activate LRRK2 through different signals rather than a single trigger.

A separate cross-sectional study of 103 women with Parkinson’s and 110 healthy controls found associations between the disease and lower body mass index, a history of gynecological surgery, and higher levels of two thyroid hormones. The authors said the association with menstrual cycles weakened after adjustment and the results require prospective validation. The study cannot establish that these factors cause Parkinson’s.

title: AI adoption boosts output but slows hiring, reshaping work
description:
Anthropic said its 66 interviews with people at 58 U.S. companies using Claude found few domestic layoffs directly caused by automation, but many firms reported slower hiring and reduced use of contractors. Respondents said AI more often increased output than cut costs. The study was qualitative, and its customer sample was not randomly selected.

A separate National Association for Business Economics survey found about one in five businesses reported widespread, measurable productivity gains. Roughly half reported some gains that were not widespread, while about 30% were not using AI or said it was too early to assess results. Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said demand for construction and chips associated with AI investment is adding to current price pressures. He said the Fed might need to raise interest rates to curb inflation.

For 2025-30, Gartner forecasts AI will create 10.6 million jobs globally and eliminate 8.9 million, while more than 20% of workers—435.5 million people—will need to change their work habits. Anthropic’s interviewees described redesigning roles and moving staff to work that AI does not speed up as ways to benefit from the technology.

Workplace bottlenecks: As AI speeds up coding, companies told Anthropic that code review, sales and strategic decision-making can become the next workflow bottlenecks (anthropic.com). Adoption trade-offs: Anthropic found top-down automation can fuel job insecurity and resistance, while distributing tools without integrating them more broadly can leave adoption uneven and limited to individual tasks (anthropic.com). Layoff notices: U.S. employers had announced more than 100,000 AI-related job cuts through October 2026, making AI the second most cited reason for reductions after market and economic conditions, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas (aktuality.sk). title: “Are We Going to Do Something about This?”: Dr. Mary Jean Brown and the Lead Poisoning Debacle
description:
It seems karmically conspicuous that I post this interview with one of the great leaders in the fight against lead just days before the US Army blows up a cache of lead azide, an explosive that will shower down in a toxic layer over Iowa and locations in neighboring states up to 100 miles away. They are doing this though a safer alternative had been available. Haven’t we learned this lesson yet? If not now, then when? Read more at https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/11/23/iowa-bomb-making-chemicals/  and https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2026/11/23/trump-orders-military-halt-iowa-detonation-plan/  

Take as much care you can. Alert friends and neighbors. Demand testing. Monitor your children. And fight against the continuing poisoning of our children with lead – and many other less well characterized contaminants in future.

Army Detonation of Lead Azide in Iowa: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oGaUXvOMBxE

Dr. Mary Jean Brown completed her doctorate at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and later became a professor at Harvard. She also served as the Chief of the Healthy Homes and Lead Poisoning Prevention Branch at the CDC. I am fortunate to have gotten to know her serving on the Children’s Health Protection Advisory Committee to the EPA (CHPAC). At our first meeting, she smiled at me across the room and pointed out the similarity in our names. Dr. Brown has co-authored some of the most important papers ever published on childhood lead poisoning and was on the ground as people realized just how badly they had poisoned children – virtually all American children – and how dire were the consequences of that rampant poisoning.

When I asked her to look into the future back in August, she pointed to the link between corruption and ill health: “I would be very interested in studying the impact of government corruption specifically on health…. Are we going to do something about this corruption or are we just going to let it go on?” This is a connection I explore in my book and blog – and that we have seen evolve dramatically during and after the midterm elections. I hope and believe people are starting to make an explicit connection between political corruption and the poisoning of our children – and us all.

Interview occurred August 5, 2026. Lightly edited for length and clarity.

JMK: Good morning, Mary Jean – it’s so good to see you!

MJB: Hi, Jean-Marie. it's nice to see you too. I don't hold out much hope for CHPAC.

JMK: I'm worried that they won't even convene it.

MJB: Right. They don't respond to inquiries, and it's like that at CDC too. It's not that they don't agree with you or that they dislike you. It's that they're terrified, you know. They can't talk.

JMK: Yes. I think that one reason this administration would want to avoid reappointing members to CHPAC is they didn't expect how much we would agree with many of the things MAHA was saying. And MAHA was their agenda. I think we would have been a force to be reckoned with, honestly. I don't think most of us ever believed they would really give MAHA the time of day after the election. But even the lip service could have gotten them in trouble with industry.

MJB: Well, there are at least two things that have happened legislatively. One is about coal-fired plants and how many toxic fumes they can emit. And then the next thing was going back from the 100 ppm soil lead standard for Superfund sites. They’ve gone back to 400, and they didn’t get any pushback on that either. I mean, I wrote a letter, and some other people wrote letters, but…

JMK: It’s hard to keep up with everything. They are flooding the zone.

MJB: Yes. It’s like drinking from a fire hose every single day.

JMK: Absolutely. I so often feel pessimistic myself. Poisoning Our Children is really a hard read – and it was hard to write. I would love to get your opinion on it, but I'm trying to show how bad things are, right? The next book is going to be more focused on solutions. It’s provisionally titled Closing the Circle: Pursuing Prevention in a Toxic World. Of course, I have to acknowledge in the first chapter how bad things are. With climate change and widespread environmental degradation, it's hard to be positive. It's hard for my students to even imagine a future. And I think if we cannot imagine that future, then we cannot get there. I don't know if you've had a chance to read Ayanna Elizabeth Johnson's What If We Get It Right?

MJB: No, I have never even heard of it.

JMK: It's good, and the question is excellent. So for the next book, I'm looking towards that. What would it look like if we got it right? And how, working backwards, can we get there? Even if we don't think it's likely, we have to try. You have had a huge success, one of the greatest successes in public health. As I told you, I start nearly every PowerPoint presentation using your graph of dramatic improvement in childhood lead levels. That affected real people. In public health, we don't always see the people whose lives we save. But you saved lives, you improved lives, and it's just an incredible success. So you have a very special perspective.

MJB: Yes. I don't think the World Bank has stood up firmly enough. If you look at just one of the things [that reducing lead has prevented] – if you looked at gasoline, for example – going from leaded gasoline to unleaded gasoline cost approximately 2 cents a gallon between 1983 and 1991. So that's not even 10 years. And the return on investment just during those 10 years was in the billions of dollars. But this is an investment that gives us dividends every single year. Now we're 30 years in. So, I think that's one way of framing the optimism: this is an incredible amount of talent that's being lost [that could be saved].

The problem is that when you start talking to people, especially capitalists, about return on investment, they don't like to talk about societal costs. They want to know that the money is going to themselves. ‘How do I get my hands on this money?’ And we're saying, no, no – everybody's going to get a piece of this money, and everybody's going to have an improved life because of that. Talents that we've destroyed in the past will be able to mature and be successful. One of the professors at Clark University in Atlanta says, you got to understand who pays and who gets paid.

JMK: I love that. It's externalized costs all the way. And I agree. This is something I wrote about more in my first book – it really is capitalism. Now, maybe it is harder, as they say, to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. I think even modifying capitalism is difficult. What do we have to do to get there? I don't know. You know, with lead, we've had all those savings of IQ points. But when you look at the data on organophosphate pesticides alone, we are now losing almost as many IQ points to that one family of pesticides. And so I do like to frame it as we could potentially have the greatest public health success ever if we controlled the chemicals. But right now, we have a public health emergency – many of them.

I would love for you to just tell me your story from the beginning – maybe with an eye to what we can learn.

MJB: Well, we don’t want to go back 76 years. How about if we just go back 40?

JMK: That would be fine. Although if there was something in your childhood – whatever inspired you to get where you are, that origin story – I'd love to hear it.

MJB: Okay. So I’ve always known I wanted to be a nurse. And part of that, I think, was the hat and the white dress and all that. But I always knew that I wanted to help people. So I applied for licensed practical nurse school when I got out of high school. And they wouldn't take me. It's a one-year degree, and I didn’t want to spend a lot of time in school. I just wanted to help people. So then...I spent the next 30 years in school. Even very early on when I was trying to get my associate's degree in nursing, I knew that there was something out there, there's something about me that I didn't…. I was a really good staff nurse, and I loved being a staff nurse. I loved going into that patient’s hospital room, looking around, seeing what needs to be taken care of, clean it up, move on to the next unit. I loved it. But there's something inefficient about doing things one at a time, right? God bless people who do it for a living.

But it just didn't seem efficient to me. And so I got my degree, my ADN, associate degree in nursing. I worked for two years in a big public hospital in Cleveland called Metro. I saw everything. Yeah, there was nothing that I didn't see while I was there.

And at the time, [this inefficiency] kept bothering me and bothering me. And then someone said, well, you know, if you get a bachelor's degree in nursing, you could do research. Which is not true.

But I packed my kids up and moved to Boston and went to Boston College. I ended up at the State Laboratory – my final semester in nursing school – working with the childhood lead prevention program in Massachusetts. At the time, we tried to differentiate between prevention and toxicity. But the threshold at which we thought kids were in trouble was 30 mg/dL at that time – in 1982.

And I started looking at the records, and I realized that we had inspectors over there, and we had pediatricians and pediatric health centers over here. And they weren't talking to each other. And these guys in the pediatric medicine – whatever they had heard as the magic lead number when they were in medical school was how they were operating. And for many of them, it was 65 µg/dL – because that's what Chisholm said -- 65, right? There had been a few other people earlier than Chisholm, who said, well, no – the threshold blood lead needs to be much lower. Byers and Lord is an article you might want to look at. It came out in the 1940s. I can send it to you if you are interested.

JMK: Yes, please.

MJB: This woman, Lord, she was a psychologist who started following up on kids who had been through the lead clinic at Children’s Hospital in Boston several years later. And she found out that, lo and behold, they couldn't read, they couldn't sit still, they just were not capable of getting….  

These were all kids who had blood at 65 or higher because they were chelated at Children’s. And so then people started thinking about, well, maybe we should lower the threshold. The National Health and Nutrition Evaluation Survey (NHANES) that Kate Mahaffey was on – who is a dear friend of mine – found that the average blood lead level of children in the United States at that time – in the mid 1970’s – was 15 µg/dL.

So if you use the three-microgram or the five-microgram threshold, virtually every child was lead poisoned. That opened some eyes. That came out in ’77, and then under Reagan, all the child health programs – teen pregnancy prevention, low birth weight, infant mortality, lead poisoning – all got lumped together under a block grant – because block grants were thought to be more efficient. And then the funding was cut by 40%.

Every lead program in Connecticut went out of business the next day. But in Massachusetts – because Massachusetts has a lot of old, lead-painted mansions – there was a critical mass of wealthy children, affluent children – and their parents were wild. Their parents were the most committed activists. It was like Mothers Against Drunk Drivers (MADD). They were out there. They managed to hold onto the Massachusetts lead program. So we had money coming in from the state, and then we got money from the Maternal Child Health Block Grant. Not every state used their Maternal Child Health Block Grant to fund lead poisoning, but we did.

Joe Biden takes an awful lot of credit for this – as far as he was concerned, lead was his legacy. He told Ruth Ann Norton he solved the problem. So when the Democrats came in again, and the CDC came back into the game – and that was 1989-90 – Congressman Louis Stokes from Cleveland was the person who pushed us. He really rammed it through. He was one of those congressmen like Clyburn. when CDC came back into the game in the 1990s, I was lucky – because I was from Massachusetts, and we were a model.

So as we tried to develop standards for the amount of lead in household dust or soil. Our first question would be, well, what's Baltimore doing?

Baltimore's first question would be, well, what's Massachusetts doing? So then, when CDC came back and then they started having grants out to the states too, I was lucky enough to get one. So now we had gone from $1,000,000 a year budget in 1982 to $3 million a year, $1 million in state funding, $1 million in block grant funding, and $1 million from CDC.

In the meantime, I had tried to address this lack of understanding and knowledge in the pediatric health care community, and quite frankly, the kinds of things that some of the inspectors were up to.

I started the case management system. So every day I got all the high blood lead levels from the laboratory that was right down the hall. And I would call the pediatric office, and I would say, Joey has a blood lead level of 70. It's really important that you call Dr. Graef, our medical consultant at Children's Hospital, because Joey probably needs to be treated. Well, they didn't want to go and ask John Graef. They didn't want to appear like they didn't know what they were talking about. So I would give them a little – nurses do this all the time – I would give them the abstract of a paper: well, here's what happens. Here's what the dose is. Here's how you do it. Then they followed up with John.

I mean, it's not rocket science. And so with this new funding from CDC, and a threshold blood lead level now at 25 micrograms per deciliter, I could hire 5 nurses. And I put a nurse in each one of the five health regions in Massachusetts and had them do what I had been doing from Boston.

And it was pretty successful. There were pockets of people who were … it was just very, very hard to move them. John couldn't make them do anything either. But for the most part, [it was successful]. I started doing a roadshow. I got accredited for continuing medical nursing education credits, and I started going around. My very first lecture I gave when I didn't have PowerPoint; I had overheads. Remember those? It was at Emerson Hospital in Arlington, Massachusetts, just north of Boston. And I came in, and I did my shtick. Everybody does the same lead lecture. Phil Landrigan actually does it better than almost anybody else because he's funnier. But so I went in there, and I did it.

And at the end, this man came up to me. At that time, most of the research on lead effects in children was done by Herbert Needleman and David Bellinger. So my lecture focused on them a lot.

And this man came up to me, and he said, “you know, your lecture just meant so much to me. I'm so appreciative.” And I said, ‘oh, thank you’. And then he looked at me, and he said, “I'm David Bellinger's father.” Thank God he didn't tell me before I started.  He was a surgeon at the hospital.

I trained the programs to do it in the inservice. Then we had 6 people going out to talk about lead. I've been to places where I projected the overhead with the plastic sheets on top on a refrigerator in the conference room, right? But it worked, and it became a model.

They liked me at CDC in those days. When the Southeast Asian diaspora started, and those kids came to the United States, they were very anemic; they were practically starving in the refugee camps. Many of them had parasites, and a lot of them ended up in Lowell, Massachusetts. Now, this is a story you can only tell in America. Lowell, Massachusetts had a Buddhist temple. The monks were Germans. But it was a Buddhist temple. And of course, the nurses were of Irish Catholic ancestry. And those three ethnic groups got together – the leaders in the Southeast Asian community, the German monks, and the nurses – and worked really well together. The CDC gave me money to put together a Southeast Asian lead poisoning prevention program in Lowell. The director, at the request of the Southeast Asian community, was a woman named Joan Seeler. Joan had worked in the refugee camps overseas for most of her career. It was very moving to walk into a room with Joan because people would come flying out of the audience or the group and say, “Joan Seeler, Joan Seeler – you saved my life!

She worked really hard, and also hired Hmong, Cambodian, Lao, and Vietnamese staff, so we covered all the language bases. It’s not there anymore, but that's mostly because they don't need it anymore.

As I was progressing through this whole thing with CDC, my boss, Ralph Timperi, the state lab director, said to me one day, “Mary Jean, I think you should get a masters degree in Public Health.” Well, that sounded all right. And then he said, “and I think you should go to Harvard.”

And I said, “sure, Ralph.” And then, I got into Harvard!

I did the one-year masters while I was working full time at the health department. In those days, you had to go to school during the day. They didn’t have part time. But they let me go half time. At the end of the first year – I used to tell my students this – that June, I felt like I was recovering from a long illness. I was so tired. I had also hired social workers for each of those regional offices because the families are in crisis – they need everything. They need nutrition and psychosocial support and rent assistance, and that is what social workers do. We figured out how to get Medicaid to pay for nurse home visits. So the nurses and the inspectors worked as a team rather than as adversaries to visit the homes. That part was going along pretty well.

And then I graduated, and I just said to Ralph, “I want the whole thing – I want the PhD.” And he was very supportive. So I left the lead program. I was working on a randomized community-based trial of nurse home visits in Rhode Island – some of my dissertation came out of that work.

When I graduated with a Doctor of Science from the program, Harvard offered me an assistant professor position. I didn’t need to go back to the lead program, and some people in the program leadership weren’t that happy with me. So it was fine – until I got to Harvard and found to my dismay that Harvard faculty is primarily dependent on outside grants for salary.

JMK: What?!

MJB: At that time NIH had no interest in lead. And whatever interest they had, there were only two people who could get money. One was Bruce Lanphear, and the other was Howard Hu. He was in California at UCLA – and is at San Diego now. He was a big occupational medicine guy. The CDC didn’t believe in nurses. First off, they thought they were too expensive. And they had a lot of men coming out of the service after they had done their 20 years – medics, or some kind of environmental or sanitarian guys – and they go into the civil service. CDC didn’t think they needed nurses. It took a long time to get them off that dime.

I was there on the permanent faculty at HSPH for three years. After I found out that Harvard wasn’t going to actually pay me, and I couldn’t for the life of me get money out of NIH, I was in luck.

And as you know, the director of the Lead Poisoning Prevention Branch at CDC opened up, and Anne Guthrie, who was at the National Center for Healthy Housing, threw my hat in the ring. And so I went through all that, and they hired me. It was actually Dick Jackson who recruited and hired me to fix the lead branch. And so I went down there and fixed the lead branch in a lot of ways – it was very different when I left, but I left under a cloud again.

Tom Frieden was director of CDC at the end of my tenure, and he had these winnable battles – about ten of them. Lead was not one of them. He hasn’t won any of them yet. But he cut lead program funding by 98% so that he could move money to these winnable battles. Some of that was personal – against me.

Well, partly because of what happened with lead in the water in DC, I was under scrutiny from a guy named Marc Edwards. He has actually blamed me for Flint – because he said that I fudged the data in DC – because we didn’t find any children who were dying, being admitted to the hospital, or an uptick in chelation. We didn’t find any serious illnesses. What we found was a whole bunch of people who had blood lead levels more than 5 µg/dL. But that’s not glamorous enough – they don’t look sick, and blah, blah, blah. He said I got away with it, and that’s why Flint happened. And when you get a reputation in the federal government – even if it’s not true – people don’t want to touch you. They want you to crawl into your desk and come out under another administration.

While I had been a branch chief, I continued to teach at Harvard. I had a program evaluation course where I brought students and CDC lead staff in the states together so they could learn about evaluation. The goal was not to get the CDC funded state staff to become professional evaluators. My goal was to get them to be savvy consumers of evaluation so they couldn’t have the wool pulled over their eyes. And the students needed to get out into the field. Some years, this was the only field opportunity they got.

So I still had the connection with Harvard. As one does, I went back to Harvard, and I taught for the next 10 years – very applied public health evaluation and how the government works – and how you can get your stuff on the agenda – because the students today have never had civics.

JMK: I know. It’s distressing. I cannot believe they have cut civics.

MJB: Yes. When I first started teaching in the permanent faculty, I taught maternal child health 101. I would start talking about the federal government, and the Chinese or the Japanese students would look up like deer in headlights. So I put together a little seminar for them and said this is not what happens in Japan, but here’s how it happens here. It was kind of a more sophisticated “school-house rock” version. Then I realized, you know what? Nobody else in this class understands either. I developed a course on how to get your issue on the political agenda. It did well, though it sputtered out the last year I was there.

I think that’s because nobody wants to go into government now. They all want to start their own companies. They shy away from government. And it’s understandable, but I don’t know who is going to rebuild this system.

I’m still working a little bit – one interview with a reporter a month And if something pops up like the lead in cinnamon.

JMK: Sure.

MJB:  I am still working with colleagues at Harvard and in Mississippi – way away from lead. Mississippi has the highest maternal mortality most years, and that hasn’t changed – 20 years it’s been like that. So we are testing whether having nurse home visits immediately postpartum for women, a lot of whom are discharged within 24 hours, reduces the severe morbidity and mortality.

JMK: What is most difficult about it? Facing the heat, the racism, the sexism – it sounds like you’ve experienced sexism throughout.

MJB: A bit of all of that, yes. I’ve had some experience working internationally. I have done community-based screening outreach programs in slums on every continent but Australia and Antarctica – because it doesn’t have one yet.

Working in Mississippi is like working in a third-world country, especially in the Mississippi Delta. There are no resources. No community hospitals anymore. The birthing center is a 2 1/2-3 hour drive. They did not do the Medicaid expansion – although women are covered 60 days after birth.

Most of the stuff that has been done around the issue has been around infant mortality. One OB said to me one day that the programs are focused on the candy. We’re not focusing on the candy wrapper.

JMK: Jeez!

MJB: So it is really hard to move things. I am not there. Everybody thinks you can do stuff remote. They forget that you can’t.

JMK: So interesting! I do have some follow-up questions. So were you saying that you've experienced some sexism and bias against nurses throughout your life?

MJB: I haven't worked in a hospital or a clinical setting for a long time. I have a daughter who is a psych nurse at a VA hospital outside of Boston. And from her stories, it sounds like it's not as bad, but it never was as bad in the service because nurses were officers. She works with patients, who, if they were enlisted, treat her like an officer.

The other thing that happens with nurses is that the way a hospital is run, the physicians are considered the product. They bring the patients in; they make the money for the organization. The nurses are considered a cost. So every time there's a merger, every time somebody gets a bright idea in the corporate world that they can make some money, they come in, and they cut the nursing staff. That's always the first thing that happens. And the fact is – and this is not my thought; a lot of people have said this – that you don't go to the hospital for medical care. You go to the hospital for nursing care. They can do almost all medical care as an outpatient nowadays. Right? You need somebody to take care of you. To take over some of the stuff that you would do on your own if you were feeling better. So that's part of it too. But now with more men coming into nursing, that may change the calculus a little bit.

JMK: Of course, as many weeks and even months as Katherine and I spent in the hospital, we know about nurses. Children's Hospital of Wisconsin, where she had her bone marrow transplants, is one place where nurses were really part of the team. It was the primary nurse, the doctor, the fellow, the pharmacist, and everybody rounding together. And that model worked so well. We had innumerable experiences of nurses being so kind and taking care of us. So thank you for that care you've given to others.

All right – the next question is, where do you think this is going? If you were going to say what the status of children's health is going to be in the year 2050, what would you say? Because in some ways, things are getting better, and in other ways, they are getting much worse.

MJB: Yes. I think we are at a very critical stage where the road splits, and it's very difficult to predict which way it’s going to go. What's happening with public health under this administration scares me to death. It really does. It wakes me up in the middle of the night. How many kids are going to die from measles or be blind from measles or have intellectual disabilities from measles? I don't know, but it's going to be a few, if not more than that, right? What if we have another big outbreak? This ‘lettuce outbreak’ that's going on right now – okay, for most people, it's a couple of weeks of diarrhea, which God knows is not pleasant, but it's usually not fatal either, or debilitating for a long period of time. There are going to be some people – especially the elderly or anybody who's frail – who are going to have a bad outcome. But most people are going to get over it.

What comes next? We don't know. Viruses mutate all the time. That's their job in the world.

So, it could be that by 2050 it will look a lot like 1950.

Or it could be that by 2050…. You know, that's not that far away. I mean, I'm not going to see it, probably, but you'll see it.

Well, first off, I think that nurses are going to take over primary care, and I don't think that's a bad thing as long as they get the education to support that work. And I'm not convinced that's going to happen. I think there's a chance that there's going to be another push to get health insurance for everybody, whether that's going to be Medicaid, Medicare for all, or whether it's going to be some kind of a hybrid model – I don't know. In my heart, I believe in Medicare for all. But in my mind, I don't think that these large corporations should be let off the hook. I think they should have to pay benefits, including health benefits for their staff. I'm tired of people who work at Walmart full-time getting food stamps. Right? I am tired of families of enlisted men in the services below the level of sergeant qualifying for WIC.

Why are we the taxpayers funding that? That should not be our job. But I think people are getting really tired of this – what I've thought of as neo-feudalism – that's going on now out there.

I think that by 2050, we will have wiped most childhood cancer deaths off the margins. I think as you're pointing out rightly, if we continue to dump so many chemicals and waste into the water, the air, into the environment, we will probably have more cancers. But I think that the treatments are going to be increasingly sophisticated. They're also going to be increasingly expensive.

So yes, are we making the wrong choice? Putting a lot of money into what we call tertiary care, which means you have to be sick before you get it, and not enough into the primary prevention? Yes, that's true.

You know, my students have asked me, what would I do if I were graduating now; what would I be looking for in a career? And so I have two answers. And it goes along with what do you think is going to happen by 2050.

The first one is that I would be looking at child labor – children going to work at very early ages. It's not a problem in the United States, but it is a problem in the rest of the world. And they are exposed to everything: sexual violence, chemical exposures, occupational hazards from machinery and sharp objects and all that stuff. And then they're not going to school.

But then the other thing, and this is what's happening here too: I would be very interested in studying the impact of government corruption specifically on health.

JMK: Yes. I mean, we can't go on like this. It's just terrible.

MJB: I think that's the answer to your question, though, about what's going to happen in 2050. Well, it depends. Are we going to do something about this corruption or are we just going to let it go on? And, you know, you have students: push one into this, just tell them, go, go, go figure it out.

JMK: I do my best, and I have had a few students who were going to law school, and then because of my courses, they pursued environmental law. And so yes, the earth needs a good lawyer, and so do people who are being poisoned. I agree with you.

The next question is somewhat similar, but with a little bit of a flip. This is the central question I now ask my students. Imagine it's 2080 or so, and imagine that the world is pretty good, maybe even better in some ways, different, of course, than it is today. What does that look like and how do we get there? Given our huge, huge challenges as we pour accelerants on a burning climate, toxify the entire ecosphere, devastate biodiversity, and thereby jeopardize political stability, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera – what would it look like if we got it right, to riff on Ayana Elizabeth Johnson?

MJB: Let me start from the beginning. Once upon a time, in Cleveland Ohio, they put the water intake 5 miles out from the shoreline because you couldn’t poison the water that far out. But of course, it happened. And then we dumped an awful lot of stuff in the ocean because God knows, you can’t pollute the ocean – it’s too big. Well, we certainly have done that with plastics. So what I see by 2080, is a lot of polluting and dangerous mining, smelting, oil refineries, the data centers – I see it being shipped into low-Earth orbit. God knows, you can’t contaminate eternity, you can’t contaminate space, right? I’m not sure that that’s right. I have a son who is an engineer, and I was just talking to him yesterday and saying, you’ve got to think about this, Tommy, because this is where it’s going.

JMK: That’s grim – because there’s already a lot of space garbage.

MJB: Right. So then there’s lower Earth orbit, there’s middle orbit, and it would just keep going out.

JMK: I think you're saying that it's harder to imagine people constraining their desires and consumption than to imagine some external fix. Wow. All right, well, Mary Jean, is there anything I should have asked you that you want to tell me?

MJB: When I look forward – just with lead, I think the future means we need to really work harder internationally. I helped write the book from the World Bank. But UNICEF has one, WHO has one, USAID had one. Everybody has one compendium with some kind of plan in it – we don’t need more of that. We know what needs to be done, we know how, and worldwide, we know where it needs to be done first. And we know what the return on the money is.

It’s hard to work in the US – every state has its own little way of doing business, and then they say, well, this isn’t Massachusetts. And so it’s hard to do that worldwide – but that’s what has to happen. Taking lead out of gasoline is a really good model. Where EPA fell apart on taking lead out of paint internationally was the enforcement arm. It has to be enforced, and that takes political will, political savvy. It takes people at the World Bank stepping up to the plate a lot harder. They need to step up. Some of the stuff that I said they should do – they took out of the book. Otherwise, that is the only way to stop it – to do everything we can to clean up the mess that’s already here and then stop putting lead in anything.

JMK: And then we need to tackle pesticides, PFAS, and plastics. I think people tremble to think about trying to back off from plastics. I mean, I have contacts in my eyes. I have plastic in my hips. But of course, we could do something.

MJB: Yes. But the plastic in your hips is going to stay there for a long time. It’s not going to end up in the water.

JMK: A while. And we could reduce plastic 75% – don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good, right?

MJB: Yes, that’s right. But see – I’m a one-trick pony. I know a lot about one toxic chemical – lead….

JMK: We need specialists for sure.

All right. Is there anything you would like to ask about my project or my experiences?

MJB: No, I'm looking forward to reading the book, and I'm hoping that a lot of that will be in there.

JMK: It is – absolutely.

MJB: I understand where your passion comes from. And I certainly respect that. And I wish that you hadn't had to go through that. I mean, it's wonderful that you have the passion and you're doing all this great work. I think you could have found something else to motivate you. But I wish you hadn’t had to lose Katherine.

JMK: Oh, oh, yes. I could have been a happy professor of medieval literature for the rest of my life, and Katherine would have been brilliant. She would have made her own contributions. And so, that's the horrible waste. What motivates me is, I would do anything to prevent this happening to other children and other families.

MJB: Yes. I know – their parents….

JMK: Well, it’s been a pleasure, Mary Jean. It always is. And I’m sorry I’m not going to get to see you at future CHPAC meetings. Was your term up, or were you going to be still doing it?

MJB: They were telling me that I was going to be just re-upped for another three years. But I haven’t heard anything back.

JMK: So we would have been able to have lunch together again if it had not been for this terrible administration.

MJB: I don’t get to Chicago often, but sometimes I do.

JMK: It would be nice to meet up!

MJB: I will let you know if I get out there. There is another lead guy there – David Jacobs. He was the Director of the HUD lead poisoning prevention: Healthy Homes. And he has been in the lead business almost as long as I, but on that side. He was also the science director at the National Center for Healthy Homes. I will give you an electronic introduction to Dave – he also wrote a book, and I’m sure he’ll be happy to tell you all about it. He’s at University of Illinois at Chicago.  

JMK: UIC has an amazing School of Public Health – they have the PEHSU there.

MJB: And if you ever decide to do some kind of a seminar, and you need somebody to speak at it, you could call me.

JMK: Thank you so much, Mary Jean!
summary: It seems karmically conspicuous that I post this interview with one of the great leaders in the fight against lead just days before the US Army blows up a cache of lead azide, an explosive that will shower down in a toxic layer over Iowa and locations in neighboring states up to 100 miles away.

title: CachyOS adds Easy Anti-Cheat v2 support; Fortnite expected first
description:
The November release of CachyOS, an Arch-based distribution, adds support for Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2, a game-protection system that checks a computer’s boot setup before allowing a game to start. Heise reported that no game was using the Linux v2 system yet and that Fortnite is expected to be the first.

CachyOS supplies a separate signed kernel and boot option for EAC-protected games, while the standard boot entries remain available. Enabling the EAC option requires Secure Boot, a trusted signing key, TPM 2.0, an enabled IOMMU and kernel lockdown. The release also includes a redesigned package installer and a recovery environment for Btrfs snapshots.

excerpt: The November release of CachyOS, an Arch-based distribution, adds support for Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2, a game-protection system that checks a computer’s boot setup before allowing a game to start. Heise reported that no game was using the Linux v2 system yet and that Fortnite is expected to be the first (heise.de, lxer.com). CachyOS supplies a separate signed kernel and boot option for EAC-protected games, while the standard boot entries remain available. Enabling the EAC option requires Secure Boot, a trusted signing key, TPM 2.0, an enabled IOMMU and kernel lockdown. The release also includes a redesigned package installer and a recovery environment for Btrfs snapshots (lxer.com, heise.de). Installer safeguards: Package Installer 2.0 adds optional AUR, Flatpak and AppImage handling; before building an AUR package, it displays the package’s PKGBUILD and install scripts and flags lines for review (lxer.com, heise.de). Snapshot recovery: The self-contained recovery image can launch from UEFI or the bootloader and test a Btrfs snapshot with a writable root before rollback. It also supports LUKS-encrypted installations (lxer.com, heise.de). Graphics startup: The new cachyos-drm-awaiter delays the display manager until graphics drivers load and can show a QR code if driver loading fails (lxer.com). Additional changes: The release also offers a CachyOS image for Windows Subsystem for Linux and includes Linux 7.3.5, NVIDIA 620.73.04 and Mesa 26.3.1 (lxer.com).
kite_context: Perspective: CachyOS developers designate the EAC kernel for gaming rather than everyday use because its lockdown mode prevents loading DKMS modules (lxer.com, heise.de). (CachyOS release notes republished by LXer)

title: Brazil cuts transfers to states and limits support for exporters
description:
The fiscal package approved by Brazil's Congress limits federal transfers to states and municipalities linked to the Kandir Law to 2 billion reais per year from 2027 to 2030. The previous arrangement provided for 4 billion reais per year through 2030. The new figure resulted from a legislative agreement; the Chamber approved the text without changes, with 353 votes in favor and 128 against. It now awaits President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's approval.

The Kandir Law exempts exports from the state ICMS tax, and federal transfers compensate for part of the revenue that local governments forgo. The adjustment also limits the interest subsidy for the Export Financing Program, which helps finance Brazilian sales abroad, to 1 billion reais per year through 2030. Opposition leaders argued that the measures will shift costs to companies and reduce state and municipal revenues.
