title: Microsoft fixes Entra Connect Health flaw exposing tenant metadata
description:
Microsoft disclosed that attackers exploited a flaw in its Entra Connect Health application programming interface (API) to read tenant metadata and the email addresses of technical contacts and administrators at affected organizations. The access was read-only. Microsoft said passwords, authentication tokens and valid cryptographic keys were not exposed, but the information could help attackers craft targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts.

Microsoft fixed the API on its servers, so customers do not need to install an update. It has not disclosed how many tenants were affected and said it found no unauthorized changes to Connect Health configurations. The company recommends that organizations review security logs and remain alert to messages that use details about their systems.
summary: Microsoft disclosed that attackers exploited a flaw in its Entra Connect Health application programming interface (API) to read tenant metadata and the email addresses of technical contacts and administrators at affected organizations. The access was read-only. Microsoft said passwords,
excerpt: Microsoft disclosed that attackers exploited a flaw in its Entra Connect Health application programming interface (API) to read tenant metadata and the email addresses of technical contacts and administrators at affected organizations (securityaffairs.com, helpnetsecurity.com, petri.com). The access was read-only. Microsoft said passwords, authentication tokens and valid cryptographic keys were not exposed, but the information could help attackers craft targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts (techzine.eu, helpnetsecurity.com, securityaffairs.com). Microsoft fixed the API on its servers, so customers do not need to install an update (scworld.com, techzine.eu). It has not disclosed how many tenants were affected and said it found no unauthorized changes to Connect Health configurations (securityaffairs.com, helpnetsecurity.com). The company recommends that organizations review security logs and remain alert to messages that use details about their systems. Metadata exposed: The API could return tenant IDs, domain names, region and licensing details, directory synchronization status and the service’s last synchronization time (helpnetsecurity.com, tweakers.net). Legacy certificate: The exposed response also included an expired certificate for an internal service decommissioned in late 2024. The certificate had remained in Connect Health storage (techzine.eu, petri.com, tweakers.net). Privileged-role controls: Microsoft recommended just-in-time role activation through Privileged Identity Management for technical contacts who also hold Global Administrator or another privileged role (securityaffairs.com, helpnetsecurity.com). Script limitation: Microsoft’s read-only PowerShell script reports current metadata values, which may differ from those accessible during the breach. The script cannot reconstruct past exposure (techzine.eu, helpnetsecurity.com).
kite_context:
Perspective: Affected tenant administrator: An administrator who discussed the incident on Reddit said the combination of real administrator addresses and tenant-specific facts could make a message posing as an Entra sync alert especially convincing (helpnetsecurity.com).
Quote: "We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes." (Microsoft, Security Affairs)
Timeline: 23 July 2026: A vulnerability was introduced into the Entra Connect Health API (securityaffairs.com, helpnetsecurity.com).
Timeline: 9 November 2026: Microsoft detected the API vulnerability (securityaffairs.com, tweakers.net).
Timeline: 19 November 2026: Microsoft deployed a server-side fix that closed the vulnerability (securityaffairs.com, techzine.eu).
Timeline: 20 November 2026: Microsoft concluded its investigation and confirmed unauthorized read-only access (securityaffairs.com, helpnetsecurity.com).

title: Quebec court suspends province’s exemption from Crown oath
description:
Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers suspended the province’s 2022 exemption from the Crown oath required of lawmakers across Canada, saying Quebec could not change the constitutional requirement on its own. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will appeal.

The dispute could affect the legal standing of legislation passed by Quebec’s newly elected assembly, while the underlying challenge has yet to be heard on its merits. Ottawa lawyer Lawrence David, who brought the case, says the oath requirement applies to the King as Canada’s head of state. Laval University constitutional law professor Patrick Taillon argues that courts could temporarily preserve laws later found invalid, citing a Supreme Court remedy in a Manitoba language case. Quebec’s legislature is scheduled to resume Dec. 1.

title: French downturn deepens, raising recession risk as German activity accelerates
description:
Business surveys released Monday showed the eurozone’s composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) holding at 51.7 in November, while Germany’s rose to 55.0 and France’s fell to 46.2, its lowest in six months. The readings point to about 0.3% growth for the eurozone in the fourth quarter, but suggest France’s economy is close to stalling. France’s economy contracted 0.1% in the third quarter, leaving it at risk of a technical recession if output falls again.

S&P Global said French companies were holding back projects because of weak demand and uncertainty ahead of the April 2027 presidential election. The government is also struggling to pass a deficit-reduction budget. Persistent price pressures could strengthen calls for another European Central Bank rate increase in December, while higher borrowing costs are already weighing on activity. Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin, however, said he expects the French economy to grow in the fourth quarter.

title: Milky Way study recasts part of Norma arm as star-forming bar shock
description:
A study published in *Nature Astronomy* suggests that a stretch of the Milky Way’s Norma arm traced by masers may instead be a star-forming shock front along the leading edge of the galaxy’s central bar. The University of Sydney-led team reached that interpretation by comparing galaxy simulations with existing maser measurements; it did not directly image the shock front or collect new observations.

The researchers say the result concerns only the maser segment near the bar’s end, not the entire Norma-Outer arm, and requires further investigation.

Unusual activity: The interpretation would place star formation in a bar shock, where strong shocks suppress star birth in many other barred galaxies (sciencedaily.com, scienceblog.com).

title: Thai appeals court cuts opposition lawmaker’s sentence to three years
description:
Thailand’s Appeals Court on Nov. 23 upheld opposition lawmaker Rukchanok Srinork’s conviction for royal defamation but cut her prison sentence from six years to three, upholding the charge tied to one 2021 social media post and dropping the charge tied to another. She faces a prison term under Article 112, Thailand’s lese-majeste law, which allows sentences of up to 15 years for each offense.

The Criminal Court granted Rukchanok bail of 500,000 baht as she appeals to the Supreme Court, allowing her to remain free and keep her parliamentary seat while the case proceeds. Rukchanok has denied wrongdoing; People’s Party leader Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut said the party would pursue the appeal.

title: Ubuntu 27.04 daily builds available ahead of April 2027 release

title: Signal adds mobile screenshot blocks as Muse privacy risks emerge
description:
Meta’s Muse AI agent revealed other people’s bank balances and private messages during internal testing, including a reminder about a Signal conversation, according to reports citing internal company posts. Signal says operating-system agents can read information displayed on a device’s screen, outside the app’s end-to-end encryption.

Signal announced default screen-capture restrictions for iOS 27 and supported Android devices on Nov. 20, while warning that the measures cannot stop agents from retrieving data already stored on a device. Signal says it cannot reliably provide the same protection on macOS and is asking Apple, Google and Microsoft for documented ways to block AI access to screens, files and notifications.

title: Sudan cites 70 alleged Ethiopia-linked drone attacks as Khartoum struck
description:
Sudan’s army-aligned government says it documented 70 drone attacks launched from Ethiopian territory between mid-February and late October, a charge Addis Ababa denies. A new drone assault hit Khartoum on Nov. 22. The United Nations said the strikes damaged a civilian neighborhood and a UN building with staff inside. Sudanese military sources alleged the drones came from Bahir Dar airport in Ethiopia. The UN said the attacks were reportedly carried out by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary force that has been fighting Sudan’s army since April 2023. Neither attribution has been independently verified.

At least four people, including a 10-year-old child, were reported killed across the capital. The strikes marked the first reported attack on a UN compound in Khartoum since the army retook the city in May 2025. Sudan has pursued its allegations through the UN Security Council, while the UN has urged an end to weapons flows, particularly drones, and a humanitarian truce.

title: Architecture as Evidence: Reading the Built Environment Through Forensic Investigation
description: Architecture is commonly examined through its visible form, materials and spatial organisation. The physical fabric of a building can also retain evidence of events and alterations that are not apparent from its present appearance. Cracks, repairs and structural changes may indicate when and how a building was modified, while photographs and material fragments can provide further evidence about the circumstances surrounding those changes. Forensic investigation examines these traces, using the built environment and its surrounding records to establish how particular events, alterations or failures occurred.

title: Swedish farm profits improve, but investment plans remain cautious
description:
Swedish farmers report improved profitability and stronger confidence than in the spring, citing lower interest rates as a factor, but investment plans remain restrained. Reports describe optimism as well as uncertainty and pessimism about 2026.

Profitability has improved in dairy and pig production, while crop farming remains under pressure. Reports on beef production cover different years: one describes gains in 2025, while another describes continued difficulty in 2024. A harvest that fell short of expectations also led crop farmers to delay investments, while livestock producers planned to spend.

title: AI sell-off exposes risks in data-center financing
description:
The AI-stock sell-off has intensified scrutiny of the debt and corporate guarantees financing data-center expansion. Nvidia’s guarantees totaled $118 billion as of Oct. 25, while its commitments to smaller cloud providers were estimated at $32 billion over the next several years. On a Nov. 17 earnings call, interim chief executive Colette Kress said Nvidia would scrutinize AI cloud companies’ financial strength and prioritize sites with visible, durable demand.

Those commitments have helped reassure lenders financing data centers and computing clusters. But analysts warn that banks may now be less willing to extend bridge loans to smaller providers whose debt they expect to resell. Nvidia’s tighter scrutiny could affect companies that lack established revenue or strong backers.

Jon von Tetzchner, CEO and co-founder of San Francisco-based Vivaldi, questioned whether many AI applications are useful. An unnamed worker at a major San Francisco AI company told the BBC he expected a downturn and feared it would affect him.

title: E-commerce processor Cleverbridge confirms theft of customers’ payment card data
description:
Cleverbridge, an e-commerce payment processor for software and subscription businesses, said attackers copied customers’ payment card data, including card numbers, expiration dates and CVV/CVC security codes. The company detected unauthorized activity on Nov. 4, 2026, took systems offline temporarily and restored them that day; its investigation later found the data had been copied.

Cleverbridge said attackers did not copy names, contact details or billing information, and the incident did not involve ransomware. It has not disclosed how attackers entered its systems, how long they had access or how many customers were affected. The company began notifying affected customers on Nov. 20 and is offering credit monitoring and fraud assistance through TransUnion’s Cyberscout.

title: UK regulators open mental health AI sandbox to test safety standards
description:
British regulators launched a regulatory sandbox for artificial-intelligence mental-health tools on Nov. 23. Studies have reported screening accuracy and patient use without establishing clinical benefit. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) will work with developers, clinicians and people with lived experience to examine evidence and safety challenges; up to five organizations will take part.

Hospitals in Kettering and Northampton have used AI software to flag possible abnormalities on chest X-rays since November 2024, while Poland says its public hospital platform now offers five certified imaging models, with clinicians making the final decisions. OpenAI has also made computer-use agents available for health-care administrative workflows, including referrals and prior authorizations.

A University of Bath survey found that students are already using generative AI for mental-health support, while a study of 140 pancreatic-cancer patients linked use of a psychological-support feature to lower anxiety and quality-of-life scores; neither establishes that the tools cause better outcomes. The UK sandbox aims to develop practical approaches to evaluating and regulating these technologies.

title: Russian strikes kill 15 near Kyiv; NATO to discuss missiles in Poland
description:
Russian attacks killed at least 15 people in the Kyiv region on Sunday, while Polish prosecutors identified three missiles that fell in southeastern Poland on Friday as Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. NATO allies were due to discuss the Polish incident in Brussels on Monday.

Eleven people died when a drone hit a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv. A strike on a supermarket in Vyshneve killed three people and wounded 15, including three children; another person died in Bila Tserkva. A Russian strike also hit a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

More than 130 rescuers worked at the Dymer building, where air-raid alerts repeatedly interrupted the search. A seven-year-old boy was rescued after nearly 14 hours under the rubble. Odesa schools were scheduled to switch to remote learning from Nov. 23 to 27 because of interruptions to heating, electricity and water.

title: Auto-detect the failed layer with the nozzle force sensor and resume (A1 / A1M)
description:
Problem
When filament stops feeding mid-print (clog, tangle, grinding), the printer keeps “printing” in the air. By the time you notice, the nozzle is several mm above the part and hours of printing are wasted. Resuming is possible in principle, but the hardest part is finding the exact layer where it failed. Measuring the part with calipers is slow and error-prone.

Proposal

  1. Add a “Resume from failure” function. With the failed part still on the bed, the printer probes several points on top of it with a cold nozzle, using the force sensor that the A1 series already uses for bed leveling. The slicer knows the model geometry, so it picks the probe points.
  2. From the measured heights the printer determines the last successfully printed layer.
  3. The printer offers: “Print stopped at layer N (Z = X mm). Resume from here?” and continues on the same part.

Optional: detect extrusion loss during printing (force sensor + filament motion data), pause automatically, and offer the same resume, so the part is still in good shape.

Why
It saves long prints and material, and it uses hardware the A1 / A1 mini already have.

Demand

  • The general request “Resume from Layer”: Feature Request: Resume from Layer
  • A community tool that already does manual resume, Layer Rescue: Layer Rescue: resume failed prints from any layer, even after a power loss

People clearly want this. Automatic layer detection would make it safe and easy for everyone.

title: UN climate summit ends without pact as fossil fuel dispute stalls talks
description:
The COP31 United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after nearly 200 countries failed to resolve disputes over fossil fuels and climate finance. The talks ran about two days past their scheduled close, making COP31 the longest COP conference on record. The final draft omitted an explicit reference to fossil fuels, prompting the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and vulnerable island states to reject it.

The draft referred indirectly to the 2023 COP28 commitment to transition away from fossil fuels but did not spell out a pathway or reaffirm the wording. Oil-producing countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, resisted explicit references to fossil fuels, while poorer countries objected that the proposal did not set concrete funding levels for adaptation. COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen said fossil fuels and finance were the main obstacles; summit president Murat Kurum said he would not put forward a replacement draft.

Countries agreed on separate measures, including a program to support workers and communities through the energy transition and a plan to assess adaptation progress. More than 80 countries backed Türkiye’s proposed goal of raising electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, but the goal was not part of an adopted overarching pact. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on possible reforms to the consensus-based negotiating process. The next summit is scheduled for Addis Ababa.

title: Canadian study finds daily cannabis use exceeds daily drinking among adults under 50
description:
Daily cannabis use is more common than daily alcohol consumption among Canadian adults under 50, according to a study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. Researchers analyzed responses from 99,920 adults in Statistics Canada’s 2023-24 Canadian Community Health Survey: 5.7% reported daily cannabis use, compared with 5.2% for alcohol and 8.5% for cigarettes.

The researchers say daily cannabis use is associated with cannabis use disorder, while smoking cannabis poses risks to lung health. About 68% of daily cannabis users reported smoking cannabis, and 41% said they began daily use after legalization. The study relied on self-reported responses and did not distinguish medical from non-medical use.

title: Deep-sea robot finds deepest volcanic deposits near Challenger Deep
description:
The remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea has found what researchers describe as the deepest documented underwater pyroclastic deposits, on the Mariana Trench wall about 6,000 meters below sea level. The rocks provide evidence of volcanic flows in the trench’s western forearc, where geologists expected little volcanic activity because the mantle is generally not hot enough to melt. The findings were published Nov. 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

The team’s observations support the idea that the Pacific Plate bends steeply as it sinks beneath the Mariana plate. That could help explain Challenger Deep’s depth and bring magma-generating processes closer to the trench. But researchers have not identified the eruption sites or established how eruptions could produce these deposits under immense water pressure. They say further sampling and radiometric dating are needed. Jason/Medea cannot reach the seafloor below 6,500 meters, while Challenger Deep extends to about 11,000 meters.

title: Study finds coding-agent instruction files grow 226% over time
description:
A new study of AI coding-agent instructions found that files such as CLAUDE.md grew by 226% over their lifetimes as additions outpaced deletions across 1,867 repositories. Researcher Kushal Chakrabarti analyzed 247,694 instruction lifetimes and attributed the pattern to agents’ imperfect recall of why older instructions were added.

The paper, revised Nov. 20, reports that comments recording the reasoning behind instructions cut excess prompt size by 99.3% in constructed tests. In small-scale tests in real repositories, the approach also improved instruction-following by 17.7%. The coding agent Claude Code is also being used for projects beyond conventional software development, including hobbyist-built apps and hardware prototypes. A separate review of the free coding agent Freebuff warns that it logs mouse and keyboard input and may use submitted information for advertising and AI training.

title: Cybersecurity firms move to secure AI agents before deployment
description:
Cybersecurity companies are moving to protect artificial intelligence systems during design and development, not just after deployment, as AI agents gain access to corporate systems and carry out tasks. Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy AI platform company Applied Compute for $4.5 billion, while CrowdStrike is pursuing AI-security acquisitions and has introduced a feature to stop unauthorized agent activity.

Microsoft President Brad Smith said AI is speeding up the discovery of software vulnerabilities, prompting a race to patch flaws before attackers exploit them. He warned that rushed updates, especially on older systems, could cause further disruptions in the coming months. Smith said Microsoft’s recent outage was caused by the interaction of software updates and network-traffic changes, not AI or a cyberattack; the company completed nine corrective measures and identified 13 more. Former OpenAI board member Helen Toner said a single emergency shutdown mechanism cannot address all AI risks.

title: Feature Request: Resume from Layer
description:
+1 for this. Here is an idea that would make resuming much easier and safer, especially on the A1 / A1 mini:

Auto-detect the failed layer with the nozzle force sensor

Problem
When filament stops feeding mid-print (clog, tangle, grinding), the printer keeps “printing” in the air. By the time you notice, the nozzle is several mm above the part and hours of printing are wasted. The hardest part of resuming is finding the exact layer where it failed. Measuring the part with calipers is slow and error-prone.

Proposal

  1. Add a “Resume from failure” function. With the failed part still on the bed, the printer probes several points on top of it with a cold nozzle, using the force sensor that the A1 series already uses for bed leveling. The slicer knows the model geometry, so it picks the probe points.
  2. From the measured heights the printer determines the last successfully printed layer.
  3. The printer offers: “Print stopped at layer N (Z = X mm). Resume from here?” and continues on the same part.

Optional: detect extrusion loss during printing (force sensor + filament motion data), pause automatically, and offer the same resume, so the part is still in good shape.

Why
It saves long prints and material, and it uses hardware the A1 / A1 mini already have.

There is clearly demand: the community even built a tool for manual resume (see the “Layer Rescue: resume failed prints from any layer” topic in Bambu Lab Software). Automatic layer detection would make it easy for everyone. Would love to see this officially, Bambu team!

title: AI safety researcher Mike Winer develops math to flag rare model failures
description:
Mike Winer, a researcher affiliated with Berkeley’s Alignment Research Center (ARC), is developing mathematical methods to estimate neural network behavior and identify rare dangerous outputs. ARC aims to explain model behavior by analyzing internal parameters rather than relying only on tests.

Winer estimates a 50% chance that people will lose control of powerful AI within five years, a 22% chance that this would eventually kill most people, and a 1% chance that ARC could help prevent catastrophe. These are his estimates, not a consensus forecast. The methods described so far focus on simplified networks and multilayer perceptrons at initialization, not the large trained models used in industry. Winer says substantial work remains.

title: Indonesia confirms 24 deaths in candy factory fire, investigates safety
description:
Indonesia confirmed 24 deaths on Monday as crews continued searching for about 30 missing people after a fire tore through the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Banten province. The company makes Milkita sweets. Search crews still faced hot spots and unstable sections of the building.

Presidential labor adviser Said Iqbal said authorities were reviewing whether safety protocols were followed and that he would summon the factory’s chief executive. Iqbal cited preliminary indications of a possible air-conditioner short circuit, but investigators have not determined the cause. Factory chief executive Steven Erwin Wijaya said the site conducted evacuation drills and had functioning fire-protection systems, including hydrants and water reserves.

Police said the fire’s intensity prevented visual identification of recovered remains. Authorities were collecting DNA samples from relatives and personal belongings to help identify the remains, a process officials said could take two to three weeks. Banten search-and-rescue chief Al Amrad said 29 people were confirmed safe, including five who were hospitalized.

title: U.S. cattle placements hit October record low as supplies tighten
description:
U.S. feedlots placed 1.891 million cattle in October, down 7% from a year earlier and the lowest October total in records dating to 1996, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported Nov. 20. The decline exceeded analysts’ expectations: placements were 92.7% of last year’s level, compared with an average forecast of 96.5%.

Feedlots with capacity for at least 1,000 head held 11.59 million cattle on Nov. 1, down 1% year over year. October marketings fell 5% to 1.62 million head, the lowest October figure since records began. Hales Cattle Letter warned that continued heifer retention could further reduce marketings and slaughter, while packers face margin pressure in 2027.

title: Trump considers NATO-style Ukraine guarantees tied to wider European security deal
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump is prepared to consider security guarantees for Ukraine modeled on NATO’s collective-defense clause, special envoy Jared Kushner said, but any commitment would require Trump’s approval and congressional and constitutional review. Kushner said Washington wants to negotiate the guarantees as part of a wider postwar European security framework, not as a standalone pledge.

A Washington Post columnist, citing a source close to the negotiations, reported that Russian President Vladimir Putin privately accepted the idea on condition that no U.S. or European troops be stationed in Ukraine. Sanctions relief was among the possible terms. The Kremlin has not publicly confirmed the account; Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has called NATO-like arrangements unacceptable and said Kyiv must agree to stay outside the alliance.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says NATO membership remains the clearest guarantee and wants any alternative to be written, specific and durable beyond Trump’s presidency. Kushner said the United States would continue discussions with Kyiv, European partners and Moscow in the coming weeks. The territorial dispute, including Russia’s demand for all of Donbas, remains unresolved.

title: Stainless vs hardened nozzle
description:
Just wanted to jump in here real quick. I have been printing with a hardened nozzle for the last 2 years. I installed it to print some CF a few weeks after I first got my A1 and never switched back to the stainless one. I didn’t think there was any difference in the print quality.

My hardened nozzle was damaged recently and I switched back to my stainless. OMG! The top layer is so smooth, much more than it ever was with the hardened nozzle. I don’t know if the hardened one was old and just wearing out over time, but the prints I’m doing now with the original stainless are MUCH smoother. I almost can’t believe how much better the print quality is.

I’m purchasing another hardened nozzle for when I need to print some CF filament, but I think I’m going to keep the stainless one in for now. It’s that much better.

Large prints tend to warp, like furniture parts. When we make 3D-printed tools and add more wall layers to make them stronger, they sometimes warp. You can see how warping looks and where it occurs in the image below. [image] In our first Bambu Lab flagstore, you can see and experience the massive CyberBr…

Personally, if a brim or mouse ears aren’t enough to reliably hold the print down, it’s usually back to the design for me. Even with glue as adhesive (eg. on Engineering plate), a bad warp may lift the plate instead (which can be hard to notice). And I don’t like glue anyway.

Cheers,

title: Farmers test soil and heat-tolerant crops as drought strains fields
description:
Farmers and researchers are adapting to drought and extreme heat with soil checks, crop trials and changes to farm work. In Poland, soil scientist Bartłomiej Glina says growers should assess soil structure, compaction and water storage before relying on irrigation. Researchers in India screened linseed varieties for late-season heat tolerance, while Romanian teams tested sweet potatoes, peanuts and cowpea as alternative crops.

A global study projects that saline soils will expand by 8% across drylands by 2100 under a high-emissions scenario. Research on heat waves found that feedback between temperature, soil moisture and atmospheric pressure can increase the intensity of the most extreme events by 10%. In Senegal, workers report shorter hours in the fields as heat intensifies. In India’s Jarandi area, drought is threatening guava and sweet-lime orchards as wells and other water sources decline.

title: Why Material Lifespan Matters More Than Ever
description: A material's environmental footprint cannot be fully understood without considering its lifespan. A product with relatively low embodied carbon may require frequent replacement, additional installation resources, and repeated disposal over the life of a building. Conversely, a material with a higher initial impact may offer greater long-term value through its durability, reducing the need for future interventions. From this perspective, longevity goes beyond being a technical characteristic; it becomes an essential component of responsible architectural design.

title: AI-related hiring shifts boost data-center trades but squeeze entry-level jobs
description:
Data-center construction is increasing demand for skilled trades, while employers in some AI-exposed fields are reducing or delaying entry-level hiring rather than making widespread cuts to existing staff. Builders in western Pennsylvania say data-center and natural-gas projects need electricians, plumbers, carpenters and other tradespeople. Research cited by Index.hr found weaker hiring among young workers in exposed occupations, with U.S. employment among 22- to 25-year-olds 19% below the comparison trend.

Gartner forecasts that AI could eliminate 8.9 million jobs and create 10.6 million worldwide by 2030, a net increase of 1.7 million; it also estimates 435 million workers could see major changes to their jobs. OECD and Eurofound analyses cited by Index.hr caution that youth employment had weakened before AI's widespread adoption and found no distinct AI-related decline among young workers across the EU.

A 2026 study found junior software vacancies fell almost 15% relative to senior vacancies after generative AI became publicly available, but did not establish that AI caused the change. Data-center projects are also generating construction work in Nevada, where union members are divided over the trade-off between construction jobs and potential service-sector job losses.

title: Oil prices hover near $92 as surplus outlook clashes with Hormuz risks
description:
Oil prices hovered around $92 a barrel for Brent and $83 for U.S. West Texas Intermediate on Monday, as steady crude exports from the Persian Gulf offset tanker attacks and fears of a wider U.S.-Iran conflict. Brent has fallen about 20% this month after President Donald Trump held off on renewed strikes following the U.S. midterm elections, though he said he could resume attacks after the New Year if negotiations fail.

The International Energy Agency expects a fourth-quarter global oil surplus of roughly 1.7 million to 2 million barrels a day. Tanker shortages and shipping disruptions could constrain exports, though crude continues to leave the Gulf. Traders are also watching the Nov. 29 OPEC+ ministers’ meeting, where producers are due to discuss their 2027 output strategy.

title: Microsoft warns AI-driven patching could fuel months of further outages
description:
Microsoft President Brad Smith warned Sunday that technology outages could continue for months as companies and governments race to patch vulnerabilities and upgrade aging systems. His warning follows separate failures affecting U.S. aviation, Microsoft services, banks, Apple and the National Security Agency; intelligence officials say they have found no evidence the incidents were coordinated cyberattacks.

Smith said artificial intelligence is making it easier for defenders to find software flaws, but those discoveries can also help attackers, while rushed fixes leave less time for testing. Older infrastructure adds to the risk: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said some critical systems, including internet-connected firmware and industrial equipment, cannot readily be patched.

Smith said Microsoft’s own outage was not caused by AI or a cyberattack, but by an interaction between an earlier software update and a newer one that changed network traffic. The company has published two incident reports, completed nine corrective measures and identified 13 more, he said.

title: Missouri judge approves Bayer’s $7.25 billion Roundup cancer settlement
description:
A Missouri judge has given final approval to Bayer’s settlement of up to $7.25 billion for U.S. claims that its Roundup weedkiller caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The deal covers people already diagnosed and those who develop the cancer later. Payments will range from $10,000 to $165,000, with Bayer funding the settlement over as long as 21 years.

The settlement is intended to resolve nearly all current and future U.S. claims, though about 200 cases remain outside it and will continue in federal courts. Bayer denies that glyphosate, Roundup’s active ingredient, causes cancer and says the agreement admits no liability. The judge rejected objections that payments were too low, saying further litigation could delay compensation for years, including for terminally ill claimants.

title: Gurman: Siri Layoffs Spared Newer AI Systems, But Problems Persist
description:
Apple's recent Siri layoffs affected employees working on the assistant's older infrastructure rather than its newer AI systems, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In his latest "Power On" newsletter, Gurman said employees have yet to notice a major difference in how Apple operates despite efforts to accelerate development and spread significant releases throughout the year. He added that the company faces growing competition from AI developers that update their models and services far more frequently than Apple's annual operating system cycle.

Within software engineering chief Craig Federighi's organization, Apple apparently follows an internal release calendar labeled A through G, with engineering work tied to specific software versions and launch windows. Depending on the release, the roadmap and features for a major operating system update are largely determined by late summer or early fall of the preceding year.

Gurman argued that this structure leaves Apple with limited flexibility to respond to competitors' breakthroughs during the subsequent development cycle. Gurman also criticized ‌Siri‌'s slow responses, limited third-party integration, and seemingly worsening dictation.

Apple is reportedly developing a more advanced AI agent, but Gurman does not expect it to arrive before late 2027. He warned that rival agents could become difficult to abandon as they accumulate users' preferences and connected accounts, although Apple's reputation for privacy and deeper platform access could help it compete. ‌Siri‌'s multistep control of Apple apps is expected to launch in December, with third-party app support following in 2027.
Tags: Bloomberg, Mark Gurman, Siri, Siri AI

title: Rise in Australian unemployment nears recession-warning threshold but has not crossed it
description:
Australia’s unemployment rate is approaching the recession-warning threshold under an Australian adaptation of the Sahm rule. The measure stood at 0.6 percentage points against a 0.75-point trigger after unemployment reached 4.9% in October. Independent economist Saul Eslake said it could cross the threshold in December if the recent pace of increase continued, with confirmation coming in data due January 21.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers told Parliament in Canberra that the government expects unemployment to exceed 5% and growth to slow below 2%, while neither Treasury nor the Reserve Bank of Australia forecasts an economic contraction. The rule tracks how quickly unemployment rises, which former U.S. Federal Reserve economist Claudia Sahm said can signal mounting strain for workers before standard recession measures confirm a downturn.

title: Anthropic mathematician says Claude outpaced him near proof's finish
description:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says the company’s Claude AI took a larger role as they worked on a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a famous problem about prime numbers. Alpöge said he guided the effort by combining two mathematical ideas, but Claude moved faster than he did near the end. Separate Lean and Mathlib groups have since verified the formalized proof.

The collaboration lasted about six weeks, from early October to Nov. 16, according to Alpöge’s account. He has not yet published a readable mathematical explanation, leaving researchers to work out the argument behind the computer-checked result.

The announcement came a day after Anthropic’s stock-market debut, prompting questions about its timing. Alpöge called the timing “horrible” and said he would have finished earlier if he could. He denied that the release was coordinated with the listing.

excerpt: AI companies are exploring alternatives to Nvidia following the Nov. 12 departure of its co-founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang. AI company Anthropic is spreading its infrastructure across suppliers, while rivals AMD and Google are building competing systems. Nvidia’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, said demand remained strong on the company’s latest earnings call (yahoo.com, forbes.com). Nvidia’s CUDA software ecosystem remains a switching hurdle for customers whose applications and teams rely on it. Anthropic uses accelerators from Nvidia, AMD and Google, though its sourcing strategy alone does not establish their relative performance or costs (forbes.com, seekingalpha.com). Switching costs: Nvidia’s CUDA libraries, developer tools and enterprise workflows can make migration costly. Customers may need to replace optimized kernels, retest model accuracy and rebuild deployment pipelines (forbes.com). Competing systems: AMD’s Helios combines 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs with 18 EPYC Venice CPUs, networking and ROCm software. AMD claims up to 30% more inference tokens per dollar than a competing system under its benchmark assumptions (forbes.com). title: Libya seeks UN probe after suspected drone strikes hit Benghazi ships
description:
The United Nations Support Mission in Libya called Monday for an immediate, independent investigation after two ships were attacked near Benghazi, urging restraint and respect for Libyan sovereignty. Satellite imagery identified the Russian Navy corvette Merkury as the ship hit inside the port on Sunday. It capsized and sank, and 10 people, including Russians and Libyans, suffered minor injuries. A Malta-flagged commercial vessel was struck offshore later, and its crew was rescued. Libyan forces intercepted more than 20 drone boats, Libyan military sources told Reuters.

The eastern Libyan administration said preliminary findings pointed to a drone attack on the Russian ship, which had stopped to refuel and take on supplies while returning to Russia under maritime cooperation agreements. It ordered a joint investigation with Moscow, requested an international inquiry through the United Nations and sought formal explanations from Ukraine about its military activity in Libya.

Libya’s rival, internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli warned that using ports and civilian facilities for conflicts abroad threatens Libyan security and state assets. The U.N. mission urged parties not to circulate unverified claims or politicize the investigation and said it was ready to assist Libyan authorities.

title: Google finds hackers using AI to run autonomous cyberattacks
description:
Google’s threat researchers say they found a cyberattack system that used artificial intelligence to identify software flaws, create exploits and carry out intrusions with little or no human direction. The system, called exploit_agent, ran on an exposed server and linked several language models. Scripts also mapped networks, guessed passwords and installed webshells. Google said the activity marks a shift from AI-assisted hacking to automated attacks.

Attackers are using open-source AI penetration-testing frameworks against real targets. Google reported that attackers exploited two PaperCut print-server flaws in August, with one campaign reaching hundreds of organizations four days after disclosure. Amazon separately documented an AI-assisted intrusion using Cairn that targeted East Asian educational institutions in September. The U.S. Government Accountability Office said AI reduces the human effort needed for complex attacks and cited a fully autonomous ransomware operation.

Google says these systems currently sacrifice stealth for speed but expects attacks to become harder to detect. Microsoft President Brad Smith warned that faster vulnerability discovery is forcing companies to patch more quickly, while rushed updates can disrupt older systems.

title: Webb and gravitational waves reveal clues to black hole origins
description:
A James Webb Space Telescope study identified a possible black hole in the young galaxy MARTA 3887, seen as it was about 12 billion years ago. Its estimated mass is 3.3 million suns—about 2.3% of the galaxy’s stellar mass. Separately, researchers analyzing 257 black-hole mergers found a concentration near 10 solar masses and a shortage between 12 and 16, a pattern consistent with some massive stars collapsing without supernova explosions.

The Webb team says a supernova or gas outflow could mimic the black-hole signal, and its evidence comes from a single observation. The merger study does not directly confirm failed supernovae; researchers say more work is needed to test that explanation.

description:

title: Dutch court blocks BYD SUV sales in EU over Defender design
description:
The District Court of The Hague has temporarily barred Chinese automaker BYD from selling its seven-seat Ti7 SUV in the European Union, ruling that its design infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s (JLR) EU design rights for the Defender. The order also halts production of the SUV at BYD’s new plant in Hungary while the case proceeds. The injunction takes effect one week after Friday’s ruling. The court said BYD had no concrete plans to launch the Ti7 in the EU. It also said it lacked jurisdiction over BYD’s UK business, where deliveries are scheduled to begin in January 2027.

BYD says it will appeal and maintains that the Ti7 was independently designed, while JLR says it takes legal action to protect its intellectual property. A final decision on the infringement claim is expected next year. BYD had planned to bring the model to Europe as it expands overseas to offset pressure on profits in China.

title: 'COP31 Was a Colossal Failure': Longest UN Climate Summit Collapses Without Deal
description:
The longest United Nations Climate Change Conference on record ended in overtime on Sunday, with the governments gathered in Türkiye for COP31 unable to reach an agreement on tackling the fossil fuel-driven global emergency.

The Turkish and Australian governments hosted the conference in Antalya. According to The Guardian, Australia's minister for climate change and energy, Chris Bowen, told reporters outside the plenary room that he hadn't slept for three days.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision, and that's very disappointing," Bowen said, hours after the latest draft drew a fresh wave of criticism. "Ultimately, looking back, many parties who are people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues, and despite many, many attempts, on reflection those red lines were not able to be met."

The European Union, Panama, and small island nations were among those that rejected the proposal. Explaining the EU's position, the Irish climate and environment minister, Darragh O'Brien, said that "it is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels."

While Big Oil-backed US President Donald Trump has ditched the Paris Agreement and declined to send a delegation to COP31, even though his country is the largest historical climate polluter, other major petroleum producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia lobbied against mentioning fossil fuels. Panama's climate minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told Politico that "the world is hostage to petroleum producers. That is the truth... And they will not stop."

In the lead-up to the conference, scientists warned that temporarily surpassing the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C threshold for temperature rise this century, relative to preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, and the world is barreling toward "an irrecoverable overshoot" of that target absent a rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions.

Jasper Inventor, head of the Greenpeace International delegation at COP31, said that "it's bitterly disappointing to leave without a clear outcome or a credible pathway to end fossil fuels. We stopped a bad deal that favors fossil fuels, but leaving without a deal is still a failure for communities on the climate frontlines. As always, it is the world's most vulnerable communities who bear the consequences of this failure. We've run out of time to avoid overshoot, but we can still keep 1.5°C alive."

Climate campaigners from around the world joined Inventor in expressing frustration that "COP31 has failed to deliver any meaningful outcomes on climate action," as Oxfam International climate change policy lead Nafkote Dabi put it after two weeks of talks. "Shame on rich polluting countries for once again turning their backs on communities fighting for survival in a climate crisis they did little to cause. Shame on the presidencies for prioritizing profits and ego over progress."

"And shame on all the countries that stubbornly blocked and distracted from discussions meant to deliver crucial funding to people watching their homes swallowed by floods, their crops wither in droughts, and their lives upended by deadly heat," said Dabi. "Instead of implementation, COP31 has delivered yet another victory for rich polluting countries and fossil fuel interests. The co-presidencies—who both remain heavily invested in fossil fuels and are profiting from climate destruction—attempted to broker a decision without a single mention of fossil fuels in favor of false solutions."

View on X

Nikki Reisch, a director at the Center for International Environmental Law, explained that "the proposed cover decision did not advance the provision of climate finance, said nothing about the root cause of the crisis, and made no mention of states' legal obligations to prevent and repair climate harm, as clarified by the International Court of Justice. On loss and damage, it fared no better as it offered little more than expressions of deep concern about mounting impacts. And a text that welcomed a scale-up of future fantasy fixes like carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies and proven-to-fail industry favorites like carbon capture and storage (CCS), without so much as a whisper about fossil fuels, would have been a massive giveaway to polluters."

Calling out the hosts, Global Climate and Health Alliance executive director Jeni Miller stressed that "the rightly rejected 'Antalya Pact' comes as climate change compounds this year's super El Niño, causing severe droughts in Fiji and Bolivia, extreme flooding in the western US, and wildfires in Southeast Asia, and putting millions of additional people at risk of hunger or famine."

Amiera Sawas, head of research and policy at the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, highlighted that "while Global North countries rejected the outcome on the basis that there was no language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, these same countries have not themselves presented serious or credible phaseout plans, nor do they intend to support others in their transitions. Many wealthy countries continue expanding fossil fuel extraction despite their international legal obligations, while developing countries carrying unpayable debt can't plan an exit at all."

"The EU and some of its most powerful member states have blocked progress or, worse, reneged on past commitments," Sawas continued. "Demanding the words 'fossil fuels' in the cover text while blocking mandated agenda items and pointing fingers at developing countries is acting in bad faith. We need real commitments to a fair and financed phaseout of fossil fuels that delivers on the Paris Agreement, not collapses it. That means a just transition, where those most responsible pay their fair share and workers, communities, and Indigenous peoples have a meaningful say in what it looks like."

View on X

Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa, declared that "this has been the worst ever COP, and its collapse needs to be a wake-up call for the world. Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook."

Romain Ioualalen, global policy lead at Oil Change International, similarly asserted that "this will go down as one of the worst COPs in history. COP hosts Australia and Türkiye have failed to steward the negotiations. This sad stalemate only benefits fossil fuel interests while people and communities will continue paying the highest price for the crisis they didn't create."

"Don't fall for the EU's attempt to portray themselves as heroes. They are the ones who are largely to blame for this result... But let's be clear: The outcome on the table was dangerous," he continued, welcoming the proposal's defeat. "Countries failed to rise to the moment, but we refuse to lower the bar. The countries and communities fighting for climate justice are not backing down, and the road to COP32 in Ethiopia must be about action."

Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, also emphasized how bad the final deal was: "After decades of broken pledges and hollow commitments, an agreement built on yet more empty promises would have been unforgivable and no substitute for the transformative action we urgently need. So the dramatic rejection of the presidency's final text by some, though underscoring the lack of consensus that's been reached, restores some level of faith in its recognition that a deal of this caliber is no deal at all."

"What matters now is not when governments reconvene, it's how they do so," he argued. "The world doesn't need more meetings with woolly commitments. We need global governments, including the UK, to come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver. That means cutting emissions fairly at home, transitioning our economies in a way that leaves no one behind, and providing the public climate finance so desperately needed to protect people, livelihoods, and our planet from unimaginable harm."

View on X

Savio Carvalho, head of campaigns and networks at 350.org, also looked ahead: "You'd think that in the middle of the worst fossil fuel crisis in history, after a year of devastating wildfires, floods, and collapsing glaciers, world leaders would finally rise to the moment. But they didn't. We averted a truly bad outcome because many countries stood up to the fossil fuel industry and rejected dangerous distractions. But we still left COP31 without a clear plan to exit coal, oil, and gas. There's no real money on the table to help countries survive the climate breakdown that is already at our doorstep."

"The world needs governments with the courage to stand with people and the planet, even when the fossil fuel industry pushes back," Carvalho added. "This isn't the end. We'll keep pushing until governments end the age of fossil fuels. Every meeting and every decision in the year ahead counts. The time for delay is over."

title: Still Alive revived
description:
Still Alive revived

Back in 2008, I blogged about a little homebrew game for the Nintendo DS named StillAliveDS and how much I liked the puzzle platformer.

StillAliveDS is a puzzle game inspired by Portal: The Flash Version, which is a 2D remake of Portal, developed by Valve Corporation.

Portal consists primarily of a series of puzzles that must be solved by teleporting the character and other simple objects using a Portal Gun. The unusual physics allowed by the Portal Gun are the emphasis of Portal.

A few weeks ago, I used my website's random button and landed on exactly that post. I wondered whatever became of the game. To my surprise, I learned that its developer, “t4ils,” had made a web version and released it under the AGPL.

Unfortunately, the website was no longer available, but the Wayback Machine still had parts of it. There was enough to recover all the client-side code.

It still worked in modern browsers, but it used an ancient version of jQuery, and the tiny DS-resolution graphics weren't great on modern systems.

So I spent quite some time “reviving” the game with the help of Claude. I wanted to keep the gameplay, look, and feel as close to the original as possible while thoroughly modernizing the game.

To nobody's surprise, Claude was able to make the game run again in no time. Refactoring the code and graphics into a modern architecture, on the other hand, took a lot of babysitting and reviewing. The current architecture is the result of many, many iterations.

Tiles and background graphics had to be redrawn from scratch while staying close to the original. Though I made the creative decision to drop a few “jokes” from the background images that I felt were a bit out of date – I don't think anyone misses jokes about Michael Jackson's looks in 2026.

Since the licensing of the original audio was a bit unclear, I decided to replace the sound effects and also extend them to cover more actions. Finding the right effects took quite a while – Claude helped me by building a “sound lab” where I could test and compare sound effects from different free sources until I found what I needed.

Even though the game now uses a modern ES module structure and web components for the UI, I decided not to use a bundler. Instead, it relies on modern browsers' module-loading support. A custom loader loads all assets into RAM once. This way, there are no external dependencies (neither libraries nor build tools), and the game can be restored from the Wayback Machine, just like the original could.

The game can be played right in your browser: Still Alive revived.

Currently, only mouse and keyboard are supported. If I feel like it, I might add controller support someday. I don't know if or how it could ever be made to support touch controls.

title: CachyOS adds signed kernel for Easy Anti-Cheat Linux v2
description:
CachyOS, an Arch-based Linux distribution, released its November 2026 update with support for Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2 through a dedicated signed kernel and boot entry for games that require it. The anti-cheat setup requires Secure Boot, a trusted signing key, TPM 2.0, an enabled IOMMU and kernel lockdown; CachyOS says users can keep their normal boot option alongside the EAC kernel. The release prepares systems for the anti-cheat but does not guarantee that any particular game will work with it; GamingOnLinux’s editor said he knew of no supported games at the time of publication.

The update also introduces CachyOS Package Installer 2.0, with optional AUR, Flatpak and AppImage support, and cachyos-recovery, a recovery environment that can restore Btrfs snapshots without external recovery media. The installation image includes Linux kernel 7.3.5, and the project also provides a Windows Subsystem for Linux image. Existing users switching to the new graphics-driver startup system must reinstall their driver profiles after updating, using the commands CachyOS recommends.

excerpt: CachyOS, an Arch-based Linux distribution, released its November 2026 update with support for Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2 through a dedicated signed kernel and boot entry for games that require it (linuxiac.com, phoronix.com, gamingonlinux.com). The anti-cheat setup requires Secure Boot, a trusted signing key, TPM 2.0, an enabled IOMMU and kernel lockdown; CachyOS says users can keep their normal boot option alongside the EAC kernel (distrowatch.com, gamingonlinux.com). The update also introduces CachyOS Package Installer 2.0, with optional AUR, Flatpak and AppImage support, and cachyos-recovery, a recovery environment that can restore Btrfs snapshots without external recovery media (tuxmachines.org, linuxiac.com, computerbase.de). The installation image includes Linux kernel 7.3.5, and the project also provides a Windows Subsystem for Linux image (phoronix.com, linuxiac.com). Existing users switching to the new graphics-driver startup system must reinstall their driver profiles after updating, using the commands CachyOS recommends (linuxiac.com). AUR safeguards: Before building an AUR package, the new installer displays its PKGBUILD and install scripts, uses static analysis to flag lines for review, and shows changes between installed and updated versions (tuxmachines.org, distrowatch.com). Recovery options: The cachyos-recovery tool can boot Btrfs snapshots for testing and regenerates kernel, initramfs and bootloader files when restoring a snapshot (linuxiac.com, computerbase.de). Kernel module limits: DKMS modules do not work with the EAC kernel, so CachyOS supplies dedicated EAC packages for NVIDIA open and 580xx drivers, ZFS and the r8125 network driver (gamingonlinux.com).

title: CrowdStrike CEO: Companies are choosing between getting hacked and shutting down
description:
Microsoft systems down. Air traffic systems down. Problems at Chase, United, and Apple. After a week of outages across big systems, the AI conspiracy theories are in full swing. CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz describes how AI agents can turn a patch into a working exploit within an hour, and how CEOs are now taking services offline rather than risk being hacked. He also discusses CrowdStrike’s new AI Kill Switch, and why slowing down the frontier labs won’t slow down the attackers.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by former Fast Company editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

So what is going on? Over the past week, we’ve seen Microsoft systems go down. Air traffic systems go down. . . . The AI conspiracy theories are everywhere. Is all this just a coincidence?

I think a few of my friends and colleagues might have their tinfoil hats on as well. The reality is it’s the bill for the Mythos moment. Nine months ago, when Mythos came out, it really set in motion everyone looking for these vulnerabilities, right? And the whole industry has been racing to find as many vulnerabilities as it can and create as many patches as it can. But what we’ve done now is hit the sound barrier of actually being able to roll out all these patches. So when you look at what’s really taking place, and you look at all the issues that were found in Black October, you’ve got Darker November.

This is like the PHP code, and now Java, that people are scrambling to find and plug these gaps in.

Yeah, exactly. I think the Java one is actually going to be worse. There are already working exploits for all of that. But what people are doing now is rushing to roll out all of these patches, and they’re making the decision: Breach or break. That is, are we going to get breached because we can’t patch fast enough, or are we just going to break something and hopefully fix it if we roll it out? That’s kind of a new norm now because the industry can’t keep up.

Technology is messy. Things happen, and we’re going to get better and better as an industry at dealing with this sort of AI speed that we’re facing. When you think about all the legacy systems that are out there, and you think about even banking-type systems, there’s a lot of legacy-type code out there, and it’s not as easy just to create a fix while everything is in midstream. So it’s not always clear, and when things are melting down, you get on these 24-hour bridges, and people are trying to figure out what actually happened. It’s a bit of fog of war.

As you describe it and go through these examples, the air traffic one seems like a particularly fragile one. Is the system fragile?

I think technology is just fragile, whether you’re in an Apple ecosystem, Android, or you use Microsoft or Google, whatever you’re using. Every day people use this, and they sort of just expect it to work, and they should. But behind the scenes, when you actually look at how complicated these systems are, how they operate, and the interaction with hardware and software, disks get full, memory gets overloaded. You would think that all this has been worked out, but there’s a lot of just making stuff work in the background. And the technology folks, the men and women who have to keep this running, literally wake up every day and are just like, “OK, what are we going to have to deal with today?”

We’ve had other kinds of cyber troubles recently: OpenAI’s agents breaking into Hugging Face, and French supermarkets hit by hackers shutting down refrigeration systems, which seem like a different order of things. Are any of these episodes an “aha” moment for you, of us sort of crossing a threshold?

When you look at the latest Patch Tuesday from Microsoft, it was 1,000-plus vulnerabilities that were fixed. And again, this has spiked. . . . I think we’ve had 25% of all the vulnerabilities ever created found in the last year. Just to give you an idea of the order of magnitude of what we have to deal with.

So all these patches come out, and now what we’re seeing is the automation by AI agents and threat actors, where they will take a patch and compare what was patched versus what wasn’t patched, and they immediately know where the flaw was. Then they automate the vulnerability exploitation of that. Within an hour, you can have all that done, where that would take a nation-state actor maybe weeks to do.

So the fact that we’re starting to see these issues come up as quickly as we are, I’m not surprised. But when you think about the refrigeration systems, this was a big one in Europe. What does AI allow you to do? There’s probably a handful of people, relatively speaking, on planet Earth who understand how to program these refrigeration systems. But when you actually take an AI agent and go, “Hey, I don’t know much about the refrigeration system. You figure out how to program it,” it will figure that out. You don’t have to be an expert in any of these technologies now. And typically they’re underprotected because it’s a refrigerator. Nobody really thought about security when they were building it.

How much of the game is becoming like “My AI is better than their AI?” You have to stay ahead of the attacks.

It’s the old Spy vs. Spy cartoon. It’s really what it is, right? Who’s going to stay ahead?

You recently launched a product called the AI Kill Switch. Which is designed to stop rogue agents. How do you know which scenarios would prompt hitting the kill switch?

If you think about industry, if there was a manufacturing problem with a big machine, there’s always the red button. It’s like, stop that thing because it could be causing bodily harm. And it’s the same scenario. Are the agents doing something they shouldn’t be doing? Are they multiplying, attacking other systems, or bringing down systems internally? You want to be able to hit the button. The challenge with the kill switch is there’s blunt force. It’s almost like pulling the plug.

You work closely with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Dario Amodei at Anthropic has called on the industry to slow down. There’s been quite a lot of noise about it, although development keeps steaming ahead. Do you give OpenAI and Anthropic advice about speeding versus slowing?

At the end of the day, the genie is out of the bottle. You can slow whatever you want down on the frontier. The open-weight models are three months behind. Just slowing them down is not going to slow the rest of the world down. But keep in mind, and I just want to make this distinction, Bob, they are called labs. Okay, labs. What happens in a lab? You develop something, it kind of works, it does great things, but when you put it in the real world, it may not actually work as intended in the lab, which is why the security industry has now moved into the safety industry and has become a great opportunity for folks like us.

Anyone can slow down. If the model is not right, if it’s not aligned, if it’s not getting the output you want, if the quality control is not there, you know what you do? You don’t release it. You go back and do another run until you get it right.

So what should any business leader do right now to improve their cyber footing?

Well, I think maybe first is go find your security and IT people and give them a hug, because they are at 110% of capacity now. I’ve never seen this before, but it’s happening across industry. Company CEOs are making a decision: Take something offline or be hacked. They’re saying, “Hey, we would rather take a massive service offline than be hacked.” They’re willing to make that decision if it’s so bad. When PHP came out, I had plenty of companies say, “Hey, we may just take everything down because it’s so bad.”

title: Netanyahu's Likud demands rejection of Palestinian statehood in unity talks
description:
Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud says a proposed Israeli unity government should reject Palestinian statehood and retain Israeli-designated security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. The demands are part of Likud’s proposed framework as Gadi Eisenkot, the centrist Yashar party leader tasked with forming a government, invites Likud to intensive talks beginning Sunday, Nov. 22.

The October election left Eisenkot’s bloc with 48 seats, Netanyahu’s with 53 and Arab-led parties with 19 in the 120-seat Knesset; a majority requires 61. Likud also seeks an agreement with ultra-Orthodox leaders on military conscription, while members of Eisenkot’s camp disagree over whether to rely on Arab parties to form a government.

Eisenkot has said he would not serve in a government led by Netanyahu and could put a minority emergency government to a Knesset vote if broader coalition efforts fail. His mandate expires Dec. 6 and may be extended by up to 14 days.

title: The real surpasses 5.90 per dollar after Lula’s fiscal plan
description:
The Brazilian real surpassed 5.90 per dollar on Friday, November 20, while the São Paulo Stock Exchange and interest rates also reflected investors’ concerns about the fiscal adjustment by Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, recorded a stock market decline during the week, and the dollar reached its highest level in more than a year.

The Senate approved the spending-containment and revenue-increase package, which aims to give the government budgetary leeway in 2027; financial traders consider it insufficient to address the deficit and public debt. In a livestream on Saturday the 21st, Lula defended the plan and denied that he would cut funds for health, education, or the minimum wage. The Chamber of Deputies was scheduled to debate it on Monday, November 23.

title: Medical AI studies report test results and validation gaps
description:
A Mayo Clinic team’s LENS vision-language model achieved 92.8% accuracy across 10 endoscopy interpretation tasks and outperformed 22 general-purpose AI models in tests on curated still images; the team’s report cautioned that accuracy may be lower in real-world use. A separate study found that Google DeepMind’s Gemini 3.0 Pro could update cancer symptom-management algorithms, but it omitted required content when revising depression guidance.

At Mary Free Bed in Grand Rapids, Abridge Scribe AI converts doctor-patient conversations into draft clinical notes, while an LSU project uses AI to monitor infants with artificial airways. Reviews found gaps in external validation for forensic dental AI and a lack of evidence that pulmonary-embolism AI has improved patient outcomes. LSU pediatric otolaryngologist Michael Dunham said “the decisions have to be made by humans based on the output of the AI”.

Exam results: Three language models scored between 89.9% and 91.3% on 1,310 anaesthesiology exam items; reviewers found that the book’s answer key was incorrect or contested for 59 of 81 disputed questions (bioengineer.org). Publication growth: Of 590 pulmonary-embolism AI papers, 375 (63.6%) appeared in 2023–25; annual output in 2025 was about 14 times the 2017 total (bioengineer.org).

For the past several weeks, 100 Mile Ford has been taking part in the KOT Auto Group’s eighth annual Coat Drive, the third time the dealership has participated. Carole Velne, an accountant with 100 Mile Ford, said they are looking to collect as many coats, gloves, toques and other winter accessories as possible. “For those that need a little bit more extra warmth at this time of year. We collect coats, hats, toques, mitts and scarves,” Velne said. “We pile them up into our truck and at the end of November they will all be taken out to the Cariboo Christian Life Fellowship (CCLF) church in the 108 Mile Ranch area.” As of Wednesday, Nov. 18, Velne said the Ford Ranger they’ve been storing the donations in is half full. She noted that they would welcome more donations to come in for the last few days of November. To donate, Velne said community members simply need to come by 100 Mile Ford during their regular hours of operation and drop off their donations. She noted that some have left bags of clothes by the front door when they come in to work in the morning. “We know times are tough. The economy is not booming the best right now. There’s just a lot of people out there who really can’t afford the proper warm jackets for the Cariboo weather up here,” Velne said. “Whatever little bit people can throw our way is just such a big help.” Donations will be accepted until Monday, Nov. 30. Afterwards, they’ll go to the CCLF, which will be responsible for distributing them. Velne said she is looking forward to seeing just how much winter wear they can raise. “I think whatever people have that would keep people warm would be gladly accepted.” **News** **Doerkson lays out immediate priorities, explains B.C. cabinet

The tar sands my uncle gave me. Well, I can’t just throw out these perfectly good tar sands, now, can I?” I spent most of that day sitting on the basement floor surrounded by my “thing piles”: keep, store, donate, recycle. It was a thoroughly exhausting day filled with micro-decisions. Somehow, we develop a strong emotional attachment to a thing, even as the thing holds absolutely no purpose in our lives. We may remember buying it, how proud we were of it, the effort it took to acquire it, or the hopes we had for it. When we hold the thing in our hands again, all those emotions come flooding back, and we hesitate to get rid of it, even though it has spent the last decade relegated to a box, at the back of a closet, in the room no one goes into. There are health implications of having too many things. Studies have linked clutter to sleep disturbances, digestive problems, poor food choices, and even relationship issues. On the other hand, having clean, minimalist spaces can make one feel light, relaxed, organized, and more productive. title: Hormuz ship attacks threaten Omani marine life as swimmer warns of pollution
description:
Repeated attacks on oil and gas carriers in the Strait of Hormuz risk contaminating marine habitats along Oman’s Musandam coast, including coral reefs and mangroves. Lewis Pugh, a British endurance swimmer and United Nations Environment Programme Patron of the Oceans, said chemical and oil pollution from damaged vessels could persist for decades and be difficult to remove.

Pugh swam about 15 kilometres in stages from the Musandam Peninsula around the Cape of Hormuz between Nov. 15 and 18. He said a tanker was struck about four kilometres away shortly after he entered the water, and he later saw a gas carrier engulfed in flames. The National reported more than 130 attacks on commercial vessels in the region since the conflict began on Feb. 28.

Iran has said it targeted ships it believed were using unauthorized routes through the strait; before the war, about a fifth of the world’s traded oil passed through it. Pugh called for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the waterway and a pollution cleanup.

title: Baltic ports carry 61% of Russia's October wheat exports
description:
Baltic ports handled 2.05 million of the 3.37 million tonnes of wheat Russia exported in October, raising their share to 61% from 52% in September. Shipments through Baltic and Caspian ports and to Central Asian countries together accounted for 80% of exports that month.

The rerouting follows interruptions to Black Sea and Azov Sea shipments. Andrey Sizov, director of the SovEcon analytical center, said damage to the Crimean Bridge has blocked the Kerch-Yenikale Canal, the only shipping route between the Azov and Black seas, and could delay the resumption of Azov Sea navigation while debris is cleared. Russia’s November wheat shipments are forecast at 2.9 million to 3.1 million tonnes, with weather and reduced river transport cited as possible constraints.

Russia’s November wheat shipments are forecast at 2.9 million to 3.1 million tonnes, with weather and reduced river transport cited as possible constraints (agroinvestor.ru). Harvest outlook: The International Grains Council estimated Russia’s 2026 wheat crop at 88.4 million tonnes, down from 90.3 million in 2025, and forecast exports of 38.5 million tonnes versus 47.8 million last season (eldala.kz). Price rebound: Russian fourth-class wheat prices rose 14% from their September low, gaining just over 1,000 rubles per tonne; Sizov cited new export routes and the removal of the export duty as factors (eldala.kz). National harvest: Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev said the grain harvest had exceeded 141 million tonnes and the oilseed harvest had reached 37 million tonnes, with seasonal fieldwork nearly complete (agroinvestor.ru).

title: Microsoft details Outlook outage causes, consumer email losses and planned fixes
description:
Microsoft said a software defect introduced in July caused its Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 outage, disrupting Outlook, Exchange Online and other services for about 12 hours. Its final incident report says the flaw affected network gateway servers and, under heavy load, stalled the process that handles incoming connections.

Microsoft confirmed it delivered all queued enterprise email, but some delayed messages to consumer Outlook mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days expired and bounced back to senders. It did not disclose how many messages were affected. The outage also delayed Microsoft Defender for Office protections and administrator actions, as well as policy and alert processing in Microsoft Purview.

Microsoft plans to limit Teams failovers to affected regions by the end of 2026 and separate gateway capacity by workload in the first quarter of 2027. It also plans to improve testing with traffic patterns that better reflect production systems.

title: Developers publish manifesto urging human review of AI-generated work
description:
Software developers and attendees at the AIE Code Summit published a “No AI Slop” manifesto on Nov. 22, urging people to take responsibility for AI-assisted work and review outputs according to the stakes. The signatories warn that AI agents can produce more code and documentation than a person can assess, while unchecked errors can be copied into later work.

A study of local open-weight models found that agents often identified the vulnerable code and formed a correct hypothesis but failed to produce a working input that would trigger the vulnerability. Separately, Together AI said an AI coding agent committed a repository credential that enabled an unauthorized party to download stored prompt samples. The company said it was continuing to review potentially exposed customer data.
