title: Trump threatens tax on U.S. tech firms building AI data centres abroad
description:
President Donald Trump threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. technology companies that build artificial-intelligence data centres overseas, saying the facilities should remain in the United States to prevent China from gaining access to computing capacity. He gave no details on the proposed penalty and said he had not discussed it with his administration, leaving unclear how it could be imposed.

Trump urged communities to accept domestic projects and negotiate payments or other benefits from developers. About three-quarters of U.S. voters opposed building a data centre in their community, with residents citing electricity prices and water use as concerns.

The administration is tightening restrictions on remote access to advanced U.S. chips and servers to prevent Chinese firms from using computing capacity hosted in third countries. Technology companies are offering communities more transparency, environmental commitments and financial contributions to secure approval for projects.

title: Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped prove Riemann hypothesis
description:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used the company’s Claude model to develop a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The claim remains subject to scrutiny. He says the approach also proves the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Alpöge said he chose the research direction, while Claude made rapid technical advances near the end; the model worked as a collaborator rather than solving the problem on its own.

The argument is available as computer-checkable Lean code rather than a conventional paper. Independent mathematicians, including Massachusetts Institute of Technology mathematician Andrew Sutherland, have compiled and rechecked the code with Lean’s kernel. Those checks verify the formalized reasoning but do not by themselves establish whether the encoded theorem matches the intended conjecture or explain the proof’s ideas to mathematicians. Alpöge says he has not yet mastered all the mathematics involved and plans to explain the work and write it up. Mathematicians expect review and comprehension to take time.

title: Spain's regional deficit forecast at four times target in 2026
description:
Spain’s regional governments are forecast to end 2026 with a combined deficit of 0.4% of gross domestic product, four times the 0.1% target set by the government and Spain’s fiscal watchdog, the Independent Authority for Fiscal Responsibility (AIReF). The research group Fedea attributes the projected gap to rising public spending despite increased regional revenues.

Non-financial spending rose 5.7% through July, exceeding the 3.5% reference rate under the spending rule. Fedea estimates that spending will rise by a further €5.832 billion between August and December. If other parts of government meet AIReF’s projections, the regional shortfall could push Spain’s overall public deficit above 3% of GDP.

title: Incredible modular space factory gears up for making drugs in orbit
description:
Like their counterparts on Earth, factories in space need a reliable delivery system. Whatever products they make in orbit will have to survive the trip home, and the vehicle carrying them should be able to go back and forth without ending as a streak of light in the upper atmosphere. Now, Luxembourg-based Space Cargo Unlimited (SCU) wants to do exactly that with REV1, a reusable orbital factory designed to bring about 2,200 lb (1 tonne) of cargo back to Earth, then fly again.

title: B.C.'s first Conservative premier in nearly a century takes office
description:
Lorne Doerkson was sworn in Friday as British Columbia’s 38th premier, leading the province’s first Conservative government in almost a century after the party won 63 seats. His cabinet has 18 ministers and six ministers of state. He said it will focus on affordability, the economy, health care and public safety.

The new government plans to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), with a bill expected in spring 2027, and has promised to raise the personal income tax exemption from $13,216 to $32,000. Doerkson will not recall the legislature for a fall session. His cabinet is due to meet next week, when it may consider orders-in-council, including action on school resources on sexual orientation and gender identity.

title: Tennessee secures $12 million federal grant for nuclear workforce training
description:
The U.S. Department of Commerce and the Tennessee Department of Labor and Workforce Development will direct $12 million to recruit, train and retain workers for the state’s nuclear industry, officials announced Nov. 18. The grant will be available to employers across the sector and has not been assigned to a particular company.

The funding is intended to prepare workers for jobs in construction, operations, manufacturing, engineering and skilled trades. The U.S. Department of Energy projects the nuclear sector will need more than 375,000 skilled workers by 2050 to maintain existing plants and support new reactors.

The Ottawa Citizen first reported a pause for the program, citing an internal document. Some media outlets then reported suspensions or cancellations of cadet meetings. The Department of National Defence issued a statement Wednesday saying that spending was being reassessed and “adjustments” would be required for some planned activities. The department clarified the next day that the core cadet program is not changing, specifically that “adjustments are being made to specific additional activities outside of the core weekly programming.” McGuinty’s statement says the full budget for the cadets this year is $265 million, which is an increase from last year and previous years. “That investment reflects our strong commitment to the program. Mayor Rob Kerslake of the District of Barriere remarked that the infrastructure funding gap is not a new topic. “It’s been around for a while,” he said. “What we’re finding in Barriere is, as we dive deeper into our asset management, it tells a story that’s not so great. We have multi-million dollar projects that we have to fund, and you know, for a small town with 1,000 ratepayers, (it’s) near impossible.” A primary pillar of Kerslake’s concern is the precarity of relying on grants to fund such projects. In an attempt to address the issue, he brought a resolution to the Southern Interior Local Government Association (SILGA) convention this year to advocate for new revenue streams for municipalities. The resolution was endorsed by the Union of B.C. Municipalities (UBCM) and is listed in its 2026 Resolutions Book. It points to “significant infrastructure deficits” among local governments across B.C., noting that many are unable to meet needs through property taxes alone. The endorsed resolution calls on UBCM to advocate for the province of B.C. and the federal government to establish a revenue-sharing model that allocates a portion of PST and GST revenues collected within municipal boundaries and electoral areas to go directly back to local governments. The bill would coordinate and shorten federal reviews for major infrastructure, energy and resource projects. title: Judge pauses discovery in Amazon’s case against Perplexity’s AI shopping assistant
description:

title: Studies link blood and brain markers to future cognitive decline
description:
Three studies examined cognitive decline: a Mayo Clinic team combined the blood biomarker p-tau217 with age, sex and genetic risk to estimate five- and 10-year risk; an analysis based in Europe and the U.S. found that later-born generations had better memory and slower decline; and a Stanford-led team tested a brain-activity score that distinguished “superagers” from people with Alzheimer’s disease.

In one example from the Mayo study, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE ε4 risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment of 5% at a lower biomarker level and 16% at a higher level. The studies do not establish that these approaches are ready for screening: the generational analysis was observational, and the brain-pattern score was less accurate in an independent cohort. Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

excerpt: Three studies examined cognitive decline: a Mayo Clinic team combined the blood biomarker p-tau217 with age, sex and genetic risk to estimate five- and 10-year risk; an analysis based in Europe and the U.S. found that later-born generations had better memory and slower decline; and a Stanford-led team tested a brain-activity score that distinguished “superagers” from people with Alzheimer’s disease (scitechdaily.com, scienceblog.com, denkstrom.org). In one example from the Mayo study, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE ε4 risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment of 5% at a lower biomarker level and 16% at a higher level. The studies do not establish that these approaches are ready for screening: the generational analysis was observational, and the brain-pattern score was less accurate in an independent cohort. Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms (scitechdaily.com, scienceblog.com, denkstrom.org). Memory gains: For each decade of later birth, participants recalled an average of 0.54 more words on memory tests, and their annual decline was slower by 0.070 words; the researchers could not determine what caused the gains (scienceblog.com). Model validation: The Alzheimer’s Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) brain-pattern model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.85 in its discovery group and 0.72 in an independent replication group, where accuracy was 0.71 (denkstrom.org). Treatment trials: AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3 are testing whether amyloid-targeting treatments can delay decline before symptoms appear. Personalized risk estimates could help guide their use if the therapies work (scitechdaily.com).

Perspective: Dung Trinh, a physician who was not involved in the ARC study, cautioned that an Alzheimer-like pattern does not guarantee future dementia. (Denkstrom)

title: Italian rail and airport strikes extend disruption after Europe-wide protests
description:
Italy’s 24-hour strike on Friday disrupted schools, some health services and local transport, while a separate rail stoppage was due to run until 8 p.m. Saturday and airport workers planned walkouts Sunday in Milan and Venice. Travelers faced further disruption from the separate rail and airport strikes. The strike called by the CGIL trade union excluded air and rail transport, and local transit operators had to maintain minimum service.

The Italian dispute centers on a proposed €26 billion budget for 2027 that the union says fails to support incomes and public services. Italy’s annual inflation reached 5.5% in October, up from 4.2% in September. Real wages remained below early-2021 levels, and the economy stagnated in the third quarter, the Financial Times reported.

The Italian stoppage coincided with coordinated youth demonstrations in more than 25 European countries, with organizers calling for investment in education, housing and welfare rather than military spending. In Switzerland, protests in several cities ended in clashes, while police in Vienna used pepper spray and made arrests after disturbances at a youth rally. Germany’s youth movement said about 87,000 people joined demonstrations nationwide.

title: Daily targeted pill plus chemotherapy shrinks metastatic pancreatic tumors in trial
description:
A phase 1/2 trial found that tumors shrank or became undetectable in 60.7% of 61 patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer who took the targeted drug daraxonrasib with chemotherapy. Tumors stopped growing in 90.2%, and 8.2% had a complete response on scans. Researchers presented the results at the EORTC-NCI-AACR cancer research symposium in Barcelona after a median follow-up of 18.3 months.

Median progression-free survival was 12.8 months, and 76.6% of participants were alive one year after starting treatment. The trial had no group receiving chemotherapy alone, so it cannot establish that the combination improves survival over standard care. The findings are preliminary, and the global phase 3 RASolute-303 trial is comparing daraxonrasib alone and with chemotherapy against chemotherapy alone.

title: Global study finds glacial lakes speed ice loss; researcher urges safety oversight
description:
A global analysis found that glaciers ending in lakes lost ice faster from 2000 to 2020 than glaciers ending on land or at sea, while a separate paper calls for formal safety oversight of hazardous glacial lakes. Lake-terminating glaciers lost an annual average of 0.66 meters of water equivalent, compared with 0.40 meters for land-terminating and 0.36 meters for marine-terminating glaciers. Ice-contact lakes explained an estimated 11% of mass loss among lake-terminating glaciers, compared with larger contributions from glacier geometry and climate.

The study counted 3,567 more lakes in direct contact with glaciers in 2020 than in 2000, a 35% increase. University of Cambridge natural-hazards researcher Maximillian Van Wyk de Vries calls for a tiered system combining satellite screening, detailed assessments, ground monitoring and, where warranted, lake lowering. He also calls for sustained funding and local early-warning and evacuation plans.

title: UK tribunal confirms secret Apple iCloud encryption order exists
description:
Britain’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal confirmed on Nov. 19 that the government had served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice seeking access to encrypted iCloud data, rejecting the Home Office’s argument that acknowledging the notice’s existence would harm national security. The decision allows Apple and civil liberties groups to argue parts of their challenges in public but does not disclose the notice’s exact demands. Judges said some details may still need to remain secret.

The dispute began with a broad demand reported in 2025. Apple disabled its optional Advanced Data Protection feature for new UK users rather than provide the requested access; a later notice reportedly narrowed the demand to British users. Apple’s legal challenge and a separate challenge to the government’s power to issue such notices remain unresolved. The parties expect a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027.

The decision allows Apple and civil liberties groups to argue parts of their challenges in public but does not disclose the notice’s exact demands. The parties expect a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027 (theregister.com, thenextweb.com). Why judges ruled: The tribunal said press reports, statements by U.S. officials and briefings it found British officials had authorized had already put the notice’s existence in the public domain (betanews.com, thenextweb.com). Encryption coverage: Some categories of iCloud data remain end-to-end encrypted even without Advanced Data Protection, and the feature remains available in the US (theregister.com). Scope challenge: Apple’s legal claims include whether the government can use the notice to regulate the security protections a company offers and whether that power extends to interception outside the UK (thenextweb.com). Other challengers: Liberty and Privacy International, alongside two individual claimants, are separately contesting the government’s authority to issue Technical Capability Notices (betanews.com, theregister.com).

title: Canada clears Bay du Nord oil project for Equinor investment decision
description:
Canada and Newfoundland and Labrador have given final regulatory approval to Equinor’s $14-billion Bay du Nord development plan, clearing the way for the Norwegian company to decide whether to build the country’s first deepwater oil project. Equinor is expected to make that investment decision in early 2027. The project, about 500 kilometres east of St. John’s, targets first oil in 2031.

The federal government forecasts that the project will generate $20 billion in government revenue and contribute $50 billion to Canada’s gross domestic product over an estimated 20-year operating life. The province is considering buying a 10% stake, while British oil company Shell recently announced it was buying a 30% share.

title: John Deere buys Orchard AI to add plant-level crop data
description:
John Deere has acquired Orchard Robotics, which operates as Orchard AI, adding its camera-based crop monitoring and FruitScope software to the equipment maker’s precision-agriculture business. The deal, announced Nov. 19, pairs plant-level data for specialty-crop growers with Deere machinery that can act on field recommendations. Financial terms were not disclosed.

The system scans trees, vines and other crops to assess fruit size, crop health and expected yield, helping growers decide when and where to thin, spray or harvest. Orchard will remain a Deere subsidiary with its existing team and products, founder and CEO Charlie Wu said. The acquisition also expands Deere’s orchard and vineyard automation portfolio.

title: Iraqi forces enter Iran-backed militia stronghold, establish joint command
description:
Iraqi government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday in the first federal deployment there in 12 years and opened a joint security headquarters under an arrangement with Kataib Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group that has controlled the area. Baghdad says the deployment will reorganize security and protect oil infrastructure after an investigation alleged oil smuggling; Kataib Hezbollah denies the accusations.

The new command, led by Federal Police and involving army, police, Popular Mobilization Forces and Energy Police units, will coordinate security across the district. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi called on troops to show restraint and said the operation aimed to bring armed groups under state authority without fighting.

Whether Kataib Hezbollah is withdrawing remains disputed: the group denied leaving, while Iraqi security sources said three of its brigades had departed and officials described a phased transfer that could take a month. Officials also announced that the main road through the area would reopen to civilian traffic on Saturday, Nov. 21. Displaced residents’ return depends on security checks, repairs and the restoration of services.

title: Germany approves 2027 electricity-tax cut tied to high power prices
description:
Germany’s governing coalition has approved a one-year electricity-tax cut for 2027, reducing the levy for households to the European Union minimum at an estimated cost of about €5 billion. The government plans to fund the cut through lower renewable-energy subsidy costs, expecting high wholesale prices to boost wind and solar revenues.

If power prices fall, subsidy costs could rise, leaving a funding shortfall. Germany’s Economy Ministry said it still expected prices to remain elevated next year; the coalition has said it would prepare a further package if savings prove insufficient. The measure still needs to be included in the 2027 budget, which parliament is expected to vote on next week.

Time really is money to many workers.

A better salary is no longer the top reason why workers will consider leaving their job in the next year—heck, it didn’t even crack the top three. For the first time since Adecco launched an annual report on the changing world of work, global workers spanning a wide range of industries are making clear that their time is more valuable.

A better work-life balance topped the reasons why workers might quit their current job, according to a survey of more than 40,000 workers in 36 countries conducted by Adecco, a Zurich-based recruitment and consulting agency. But the second and third reasons why workers might switch jobs—seeking out more flexibility and the opportunity to work remotely—also speak to how people are reevaluating how work fits into their lives, and not just the money it provides, according to the report.

At a time when workers are increasingly being asked to operate alongside AI agents or even robots, as the report found, they seemingly want to retain some of their humanity. And organizations that don’t want to see a mass exodus of humans should take note, according to Denis Machuel, CEO of Adecco.

“We cannot simply ask people to keep pace with technology,” Machuel said in a foreword to the report. “We need to build trust and confidence, to adapt, to give people the freedom to learn and experiment, and protect the flexibility and balance they value.”

The survey also highlighted that across seven key indicators, employees generally reported being somewhat less satisfied this year than last. But the biggest decreases were related to flexibility regarding both their working schedule and working location. 

That’s why the report’s findings also speak to the ongoing tension surrounding stricter return-to-office policies, as Machuel told The Guardian.

“Every company that wants to bring people back to the office struggles with actually implementing these measures to their full extent,” he told the outlet. As for companies with a strict policy of five days per week? “It doesn’t work,” he added.

WORKERS WANT AI

As artificial intelligence continues to reshape how people work, employers play a key role in how that plays out. The survey found that when AI tools are well integrated into everyday workflows, workers save time for higher-value work—and they feel less overwhelmed by the technology as a result.

Nearly three-quarters of workers surveyed use AI agents at work, while 14% work alongside robots, the survey found. These “hybrid workers,” as Adecco dubbed them, report feeling far and away more empowered to shape their work going forward. Compared with their non-hybrid counterparts, these hybrid workers were overwhelmingly more likely to say they’re able to perform at their highest level, that their sense of autonomy over their work has increased in the past year, and that they proactively experiment with different ways of using AI at work.

Once again, employers should take note, Machuel says.

“When workers help redesign how work gets done, and receive the training and clarity to adapt, AI creates more value, and change becomes easier to navigate,” he said in a statement. “AI delivers its greatest impact when it happens with people and not to people.”

title: Astronomers track stellar merger as Andromeda giant engulfs companion
description:
Astronomers have reconstructed the first observed case of a giant star engulfing its companion, tracking the pair through their merger in the Andromeda Galaxy. The system, AT 2025abao, began brightening in 2018 as the smaller star spiraled through the giant’s shared envelope of gas; the plunge ended in a powerful eruption in late 2025. The study appeared in the journal Nature on Nov. 18.

The analysis indicates the smaller star crashed into the giant’s core rather than surviving in a close orbit, but researchers say decades of further observations are needed to rule out a remnant. The observations recorded common-envelope evolution, a process used to explain how some binary stars tighten their orbits.
summary: Astronomers have reconstructed the first observed case of a giant star engulfing its companion, tracking the pair through their merger in the Andromeda Galaxy. The system, AT 2025abao, began brightening in 2018 as the smaller star spiraled through the giant’s shared envelope of gas; the plunge
excerpt: Astronomers have reconstructed the first observed case of a giant star engulfing its companion, tracking the pair through their merger in the Andromeda Galaxy. The system, AT 2025abao, began brightening in 2018 as the smaller star spiraled through the giant’s shared envelope of gas; the plunge ended in a powerful eruption in late 2025. The study appeared in the journal Nature on Nov. 18 (livescience.com, researchmatters.in, tribune.com.pk, birgun.net). The analysis indicates the smaller star crashed into the giant’s core rather than surviving in a close orbit, but researchers say decades of further observations are needed to rule out a remnant. The observations recorded common-envelope evolution, a process used to explain how some binary stars tighten their orbits (arstechnica.com, researchmatters.in, birgun.net). Ejected material: The final plunge sent about one-tenth of the giant’s envelope into space at speeds reaching 900 kilometers per second, according to the team’s analysis (researchmatters.in, arstechnica.com). Energy accounting: Only about 1% of the energy released in the companion’s final descent emerged as light; most drove the fast-moving ejected gas (arstechnica.com). Telescope follow-up: The James Webb Space Telescope observed the eruption 47 days after its peak, while data from multiple ground and space observatories helped trace the system’s changes (universetoday.com, researchmatters.in). Gradual brightening: Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant grew two to three times brighter in visible light while its temperature stayed nearly constant, a change the team linked to frictional heating as the companion spiraled inward (arstechnica.com).

That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material." title: New York mayor proposes 2032 Rikers closure, seeks fewer detainees
description:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday proposed closing the Rikers Island jail complex by the end of 2032, five years after the current legal deadline, and replacing it with four smaller jails in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Manhattan. The plan depends on reducing the city’s jail population from about 6,600 to roughly 4,100 through diversion and supervised-release programs, easier online bail payments and faster court proceedings.

The city says the borough jails will open in stages from 2029 to 2032 and that people needing intensive psychiatric or medical care will move to hospital beds. The administration also proposes spending $146 million next fiscal year on treatment, education, job training and related support.

The city is expected to miss the August 2027 deadline set by city law. Mamdani has blamed delays under former Mayor Eric Adams and pandemic-related disruption. The City Council must approve a revised legal deadline, and the mayor’s office says it plans to introduce legislation to do so.

title: Bessent says Trump and Xi agreed humans must oversee military AI
description:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that humans must remain involved in military decisions involving artificial intelligence and that AI should not act autonomously in major military operations. His account added military detail to Trump’s earlier general remarks about cooperation on safeguards after his Nov. 19 meeting with Xi in Shenzhen.

Bessent described the human-control principle as separate from the two countries’ competition to lead AI development. Trump, speaking at a White House news conference on Nov. 20, also said the leaders had agreed on joint guardrails but did not define them. No implementation plan or timetable was reported.

Trump also threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. companies that build data centers abroad, saying he wants the facilities built domestically. He gave no tax rate or enforcement details and said he had not yet told his officials about the plan.

title: Saudi strikes on Hodeidah port threaten Yemen's key aid route
description:
The Saudi-led coalition struck Yemen’s Red Sea port of Hodeidah on Friday after warning civilians to leave, saying it targeted facilities used to smuggle weapons and ballistic missiles. Hodeidah is a main entry point for food and other supplies to Houthi-held northern Yemen. The United Nations warned that escalation could threaten aid routes relied on by millions. Yemen’s information minister said the port remained fully operational and goods would continue to flow.

The coalition also reported strikes against Houthi military capabilities in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz. In southern Saudi Arabia, it said air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles aimed at Jazan, with debris falling near the Shuqaiq area. The Houthis claimed attacks on a power station there and Jazan port.

Air India and Air India Express suspended flights to and from Jeddah until Nov. 24, while flights to Riyadh and Dammam remained suspended until Nov. 30, the Indian embassy in Riyadh said.

title: Italy provisionally approves Tesla driver-assistance system before EU-wide vote
description:
Italy has provisionally authorized Tesla Assisted Driving, becoming the first of the European Union’s four most populous countries to permit the supervised driver-assistance system. The transport ministry recognized a Dutch provisional type approval on Nov. 19, and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini announced the decision the next day. Tesla says the feature will roll out soon through a software update and cost €99 a month.

The system can steer, brake and accelerate, including on urban routes, but is classified as Level 2 assistance: drivers must stay alert and remain responsible for the vehicle. Italy is the 12th EU country to authorize it. Together, those countries represent about 29% of the bloc’s population, short of the 65% required for EU-wide approval.

The European Commission’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles is expected to vote in December. Germany has indicated it would support approval after Tesla agreed to changes, while France and Spain have not recognized the Dutch authorization. Italy’s provisional permission follows the EU’s separate approval process and is valid through April 10, 2029.

title: Ottawa threatens Stellantis with lawsuit over planned Brampton plant sale
description:
Canadian Industry Minister Mélanie Joly warned Stellantis on Friday that the federal government could sue it for hundreds of millions of dollars unless it keeps its idled Brampton, Ontario, assembly plant open instead of selling it to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel. The warning follows Ottawa’s notice that Stellantis breached a 2022 agreement tied to up to $529 million in support for retooling its Brampton and Windsor plants. Joly gave the automaker 30 days to show it will correct the cited breaches.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford described a closed-door meeting with Stellantis, Ontario officials and the Unifor union as “challenging” but “productive.” Unifor president Lana Payne said Stellantis had not changed its decision to sell, although proposals were presented and talks will resume next week. Stellantis says it plans to repay $24 million in support for Brampton, while Ottawa warns the company may owe substantially more. The sale is expected to close before the end of 2026.

title: Polish nuclear developer signs pact to expand reactor component procurement
description:
Poland’s state-owned nuclear developer, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ), has signed a letter of intent with U.S. partners Westinghouse and Bechtel to prepare to procure another batch of long-lead components for the country’s first nuclear plant, a three-reactor project planned for the Baltic coast. The main construction contract remains under negotiation, with signing expected in 2027.

The U.S. partners will also help PEJ discuss financing for component purchases with export credit agencies. The letter sets a framework for negotiating expanded procurement but does not authorize full-scale manufacturing. Polish authorities say the next step is to develop agreements covering the additional components.

title: Iran hardliners urge tanker convoy to challenge US oil blockade
description:
Iranian hardliners are urging Tehran to send an oil-tanker convoy through the U.S. naval blockade, while satellite imagery and ship-tracking data show more than 14 tankers gathered near Kharg Island, the country’s main export terminal. Iranian officials have not confirmed a decision to send a convoy. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran would pursue oil exports and negotiations, adding that “the naval blockade must be broken”.

Kharg handles about 85% to 90% of Iran’s crude exports, and alternative facilities such as Jask cannot replace its capacity. Energy-intelligence firm Kpler projects that Iran’s revenue from crude and condensate exports could fall to zero by mid-December; about 43 million barrels were reported stranded inside the blockade zone.

The United States expanded enforcement on Nov. 18 to cover ship-to-ship transfers, warning that vessels receiving Iranian cargo could be stopped, boarded or seized. A transfer of about 200,000 barrels near Kharg was observed on Nov. 17, but analysts cautioned that it does not establish that a convoy is underway.

title: Anthropic shares fall 8.5% as investors scrutinize AI economics
description:
Shares of Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot and the first major frontier-AI lab to trade publicly, fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday, its first full trading day, after briefly approaching the $83 IPO price.

Anthropic reported third-quarter sales of $17 billion, up 47% from the previous quarter, and a $23.29 billion loss. Revenue growth slowed from 144% quarter over quarter in the second quarter, and compute spending grew faster than sales, according to the company’s filing and financial analysis.

Wall Street analysts are not expected to begin coverage for several weeks, and Anthropic’s first earnings report as a public company is months away. Its amended IPO filing remains a key source of company-specific financial information in the near term. Index-tracking funds could also buy as much as 30% of the company’s shares by year-end, according to analytics firm Intropic.

title: Eurozone pay growth edges up as Brescia factories lose momentum
description:
Negotiated wages in the euro area rose 2.57% year over year in the third quarter, up from a revised 2.45% in the previous quarter, the European Central Bank said Friday. Wage growth remained well below the 5.51% peak recorded in 2024. Bloomberg said the figure reassured the bank that inflation triggered by rising energy prices was not spreading.

Separately, manufacturing growth in Italy’s Brescia province slowed to 1% year over year in July-September, while production fell 0.7% from the previous quarter, according to a survey by manufacturers’ association Confindustria Brescia. The association cited high energy costs and weak domestic and international demand as pressures on companies.

title: IEA warns Hormuz crisis will permanently reshape global energy priorities
description:
The International Energy Agency’s 2026 World Energy Outlook says the Iran war and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have caused a historic shock to energy supplies, with lasting effects on how countries secure power and fuel. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said he sees no credible route back to the pre-crisis energy system.

The agency says the shock is strengthening the case for electrification and domestic energy sources, including renewables and nuclear power, but also encouraging some countries to retain coal as backup. Under current and proposed policies, electricity is projected to supply 29% of final energy use by 2035, below the 35% goal set at the COP31 climate summit. Oil demand is expected to level off around 2030; coal demand is projected to fall 14% from 2025 to 2035, while planned liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity could exceed demand by 70 billion cubic meters in 2035.

The outlook also warns that demand growth will strain power networks: the world needs at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines over the next decade and upgrades or replacements for another 15 million kilometers. Major grid projects can take five to 15 years to plan, permit and complete. The IEA says its scenarios are possible pathways, not forecasts.

title: Solar EV maker Aptera completes first customer-bound vehicle, delivery pending
description:
Aptera Motors, a California solar-electric vehicle developer, has completed its first vehicle intended for sale to a customer, but has not delivered it. The three-wheeled car was built for Martin Hartono, chief executive of GDP Venture, and is intended for export; Aptera has not announced a delivery date or destination country.

The company says body-integrated solar panels can provide up to about 40 miles of driving per day in favorable conditions. Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash on Sept. 30 and said its cash would not cover operations for the next 12 months; it estimated that starting production requires about $25 million. In October, it said it planned to begin building its first 40 production vehicles by year-end, with customer deliveries targeted for early 2027, subject to financing.

Poland seeks stronger NATO air defences after missiles hit near drills
description:
Poland said it would ask NATO for additional support to defend the alliance’s eastern flank after Russian weapons crossed into its airspace and crashed near a European military exercise in the southeast. Warsaw confirmed that a Kh-101 cruise missile fell at one site and said a second missile and a jet-powered drone likely fell at two others; officials reported no injuries or significant damage in Poland. NATO scrambled aircraft in response, and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday, Nov. 21.

The incursion coincided with Koalicja 2026, a two-week exercise involving troops from 11 countries preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. The French- and British-led multinational force is training to deploy after a ceasefire to help stabilize Ukraine and rebuild its military. The exercise began Nov. 9 and was scheduled to end Nov. 22.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the timing suspicious but said a connection to the exercise remained a hypothesis. NATO condemned the airspace breaches as “grave violations,” while European Union and national leaders voiced support for Poland. Warsaw also said U.S. officials could examine recovered debris, as Tusk challenged President Donald Trump’s public suggestion that prior incursions had been mistakes.

Warsaw confirmed that a Kh-101 cruise missile fell at one site and said a second missile and a jet-powered drone likely fell at two others; officials reported no injuries or significant damage in Poland (rapporteur.com, bbc.co.uk, elpais.com). NATO scrambled aircraft in response, and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday, Nov. 21 (bbc.co.uk, rfi.fr). The incursion coincided with Koalicja 2026, a two-week exercise involving troops from 11 countries preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. The French- and British-led multinational force is training to deploy after a ceasefire to help stabilize Ukraine and rebuild its military. The exercise began Nov. 9 and was scheduled to end Nov. 22 (euobserver.com, pbs.org, elpais.com). Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the timing suspicious but said a connection to the exercise remained a hypothesis. NATO condemned the airspace breaches as “grave violations,” while European Union and national leaders voiced support for Poland. Warsaw also said U.S. officials could examine recovered debris, as Tusk challenged President Donald Trump’s public suggestion that prior incursions had been mistakes (politico.eu, france24.com, bbc.co.uk). title: Radiant expands California and Tennessee sites for 2028 microreactor deliveries
description:
Radiant is expanding its manufacturing operations in El Segundo, California, and developing an 81-acre production and fueling campus in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, to prepare its Kaleidos microreactor for commercial deployment. The California expansion adds about 200,000 square feet and represents an investment of more than $100 million; the planned investment in the Oak Ridge project is about $280 million.

Radiant expects to begin operating its Tennessee fueling facility in 2027 and start commercial deliveries in 2028. Its first Kaleidos unit is at Idaho National Laboratory for testing, and the U.S. Department of Energy has approved its safety analysis ahead of a full-power test campaign.

title: Poland seeks propane market investigation as shortages disrupt corn harvest
description:
Poland’s agriculture ministry has asked the competition regulator, UOKiK, to investigate propane prices and supply after shortages and high costs disrupted corn drying during the harvest. Temporary rules allowing LPG truck drivers to drive up to 11 hours a day, instead of nine, run from Nov. 6 to Dec. 6. The ministry has also pressed the energy ministry and fuel supplier ORLEN Paliwa to help secure deliveries.

The shortage has led some grain collection points to stop accepting wet corn, while others have increased deductions for moisture, according to Poland’s farmers’ chambers. The ministry has not announced drying subsidies, a price reduction or guaranteed deliveries. It says the regulator will examine possible restrictions on competition and unfair use of suppliers’ contractual advantage.

title: COP31 talks overrun as vulnerable nations seek climate finance
description:
COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued past their scheduled Friday close as representatives of climate-vulnerable countries pressed for firm funding commitments to prepare for worsening climate impacts. The summit’s nearly 200 countries remained divided over a political agreement, including whether it should call for a transition away from fossil fuels.

Ghana’s Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who leads the African negotiating group, said public adaptation funding from developed countries totaled $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024, compared with an estimated need of about $305 billion annually by 2035. The revised draft offered no detailed commitments on the issue; a report is expected before the 2027 climate conference in Ethiopia.

Pacific island representatives also pointed to a funding shortfall for climate resilience: the Pacific Resilience Facility remained about $300 million short of its $500 million goal after a summit event drew just one new offer, $5 million from Australian mining executive and philanthropist Andrew Forrest. At a late Friday plenary, delegates approved technical decisions but left the main political text unresolved. COP31 President Murat Kurum said a new draft was expected Saturday.

title: Japan clinic group SBC reports breaches exposing 1.6 million people
description:
SBC Medical Group, a Japan-focused medical clinic operator, disclosed two cyber incidents on Nov. 20 involving unauthorized access to its website databases and administrator accounts on Tribeau, a third-party booking platform. The database intrusion exposed basic information on 1,624,000 people, including names, contact details, birth dates, patient card numbers and passwords. Other affected records included reservation requests and website inquiries. The Tribeau incident exposed booking and treatment information for thousands of people.

SBC said it discovered the breaches on Nov. 16 and is still investigating. It has not confirmed whether electronic medical records were accessed in the database incident. Tribeau's operator said the platform incident did not expose medical records, passwords, email addresses or home addresses. About 20,000 employee account records were also compromised, including bank and tax-related information for 459 workers. SBC has not determined the incidents’ financial impact.

title: UK and EU seal food trade pact, but checks remain until 2028
description:
The United Kingdom and the European Union concluded a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement on Nov. 20 to remove export health certificates and routine border checks for most covered food, animal and plant products, including poultry and eggs. The arrangements are expected to take effect on March 1, 2028, after legal approval and domestic implementation. Businesses must meet current requirements until then.

The deal also requires Great Britain to align with relevant EU rules as they change, including those covering animal health and welfare, food safety, antimicrobial resistance and organic production. The National Farmers’ Union wants clarity on avian-influenza controls, veterinary medicines and organic standards. Organic poultry and egg producers will have a 12-month transition period for specified housing and production changes.

The Association of Independent Meat Suppliers welcomed the agreement but said exporters would continue to pay certification and border-delay costs until it takes effect. The British Veterinary Association called for a smooth transition and continued border biosecurity, noting that official veterinarians have issued about one million export health certificates since Brexit.

title: Cosmology researchers test rival accounts of dark energy and cosmic expansion
description:
Researchers have proposed two different explanations for dark energy, the component estimated to make up about 70% of the universe’s energy. A team from the University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield says quantum chromodynamics (QCD)—the established theory of the strong nuclear force—could account for the observed acceleration of cosmic expansion through properties of the quantum vacuum, without requiring a new particle or field. The team found that its model fit observations of supernovae and early-universe radiation about as well as standard cosmological models.

Separately, a University of Ottawa study tested a model called CCC+TL, which attributes effects usually assigned to dark matter and dark energy to changing physical constants and “tired light.” The researchers say it matched several observations, including light-element abundances and cosmic-chronometer measurements. The model also estimates the universe is 26.7 billion years old. Both proposals remain theoretical, and the QCD team plans to test its calculations against future space-telescope data.

A team from the University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield says quantum chromodynamics (QCD)—the established theory of the strong nuclear force—could account for the observed acceleration of cosmic expansion through properties of the quantum vacuum, without requiring a new particle or field. Galaxy tests: The Ottawa researchers applied CCC+TL to 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and reported that it reproduced their rotation curves without dark matter (universetoday.com). Cluster comparison: They also tested the model against the merging Bullet Cluster and found that its predicted additional gravitational effect was consistent with observations. The researchers described the result as an early proof of concept (universetoday.com). QCD calculation: The University of British Columbia researchers say their calculation yields a characteristic energy scale close to the observed dark-energy scale using known physical constants and no additional fitting parameters (phys.org).
kite_context: Quote: "The most striking result is that the observed dark-energy scale emerges naturally from known physical constants, without the need for any additional fitting parameters." (Ludovic Van Waerbeke, professor at the University of British Columbia, Phys.org)

title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

title: Researchers test lunar-soil bricks and oxygen extraction methods
description:
University of Arkansas researchers used simulated lunar soil to print small, interlocking bricks without binders, while a separate team found that plasma treatment can release oxygen and oxygen-containing gases from lunar-soil simulants. Both experiments aim to reduce the supplies future lunar missions would need to transport from Earth, but neither method is ready for practical use: the bricks need to be stronger, and oxygen yields must increase substantially.

The brick study, published in *npj Advanced Manufacturing*, used laser powder bed fusion; the oxygen-extraction research, published in *Scientific Reports*, adapted plasma processing used in semiconductor manufacturing. Researchers still need to test the brick process in lunar vacuum and low gravity and determine whether oxygen extraction can be improved and scaled up economically.

Block design: The test pieces included cross- and H-shaped forms, demonstrating different shapes for potential construction components (sciencedaily.com). Mineral reactions: The plasma altered oxygen-bearing minerals, some of which reacted more readily than others. Researchers say they need to understand these differences to improve efficiency (phys.org, newspaceeconomy.ca). Resource rationale: Oxygen is needed for astronaut life support and as a component of rocket propellant. Lunar soil also contains silicon, aluminum and iron (phys.org, newspaceeconomy.ca).

title: EU transfers record €7.9 billion to Ukraine, ties future funds to reforms
description:
The European Commission transferred €7.9 billion to Ukraine on Nov. 20, the largest single payment under the EU’s Ukraine Facility, to help meet financing needs and keep public administration running during Russia’s war. The ninth payment brings support under the Ukraine Plan to €40 billion since mid-2024; €5.1 billion of this tranche comes from a separate EU loan for 2026-27.

The payment followed Ukraine’s reported completion of 16 reform and investment steps, including measures on the judiciary, anti-corruption, energy and public-asset management. A further €15.7 billion remains available through the end of 2026 if Ukraine meets agreed conditions; more than €14 billion is available under the loan, including €10.2 billion for the defense industry and €3.9 billion for budget support. The Commission has also proposed up to €45 billion in support for 2027, when Ukraine faces a projected €70 billion funding gap.

title: GAO urges safeguards as AI accelerates cyberattacks and vulnerability discovery
description:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO), a congressional watchdog, said in a report published Nov. 20 that artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster and more precise while expanding defenders’ capabilities. Generative AI can produce convincing phishing messages and deepfakes, and emerging agentic systems can carry out multiple attack stages with limited human input. The GAO outlined 16 policy options, including stronger testing and oversight of AI security tools throughout their lifecycle. The options are a menu for policymakers, not mandatory rules.

Technology disruptions affected services including Microsoft Outlook, United Airlines and the Federal Aviation Administration over the past week. Companies and agencies said those outages were not caused by cyberattacks. Separately, cybersecurity researchers have documented attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe that altered temperature controls. AI-assisted discovery of flaws in old software is accelerating both patching and exploitation, and hurried software updates can themselves cause service problems.

Unmaintained software and exposed equipment remain entry points for attackers. VulnCheck reported that more than 100,000 vulnerabilities had been disclosed so far in 2026, more than twice the 2025 total, while known vulnerabilities were being exploited 33% faster than in the previous year, NPR reported. The GAO’s policy options leave decisions on testing, governance and workforce measures to lawmakers, agencies, standards bodies and industry.

title: Canadian military to continue howitzer avalanche control at Rogers Pass
description:
Parks Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces have put plans to end Operation Palaci on hold and say there is no set end date for the military’s howitzer-based avalanche-control program at Rogers Pass in southeastern British Columbia. The military will continue supporting the operation while the agencies develop a transition plan. The decision reverses a plan to end military involvement after the current season, when the agreement expires in August 2027.

The operation triggers controlled slides above the Trans-Canada Highway to reduce the risk of larger avalanches and also protects a railway through the pass. The Department of National Defence had previously cited changing military priorities and plans to retire older artillery systems as reasons not to renew the agreement.

title: Apple tightens Mac access for rival agents as it develops its own
description:
Apple’s macOS 27.3 beta tightens approval requirements for third-party apps seeking broad access to Macs. Separately, a job listing indicates Apple is developing its own agent to operate apps, browse the web and write code; Apple has not announced it as a product.

A now-removed Apple job listing described agents that could plan multistep tasks across apps, browsers, command lines and application programming interfaces, and coordinate specialized subagents. The project remains at an early stage; Apple has not confirmed a product, launch date or whether the agent will be part of Siri.

In the beta, users can narrow some permissions, approve access each time and see an indicator when one app controls another. Previously granted permissions remain active, however, and Apple has not explained what permission model its own agent would use.

The companies plan to combine Telekom’s infrastructure and integration expertise with Mistral’s models and software for industrial and regulated sectors, emphasizing that customers should retain control of their data.

Telekom says its Munich Industrial AI Cloud provides a foundation for sovereign AI in Germany, while Mistral has opened a Munich hub to develop physical and industrial AI. The companies have described plans for a strategic partnership, not a fully developed joint offering.

title: South Africa records 5,590 murders as violence remains widespread
description:
South Africa recorded 5,590 murders from July through September, 204 fewer than in the same period a year earlier, Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said Friday. An average of about 60 people were killed each day. Murders continued to decline, while police said violence remained concentrated in specific areas.

The murder victims included 4,819 men, 581 women and 149 children; police could not verify the age and sex of 41 victims. Police also recorded 9,908 rapes. Of the 9,705 cases in which the victim’s age and sex were verified, 4,362 involved victims under 18.

The figures followed two mass shootings that killed 17 people earlier in the week. Cachalia said such incidents were concerning and often linked to organised crime. title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow Waves Decline in the Aging Brain
description: Cerebrospinal fluid is manufactured by the choroid plexus, flows through the brain, and drains into the body via the glymphatic system. This current carries away metabolic waste from the brain, particularly during sleep. Unfortunately cerebrospinal flow and drainage declines with age, allowing the buildup of metabolic waste in the brain, such as the protein aggregates that contribute to neurodegenerative conditions. Evidence suggests this to be a meaningful contribution to degenerative aging in the brain. Most research in recent years has focused on drainage, but here researchers look at the flow of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain more generally. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates around and within brain tissue, performing multiple functions, including cushioning the brain and transporting solutes from brain tissue to brain exit routes. But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. description:
Andhra Pradesh approved exploring the use of small modular reactors (SMRs) as an alternative to thermal power on Nov. 20, under an order issued by K Vijayanand, the state’s special chief secretary for energy. The approval followed a proposal from the Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation (APGENCO). It allows the state to study the option, not build a plant.

The state may consider sites of retiring thermal power plants or other suitable locations, but will consider building plants after SMR technology stabilises. The order permits private-sector participation and directs APGENCO’s managing director to take the necessary next steps.

title: PostgreSQL 19 adds online table repacking and query-plan controls
description:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19 on Nov. 19, adding a REPACK command that can reorganize tables while reads and writes continue, alongside new controls for query execution plans. The changes address database maintenance and application workloads, including large production systems where maintenance can otherwise interrupt table access.

The release also improves autovacuum, logical replication and SQL features, including a new way to wait for replicated writes to reach a standby server before reading them. PostgreSQL 19 is available for download, with packages and installers for Linux, Windows, macOS and other supported platforms.
summary: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19 on Nov. 19, adding a REPACK command that can reorganize tables while reads and writes continue, alongside new controls for query execution plans. The changes address database maintenance and application workloads, including large
excerpt: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19 on Nov. 19, adding a REPACK command that can reorganize tables while reads and writes continue, alongside new controls for query execution plans (heise.de, linuxiac.com). The changes address database maintenance and application workloads, including large production systems where maintenance can otherwise interrupt table access (linuxiac.com, ithome.com.tw). The release also improves autovacuum, logical replication and SQL features, including a new way to wait for replicated writes to reach a standby server before reading them (linuxiac.com, heise.de). PostgreSQL 19 is available for download, with packages and installers for Linux, Windows, macOS and other supported platforms (linuxiac.com). Repacking limits: REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) still requires a brief table lock to switch files and uses extra disk space. Concurrent mode does not support partitioned tables and can present an empty table to transactions holding older snapshots (ithome.com.tw). Bulk inserts: Project testing found that faster foreign-key checks nearly halved the time required for some bulk-insert workloads (linuxiac.com, heise.de). Plan controls: The pg_plan_advice extension can specify join order and scan methods; its companion, pg_stash_advice, applies stored guidance by query ID. Fixed plans may perform worse if data distributions change (linuxiac.com, ithome.com.tw). Upgrade checks: PostgreSQL 19 rejects startup configurations containing the old io_workers setting or RADIUS authentication entries, and older pg_dump files made with standard_conforming_strings disabled may not restore correctly (heise.de).

Timeline: 15 October 2026: PostgreSQL 19 release candidate 1 was published (heise.de)
Timeline: 12 November 2026: Developers issued release candidate 2 after finding more bugs (heise.de)

Did you know: Eight to 10 substantial features were removed during the beta period, including SQL/PGQ graph queries and UPDATE/DELETE... FOR PORTION OF (heise.de).

title: U.K. government ordered to reveal secret Apple backdoor demand
description:
Macworld

The U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government must confirm that it demanded access to Apple customers’ data in 2025.

Early last year, the Washington Post was tipped off about the secret order, or “technical capability notice,” which ordered Apple to “create a back door allowing [U.K. authorities] to retrieve all the content any Apple user worldwide has uploaded to the cloud.” At the time, we warned that such an order would instantly compromise the security of more than two billion Apple users across the globe.

Apple resisted, choosing to remove the ADP feature from U.K. iPhones rather than comply with the order, and it was subsequently reported that British politicians had given up on the scheme. But while it was common knowledge that the attempt had been made, the Home Office refused to acknowledge this, arguing that revealing the existence of the order would damage national security and the public interest.

Apple itself was not permitted to disclose that it had received a technical capability notice. Until now the company has adhered to this even while commenting in carefully non-specific terms on the situation. At one point, for example, it stated that “we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products, and we never will” without actually confirming it had been ordered to do so in this case.

But now, finally, as TechCrunch reports, the national security argument has been put to rest.

Having noted that “anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges indicate that they “reject the respondent’s contention that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the fact that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice.”

It should be noted that this judgment refers to the existence of the order rather than its specific details. The judges say this is “another matter” which “is better addressed separately.” The case, in other words, is not finished yet.

title: Milky Way bar shock may explain part of disputed Norma arm
description:
A study led by Hillary Davis, a University of Sydney PhD graduate, finds that masers assigned to the Milky Way’s Norma spiral arm align instead with a shock front driven by the galaxy’s central bar. The result suggests that at least part of the supposed arm may be a star-forming region along the bar rather than a spiral arm.

The researchers compared observations of masers—microwave sources associated with regions where massive stars form—with large-scale computer simulations of galaxy evolution. Star formation is often suppressed along bar shock fronts in nearby galaxies, making the proposed activity in the Milky Way’s bar unusual. The study also constrains the bar’s dimensions and rotation speed.

title: California subpoenas Nvidia over China chip risks and investor disclosures
description:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has subpoenaed Nvidia for information on whether advanced chips or confidential data reached China and whether the company misled investors about those risks. The inquiry examines possible violations of California securities law; it does not accuse Nvidia of breaching federal export controls.

The subpoena follows the resignation of Nvidia co-founder and former chief executive Jensen Huang. Reports linked Huang to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of having ties to Chinese intelligence. The two are not related. Authorities are separately investigating whether Megaspeed diverted restricted Nvidia chips; the company says it operates lawfully.

The California inquiry adds to a reported Securities and Exchange Commission review of Nvidia’s disclosures and congressional scrutiny of chip sales to China. Huang has agreed to answer questions before House committees on Dec. 1, followed by Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. Nvidia’s board has said it will not reinstate Huang.

title: Bangladesh sets 18-month push for safe Rohingya repatriation
description:
Bangladesh will intensify talks with the United Nations and bilateral partners to secure the safe return of Rohingya refugees within 1 to 1½ years, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide during its 2017 military campaign. Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry described repatriation as the only viable solution to the crisis, while Kobir said it would not happen immediately.

Myanmar’s civil war has continued since the 2021 coup, and the Arakan Army controls nearly all of Rakhine State, where most refugees would return. Myanmar’s government rejected the ruling as unfair and said the 9-6 decision was not unanimous.

United Nations General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman urged Myanmar to bring the displaced Rohingya home during a Nov. 20 visit to camps in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar. At the United Kingdom’s request, the U.N. Security Council has scheduled consultations on the ruling for Nov. 25 and a private meeting for Dec. 7. An analyst told the Associated Press that China and Russia could block council action.

title: North Carolina regulators defer Duke solar procurement after canceling 2026 bids
description:
North Carolina regulators have confirmed that Duke Energy will not solicit solar bids in 2026, shifting some planned procurement into later years. The commission’s decision approving Duke’s carbon-reduction plan calls for 2.3 gigawatts of additional solar to come online by 2034, but leaves more than a gigawatt of planned procurement unfulfilled this year.

Clean-energy groups say skipping a year of bidding could lead to higher costs because tariffs and inflation may push solar prices up. Regulators cited federal tariffs and expiring tax credits as factors making solar more expensive, along with lower near-term demand after state lawmakers repealed a carbon-reduction requirement. Duke must tell the commission by Nov. 26 how it will meet its solar projections.

title: European Commission confirms AI-assisted attack as internal apps return
description:
The European Commission has confirmed that attackers used artificial intelligence tools in a cyber campaign that disrupted its internal services. The EU executive body first detected the incident in October. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said most temporarily disabled applications have been restored. The investigation continues, and officials have found no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, he said.

The Commission has not identified the attackers or named the AI tool used. CERT-EU, the EU institutions’ cybersecurity service, had warned about the publicly available ARTEX framework, which can use AI to find vulnerabilities, but officials have not confirmed that it was involved in this incident.

The confirmation followed questions about why the incident had not been publicly disclosed earlier. Regnier said the Commission followed its usual procedures and kept response measures out of public view so they could remain effective. He said the institution notified CERT-EU, the European Data Protection Supervisor and affected internal services.

title: Trump replaces national cyber director after outages disrupt US services
description:
President Donald Trump replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross with Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies as acting director after a week of outages disrupted aviation, banking, communications and government systems. The incidents have drawn scrutiny of the administration’s response, although officials say there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or a connection among the failures.

A source familiar with the White House’s thinking said Trump supported Cairncross’s removal because he lacked strong cybersecurity credentials. Trump said Friday, “I didn’t think that person was good enough”. Axios reported that Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pushed for the change on similar grounds. Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive, said he was proud of his work in the role. Davies has held cybersecurity and technology leadership jobs at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens.

Davies will serve temporarily. A permanent director must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, which Democrats are due to control in January. Cybersecurity experts say companies’ rapid efforts to patch software vulnerabilities may be behind some disruptions, as advanced AI tools make those flaws easier to find.

title: Data center electricity demand set to double as grid rules tighten
description:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts that global data-center electricity use will nearly double to about 1,000 terawatt-hours a year by 2030, with artificial intelligence driving roughly three-quarters of the increase; associated emissions could rise about 70%. On Thursday, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, 62-33. The bill would require data centers to pay for grid costs and shorten approval timelines for energy infrastructure. It now goes to the House after the Thanksgiving break.

The Senate measure has divided lawmakers: supporters say it could fund grid expansion and accelerate clean-energy connections, while opponents warn that faster approvals could spur gas-fired power and data-center construction. A Harvard-led study estimated that 403 U.S. hyperscale facilities used about 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually and were linked to roughly 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Oregon regulators approved rules requiring new Pacific Power data centers to cover their energy costs starting Jan. 1, 2027. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek has also called for state oversight legislation during the session beginning Jan. 11, 2027.

title: WHO warns rising drug resistance is eroding last-line antibiotic options
description:
Drug-resistant bacterial infections are increasing across regions. The World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control report that European Klebsiella pneumoniae infections rose 72% from 2019 to 2025, while resistance in monitored E. coli infections also increased. Globally, one in six laboratory-confirmed common bacterial infections was resistant to antibiotics in 2023, according to the WHO.

When standard antibiotics fail, clinicians may turn to carbapenems, but resistance to these last-line drugs is also rising. In the Americas, carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae increased from about 15% in 2015 to 26% in 2024; median resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii was 77% across the seven reporting countries. Health authorities are calling for stronger infection prevention, laboratory diagnosis and surveillance; the Pan American Health Organization’s 2027–2031 action plan was approved in September.

title: AI expansion exposes constraints in chips, power and cloud economics
description:
Anthropic’s U.S. securities filing identifies power, cooling and networking—not just graphics processors—as potential constraints on expanding artificial-intelligence services. NVIDIA operations executive Deb Shoquist described how expanding its data-center systems depends on suppliers’ technical capabilities, investment capacity and factory output, including critical chip supplies from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC).

Vertiv Chief Executive Giordano Albertazzi said modular construction can cut AI-factory build time by up to 50%, while digital-twin simulations can shorten design work from 30 days to three. Oracle argues that operators must measure the full cost of serving successful AI requests—including computing, data movement and retries—rather than focus only on model prices. New research finds that cloud-computing providers’ customer service-level penalties can exceed data-center outage compensation by more than four times.

title: Report details alleged Qubole intrusion potentially linked to cardholder data leak
description:
BleepingComputer has reported an alleged intrusion involving Qubole, identifying it as a suspected third-party provider in attacks linked to files published by ransomware group n0n. The group tied the files to JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard. Attackers allegedly used compromised Qubole credentials between Oct. 14 and 26 to access customer cloud environments, according to BleepingComputer; the three financial companies disclosed incidents involving vendors on Nov. 19. The companies have not confirmed Qubole as the affected supplier, and the group’s claims and leaked files have not been independently verified.

BleepingComputer reported that the attackers said they took 53.9 gigabytes of data across 30,743 files from Qubole and claimed to possess nearly a petabyte of data from customer networks. The reported customer records include marketing and contact information. Visa said card numbers were not affected, Mastercard described the exposed information as non-payment data, and the companies said their payment networks were not affected.

Researchers said the Visa-linked files appeared to contain customer contact details and restaurant-booking information. The companies have not identified the suppliers or disclosed the total number of affected customers; JPMorgan said it would contact affected customers where appropriate and offer credit monitoring.

title: Russian barrage kills 11 in Ukraine; three objects fall in Poland
description:
Russia launched more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, at Ukraine overnight on Nov. 20, killing at least 11 people, Ukrainian officials said. The strikes damaged three bridges in Kyiv and hit railway, energy and other infrastructure. Kyiv and other regions reported disruptions to electricity, water and heating. The attack followed Russian strikes in Kyiv the previous day that damaged foreign embassies and Ukraine’s Nov. 17 attack that damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Polish authorities said three objects from the attack entered the country and fell at separate sites: two were believed to be missiles and the third a jet-powered drone. No injuries were reported, and NATO scrambled aircraft. Poland called the incursion a provocation and said it would seek more NATO support for the alliance’s eastern flank.

France called for a U.N. Security Council meeting over the Russian strikes. Separately, Moscow invited representatives of Britain, France and Germany to talks in the Russian capital. France said any dialogue must lead to European participation in the next negotiations with Ukraine and the United States. Russia has said a visit to Moscow would not itself guarantee European participation in peace talks.

title: US Senate rejects Iran withdrawal measure as Gulf energy routes face disruption
description:
The U.S. Senate on Nov. 19 voted 51-48 against a measure that would have directed President Donald Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. The resolution, rejected as the U.S.-Israeli war continues, had passed the House in September.

A Pentagon official put U.S. war spending at $48.3 billion through Nov. 13, excluding damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East and effects on the global economy. Iran has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi forces in Yemen have targeted Saudi oil infrastructure and ships.

Trump said he would defer a decision on any major new strikes until after the start of 2027. Democrats, due to take control of Congress on Jan. 3, have said ending the war will be a priority.

title: France begins 2027 budget review as debt concerns deepen
description:
France’s Senate begins reviewing the government’s proposed 2027 budget on Nov. 20, with fiscal strains and a bond-market selloff adding pressure to a government that lacks a majority in the National Assembly. France has also faced cost-of-living protests, while the approaching presidential election narrows the government’s options for securing parliamentary approval.

France needs to reduce borrowing by about 5% of gross domestic product to stabilize its debt ratio, compared with about 2.5% for the United Kingdom. France also has less room to raise taxes because its tax take is already higher. The Senate may seek a compromise, but France’s presidential election is scheduled for April 18 and May 2, 2027, followed a few weeks later by a parliamentary election.

The Senate may seek a compromise, but France’s presidential election is scheduled for April 18 and May 2, 2027, followed a few weeks later by a parliamentary election (bloomberg.com, piie.com). Public distrust: Nearly 80% of people surveyed said the 2027 presidential election would not solve France’s problems, according to a poll cited by Le Monde (lemonde.fr). Investment debate: Nearly €200 billion in investments had been announced at Choose France events over nine years, according to Economy Minister Roland Lescure (lesechos.fr).

In other words, the grant deadline and the boiler deadline are working against each other. Wait for a midwinter breakdown and you could find yourself choosing the fastest available boiler instead, but start now, and you have time to establish whether a heat pump is suitable, compare installers and apply for the funding. title: EU-UK reset faces tuition-fee dispute over implementation
description:
European Union governments and Britain disagree over whether they must settle university tuition-fee talks before new UK-EU trade and mobility agreements can take effect. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders agreed on the package at a Brussels summit on Nov. 20. It would ease food trade, link emissions markets and create a youth mobility scheme. EU member states say adoption depends on equal tuition treatment for EU students, while Britain says the agreements will proceed separately.

The food deal is expected to remove most certificates and checks from March 2028, including for goods moving between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland’s agriculture minister, Andrew Muir, said paperwork on those routes would fall but not disappear. Britain would align with EU food and plant-safety rules, and British experts would advise on future standards without voting on them.

UK food, drink and feed exports to the EU fell 26% in value from 2019 to 2025, while certificates for shipments typically cost £150 to £250 each. The emissions-market link is scheduled for 2028, and the youth scheme is due by January 2030. The two sides have six months to continue tuition-fee talks.

title: Poland targets early 2027 signing of $50 billion deal with U.S. nuclear builders
description:
Poland expects to sign an engineering and construction contract with U.S. firms Westinghouse Electric and Bechtel in early 2027 for its first nuclear power plant, a project valued at about $50 billion. Polskie Elektrownie Jadrowe (PEJ) said the main commercial terms had been agreed and detailed provisions were still being finalized. PEJ head Marek Woszczyk said the contract would most likely be signed by the end of March.

The planned plant on the Baltic coast will have three Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. Poland aims to begin construction of the first unit in 2028, with the reactor scheduled to enter service in 2036. The project is part of Warsaw’s effort to reduce coal use and strengthen energy security. Woszczyk said the later contract signing would not alter the project schedule.
